speechtext: That in accordance with the recommendation contained in the 28th report of the Select Standing Committee on Standing Orders, that portion of the 49th rule of this House which limits the time for receiving petitions for private Bills, be suspended in reference to the petition of John Henry and others praying for ait Act of incorporation under the name of the Westminster Bridge Company, presented this day, and that it be read and received forthwith.

Before that is adopted, I want again to draw attention to the great abuse that has been perpetrated on this House during the present session by presenting petitions and introducing Bills quite regardless of the rule which should govern the House. There is no doubt whatever that we have paid no attention to it for some months past. If the rules are of any value, they should be observed as -closely as possible. There is no doubt that exigencies may arise which would justify a departure from the rule, but we have departed from it so frequently this session, without any apparent effort on the part of the government to keep the House to an observance of the rule, that it seems to me some one ought to draw attention to it, and that either we should regard the rule or abolish it entirely.

I do not at all agree with my hon. friend. I think the rule this session has been violated much less frequently than in former sessions, and I think I can appeal to the sense of the House that of late years the practice of introducing private legislation after the time fixed for it has passed, has been seriously checked. But, of course, circumstances have to be considered, and sometimes it is well to suspend the rule.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before the Orders of tbe Day are called, I wish to rise to a question of privilege. In his utterances on the 31st of last month in the House of Commons, the member for West Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) made a most cowardly attack
Order.
Order.

I take back the word ' cowardly.' He made a very unfair attack on me, and if it had only been stated in this House and had gone no further than this House, knowing Mr. Scott, I would not have deemed it worth my while to reply to it. However, it has been made the occasion of very heavy headlines in the government organs in Toronto, the ' Star ' and the ' Globe,' accusing me of being one of a body of grafters who cleared $15,000,000, in connection with the late government, out of some western railways. I want to say that the member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) some years ago made practically the same charge. I answered him then in this House very fully, and my answer has never been contradicted. I want to say that there is absolutely not a shadow of foundation on which to build that statement made and repeated in this House by the member for West Assiniboia, after I had contradicted the same statement made some years ago. when it was made by the other member (Mr. Davis). M.v connection with these two roads was purely a business one, and it was long before I was a member of parliament, and before I practically took any interest in politics. The Qu'Appelle, Long Lake and Saskatchewan Railway had been under charter for many years with a subsidy, and no one could be found to build it. After the North-west rebellion, the late Sir John A. Macdonald was very anxious to have that road built for political purposes, as I think we all know. The then government tried to get Mr. Onderdonk and Mr. Ross to build that road and had failed, as these gentlemen would not take it up for the subsidy and the land grant. Sir John Macdonald then asked me if I could by any chance interest people in England to raise the money to carry out that work. The charter I had nothing to do with. I had no interest directly or indirectly in the charter which belonged to some gentlemen in New Brunswick, and the late Hon. Mr. Mclnnes and some of his friends. After negotiations in England, I succeeded in raising the money by the sale of the land grant and the sale of the bonds. In that agreement it was quite understood that for five or six years that road would not be able to earn enough money to pay its interest. The bankers lending the money required an undertaking from the Canadian Pacific Railway that they would operate flint road for six years 329	.
free of charge, and a deposit was rnade with the bankers in London for the amount compounded each year to pay six per cent interest on the bonds. Since that amount has been exhausted, the bondholders have received no money, except the small interest they get from the government subsidies. To show hoyv utterly wild and reckless the statements of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Scott) are, I may say that the whole bonded indebtedness of that road is $15,000 a mile, lower than the amount authorized, I think, on any prairie road we have chartered this year. The whole of this money, every pound of it, was spent upon the road. My firm received out of it less than the ordinary business commission-not half of what would be charged under ordinary circumstances. There was not enough money possibly to be raised to pay more than that. The bankers said:	We would give so much money
for that security, if you can get a contractor to build the road for that. The contractor secured was Mr. Jas. Ross, who had no interest in that road at all. Mr. Jas. Ross, as contractor, built that road, and he was paid his estimates as they went along, and his interest in the road ceased when the contract ceased, just the same as in the case of any ordinary contractor.
Resulting from that, Mr. Ross looked into the Calgary and Edmonton Railway. About that time there was a charter in existence covering the Calgary and Edmonton Railway and carrying a land grant of 12,400 acres per mile. That charter for that railway was hawked about from one end of this continent to the other. It was submitted in England, trying to raise money to build the road, and the effort was unsuccessful. Subsequently, a new charter was obtained by some people-I was not one of them-with a grant of 6,400 acres per mile and $80,000 a year for twenty years in lieu of government service. The government retained one-third of the land grant to protect them against any deficiency in case the railway had not earned $80,000 a year through government business during that time. The government still own that land grant, and I have no hesitation in saying that that land grant covers all that the railway company owes the government. The road was financed in precisely the same manner as I have described in connection with the Qu'Appelle, Long Lake and Saskatchewan Railway. Five million five hundred thousand dollars were raised in cash by the sale of the land and of the bonds. I myself took nearly $200,000 in these bonds, paying par for them. These bonds I have held and they have been down to twenty-five cents on the dollar since that day. Now they are at a better rate because of the improved conditions of the road. I may mention that the Qu'Appelle, Long Lake and Saskatchewan bonds are quoted in the market to-day at about sixty cents



on tlie dollar, so that I did not get very rich on that transaction ; in fact I think It was unfortunate for me. The Calgary and Edmonton Railway was, as I have said, financed precisely in the same way hy the sale of the bonds. I should judge that so far from any of the members from the North-west finding fault with the financing of these two roads, they should hold them up as an example, and as an absolute contrast to any other road that has been built in the North-west as a branch or a small concern. I say that for this reason, that these two roads were built for honest cash put into them
The hon. member will, I suppose, conclude with a motion, because I think the question of privilege is exhausted now', and we are entering into a discussion.

Yes, I will conclude with a motion. Every dollar that went into the construction of the road was paid in cash. There were no arrears or wages, there were no debts on the road. Contrast that with any other road that was constructed in the North-west at that time. Every one of these branches or small concerns failed when they got partly constructed, leaving debts to tradesmen, to contractors and to labourers. The Manitoba and North-western, the North-west Central, the old Hudson's Bay Railway, and in fact every branch road failed until they came into the hands of strong companies. Some of these roads which are now controlled by Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann receive precisely the same bonus that was given to the two roads with which I was connected, namely, a land grant of 6,400 acres per mile, and so many thousand dollars a year for twenty years.
I defy any man in this House or in this country to put his finger upon one single transaction in connection with the building and financing of these two roads, that is not absolutely straightforward and honourable. And so far as my being ashamed of my connection with these two roads, I think that I can point, and my firm can point, with a great deal of pride, to these difficult undertakings that we successfully financed; and the latter, financed at the time of the Baring failure, a time of great financial crisis in Great Britain. I am not aware of having in any shape or way made myself disagreeable to these members from the North-west. I do not know why they should go out of their way to make statements, which one can hardly believe they didn't know to be absolutely false, because they had been denied before. I can only challenge the gentleman who made the statement, or any gentleman in this House, to produce one single fact in relation to my connection with these two roads, which I may not be proud of.	.
When I was connected with those roads, I was not in any shape or way in politics.

I had nothing to do with the chartering of those roads. I took charge of the financing purely and simply as a matter of business, and as a matter of business I think they were very successfully carried out ; and all the people connected with them will testify that I looked after their interests solely, and that the money that was expended on the roads was expended absolutely under their direction, and not under the direction of the men having charge of the financing. The capital stock of the Qu'Appelle, Long Lake and Saskatchewan Railway was $200,000, and that of the Calgary and Edmonton $1,000,000. If you add these two sums together, you will not have more than half the amount of the sum which I am accused of robbing the country of. The whole of the money which I have mentioned as having been' raised was put into these two roads. I hope that the papers will give this statement as much prominence as they gave the charge aginst me, made by the hon. member for West Assiniboia. That charge was printed with great prominence, with startling headlines, which were very misleading to any who might not read the speech in full.

Mr. Speaker, if I might be permitted to make a remark in reply to the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat, I might say that it is regrettable that the hon. member has not read the actual words I used, but has taken the perhaps not quite accurate reports of my statement in the newspapers. I took pains to state on that occasion that I was making no reflection at all upon the junior member for West Toronto, but was merely making before the House a comparison of the railway legislation proposed by the government at the present time with certain railway legislation which had been put through parliament by previous governments. Unfortunately, I had not the privilege this morning of hearing the full statement or explanation made by the hon. gentleman, and I am not quite aware whether he challenged the figures I placed before the House the other evening. These were not voluminous, and it will take me only a moment or two to go over them again. The Qu'Appelle, Long Lake and Saskatchewan Railway was stocked for $201,000, and was bonded for $3,809,140. The total debt upon the road is therefore $4,010,140. The total cost of the railway, as shown by the records left in the Department of Railways and Canals by the previous government, was $2,539,600. I made no reflection, as I state, upon the hon. gentleman. He has taken pains, since I came into the House, to deny that there was anything in the building of these roads not entirely straightforward. I made no such accusation against the promoters of these roads or against the hon. gentleman ; but in view of these figures, I think the hon. gentleman is going a considerable length in

boasting that none of the labourers or contractors on these roads lost any money or failed to receive their wages or their pay. I say that the total money raised in connection with that one road was $4,010,140, and the total cost was only $2,539,600, leaving a balance in the pockets of the promoters, after they had paid all the contractors and labourers, of $1,470,000. Surely there is no great reason to be found in these figures for the boast that the labourers and contractors did not fail to receive their pay. In addition to that there was a land grant given in connection with the Prince Albert Road of 1,619,200 acres. I put the value of this the other evening at $2 per acre, and I understand that the company was able a little over a year ago to sell the lands at that figure to the Saskatchewan Valley Land Company. I gave the value of the land at $2,238,400. I regret to find that 1 made a little error there-a little matter of $1,000,000. The value of the land grant is $3,238,400 ; but, of course, a little matter of $1,000,000 in the total amount of the improper profits which these promoters obtained out of these roads does not amount to very much after all. Then, I gave the amount of the subsidy of $80,000 a year for twenty years at $1,600,000, and I said that over and above the cost of the road, it appeared that the promoters got away with $5,30S,940. The accurate figure is $6,308,940. That is the history, as I stated, of the Qu'Appelle, Long Lake and Saskatchewan Railway. The history of the Calgary and Edmonton is very similar. May I ask the hon. gentleman, as I did not hear his statement this morning, if he denies any of these figures ?

Yes, I deny them absolutely. I can quite understand that the hon. gentleman, making the statement he does, brings the figures out as he has done now. He assumes that the money was not put into the road, and that the $80,000 a year is still going to the promoters, though it has been assigned to the bondholders. The company does not own all the land ; the government possess one-third of the land. The lands of the company and the bonds were sold, and they produced $3,700,000. The contract for the road was $2,500,000. The bondholders, as I have stated, insisted on having a deposit which would pay them 6 per cent interest on their bonds for six years. That money was got by selling the bonds and the land grant to produce that $3,700,000.
Will the hon. gentleman allow me to ask him a question ?
Order.
I merely wish to ask to whom was the land sold ?

I state again that every dollar that was raised by the sale of the lands and the bonds was put into the road-
$2,500,000 into construction and $1,000,000 or $1,250,000 with the bank in London to provide for the interest. It may be quite true that the people who bought that land bought it at the nominal value of a dollar an acre; but they held it for thirteen years, and were only able to sell it this year. The men composing the Lonk Lake Land Company are all over England ; and if that land had gone up to $10 an acre, that would have nothing to do with the original cost; that cannot be controlled by anybody. But what I state is that the whole amo,unt for which the two roads were bonused went into the cost of the roads. The money was deposited with two bankers, one of whom was Morton, Rose & Company, it was then, for the security of the bondholders, and for six years the bondholders were paid 6 per cent interest. Since then they had nothing on the Qu'Appelle and Long Lake except the 2 per cent from government subsidy which was assigned to Morton. On the Caigary and Edmonton, after the amount paid on that was exhausted, the bondholders only received one year 2 per cent, other years 1 per cent, and in the past year, owing to the prosperous times, 4 per cent. All these contracts were made with the approval and sanction of the government, and the government has copies of them in the department here. The statements I make can also be verified by writing the bankers, Morton, Grenville and Chapman, successors to Morton, Rose & Company. The figures I give are absolutely correct. I make the statement that the promoters of that road did not get even an ordinary commission on a business transaction, and that there never was a business transaction put through in this country more creditable to all 'concerned.
Does the hon. gentleman deny the accuracy of the figures I quoted ?
The hon. gentleman said that there was a difference of a million and a half which the promoters put into their pockets. I deny that absolutely.
My question is whether or not the figures I quoted are accurate.. Does he deny those figures ?
I do.
They are from the blue-books. They are mattei-s left on record in the Department of Railways and Canals by the Conservative government before 1896.

I hope that the hon. gentleman will be fair, as this is a personal matter, and I am stating what is absolutely correct. He talks about $200,000 of stock and he assumes that the $200,000 was put in in cash. I assure him it was not put in in cash. Capital stock in those days and to-day is seldom put in in cash. There is nothing in the agreement with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway providing that the

capital stock should he paid for in cash. I gave the figures, and if the hon. gentleman chooses to distort them I cannot help that.

The hon. gentleman has spoken all around the figures. I want him to say whether or not the figures which 1 took the trouble of reading a few evenings ago from the records of this government are correct. There was another little matter in which the hon. gentleman was interested, known as the North-west town sites scandal. I asked him on this floor one eveniug whether he denied the matter which appeared in the report of certain commissioners appointed to look into the case of the Northwest town sites. He denied most emphatically and absolutely everything that appeared in the report of those commissioners, yet the whole of that report consists of sworn evidence, given by residents of the territories, some of them political friends of the hon. gentleman. Certain statements made by my hon. friend do certainly take away from the seriousness of the position, as I explained it the other evening. But even giving him full credit for every piece of explanation he has been able to make, there are still left in this transaction very enormous profits to the promoters of these two railway companies, of which my hon. friend admits he is one.
I was not a promoter of either. I deny it absolutely.
Was the hon. gentleman not interested and associated in the building of these two roads ? The explanation he has already made absolutely places him in that position. Let me just a moment or two

I rise to a point of order. The hon. gentleman has made a statement which the hon. member for West Toronto distinctly and emphatically denied, and now the hon. gentleman is attempting to reiterate the statement. Is he not bound to accept it.

When a statement is made by an hon. member on a matter affecting him personally, every other member must accept it. Therefore the hon. member for Assiniboia will have to accept the statement of the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) regarding the question of promotion.

I am bound to accept any statement made by any hon. gentleman on a personal matter, but what I was pointing out was that, by his explanation of the facts, the hon. gentleman has put himself in the position of one who was associated with certain others in the building of two lines of railway. The Calgary and Edmonton road issued common stock to the extent of $1,000,000 and bonds to the extent of $5,474,573, making a total indebtedness of $0,474,513. My hon. friend said he never

did anything to earn the enmity of the members or the people of the North-west Territories. Why, certainly not. The people of the North-west Territories, or the members at all events, have not the slightest enmity towards my hon. friend, but when he takes credit to himself and his associates for having conferred any great benefits on the people of the North-west Territories, he is going a great deal further than the occasion justifies. There is a debt on the Calgary and Edmonton Railway, through the efforts of my hon. friend and his associates, of - $6,474,513. But the whole cost of that road, as shown by the reports in the Railway Department, was only $3,573,562, showing an excess of debt over cost of $2,730,951, which is a burden on that road and on the struggling settlers who have to pay freight rates sufficiently high to enable the company to meet the interest at the rate of six per cent. The land grant was about 1,888,000 acres. My hon. friend from Alberta says that the company sold no land for less than $3 an acre and this year they are selling lands at $4 and $5 and higher, and within that area are several town sites, the lots in which sell at a figure very much in excess of $3. But taking $3 as the price, you have on the land grant of 1,888,000 acres $5,664,000. I understood the hon. gentleman to say that the land was sold at the time of the construction of the railway. The land of the Prince Albert branch was only sold last year to the Saskatchewan Valley Land Corporation at 82 per acre. The company was given a subsidy of $80,000 per year for twenty years, which makes $1,600,000. This shows a total profit on the Calgary and Edmonton of $9,994,951. Let me repeat the figures :

My hon. friend by his explanation, says that those interested in these railways-he does not wish them to be called promoters- those who obtained the legislation from the Conservative government, did not obtain the full advantages shown by these figures, but suppose we cut the amount down by one-half, you will still have a sum of about $8,000,000, or more than one-half the outside amount which the Grand Trunk Pacific

is going to cost the people during the next fifty years. As regards the advantage to the territory from the building of these lines, the Saskatchewan valley would have been much better developed by the continuing of the Manitoba and North-west Railway from Portage la Prairie to the Saskatchewan valley from east to west, and the hon. member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) will be able to show the House that the freight on wheat charged on that line from Regina to Prince Albert is 29 cents per hundred pounds. That has been the charge ever since that railway was constructed.
Twenty-nine cents per 100 pounds. I venture to say that when the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway is constructed there the people in the neighbourhood of Prince Albert will have the advantage of a freight rate not more than 60 per cent of that amount. I pointed out that these roads had failed to effect the purpose, for which they were intended, had failed to develop the Saskatchewan valley, which was tapped by these roads at only two points. And the people who were interested in the construction of these roads, by their success in their application to this parliament when the Conservative party was in power, blocked for ten years the extension of the Manitoba and North-western Railway. Why did they come down here to agitate for the construction of these roads when, by the extension of the Manitoba and North-western Railway, the Saskatchewan valley could have been quickly and successfully opened ? Because the Manitoba and North-western in those days was in the hands of people not so closely allied with the Conservative party ; the Manitoba and North-western pebple could not be squeezed out of their holdings at that time. Then other action was taken; these other roads were built from the south to the north to tap the Saskatchewan valley.

I rise to a point of order. I do not think that on a question of privilege, in which the hon. junior member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) refers to a statement that he was one of those who made a profit of $15,000,000 and was a grafter, it is open to my hon. friend to discuss the question of freight rates and other matters connected with the administration of that particular railway. I do not think it is in order; this Is a matter of privilege, and discussion should be confined strictly to the question of privilege.
I understood that my hon. friend moved that the House do adjourn.

With regard to the motion to adjourn, 1 may say'that when a motion to adjourn is made the question which is to be discussed is the question which is brought up by the member who makes that motion and the discussion should not go outside of that question.

Mr. Speaker, I am within your judgment if I am not speaking strictly to that question. I am speaking of the effect of the building of these two lines of railway ; and I was explaining that one effect of their construction was the blocking for ten years of the extension of the Manitoba and North-western Railway.

I am afraid that is going a little outside the question. I understood that the motion of the hon. junior member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) was concerning his connection with those railways, and I think then we should not enter upon the discussion of the whole question of freight rates on these railways.

I was endeavouring to keep myself strictly to the discussion of the connection of my hon. friend with these roads, and to the result of liis connection with them, and I say that one of the worst results of this and of the building of these lines of railway was the blocking for ten years of the extension of the Manitoba and North-western, and it is the opinion of the people of the west that the reason why the Manitoba and North-western was thus blocked at that time was that the owners of the Manitoba aud North-western could not at that time be squeezed out of their holdings. Because they could not be squeezed out, other action was taken, they were in time squeezed out, and I understand my hon. friend the junior member for West Toronto now stands in the position of one of the chief holders also of the Manitoba and North-western. Let me repeat again, I have not made any personal reflection on my hon. friend. I said distinctly that I understood he was perfectly right in getting all he could get so long as he did not transgress the law. He simply took advantage of the law put on the statute-book when the Conservative party was in office. I am bound to say that when it can be shown that an hon. member of this House at some previous time in his career has profited to such an enormous extent through the Canadian Pacific Railway, through the Calgary and Edmonton Railway, through the Long Lake and Saskatchewan Railway, through his connection with town sites in the North-west and other matters for which the Conservative government was responsible, when he and his associates have profited to such an enormous extent, to the extent of millions of dollars through legislation placed upon the statute-books, it ill-becomes him to come down to this House, as the hon. gentleman has done in the last few years, and take the position that no more subsidies should be granted, that no more of the people's money should be expended for the construction of railways. That seems to put him in this position-I make no direct charge-to put him in this position, that he and his associates having got their clutches firmly upon Manitoba

and the North-west Territories, he does not wish to see any other railways, independent or competing railways, constructed there to give the people of those provinces the benefit of competition. He and his associates seem to take the position that they must be left for ever with their clutches on the people of Manitoba and the west, so as to be able to charge rates at their own sweet will and to tax the people of that country as they have done during the last twenty years.

I wish to say a few words with reference to this discussion. I asked the bon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier), while he was speaking on this question, to whom the lands were sold. I understood him to say that the land received in connection with the Regina, Long Lake and Saskatchewan Railway was sold, along with the bonds. I do not doubt the hon. gentleman's word, but it seems to me very strange that this land was sold twelve years ago and that I myself, not twelve months ago, bought some of it from the firm with which the bon. gentleman is connected, the firm of Osier, Hammond & Nanton. The hon. gentleman has stated that when a railway was built he had nothing to do with political matters, but at the time this railway was projected we who live at Prince Albert went to the expense of sending a delegation down here to press for the extension of the Manitoba and North-western Railway. The hon. gentleman who then represented Saskatchewan in the interest of the Conservative party in this House made that application and the delegation were told not to say a word about the Manitoba and North-western Railway, that it would be all fixed up, and that friends of the government had hold of the matter and were going to have two other lines built into that country. As has been well pointed out by the hon. member for East Assiniboia (Mr. Scott), had the Manitoba and North-western Railway been extended at that time, there would not now be the necessity for subsidizing the Canadian Northern Railway, and the development that is now taking place in that country would have taken place thirteen years ago. Rut, as I said before, when our delegation came down to press for (he extension of the Manitoba and North-western Railway they were told: Do not say a word about it ; close friends of the government have taken up that proposition and are going to put it through-and it was put through. My hon. friend beside me suggests that the firm of Osier, Hammond & Nanton could not wait. This proposition was put through, these gentlemen voted this cash subsidy for this railway, and when these parties got the right to build their railway, how did they treat the settlers in that country? Let me point out to you how they made money. When they came to Sas-Mr. SCOTT.
katoon they found a town which had been built up by the settlers. Did they go into the town? No, they shunted across the river and built a town of their own and the golden shekels are now flowing into the pockets of the company from that new town. When they came to the town of Duck Lake did they enter it ? No, they went two miles away, built a town of their own and ruined the people of Duck Lake, and the golden shekels are now running into their pockets from that town site. When they got to Prince Albert they did not go into that town, which had been there for years and which had over 1,500 inhabitants. until the people gave up to them one-lialf of their property, and no doubt ah the present time the golden streams are flowing into the pockets of that company from the money they are realizing from that town site.
They say that the land was sold as a bond. Why, the land has been and is being sold by the firm of Osier, Hammond & Smith, in Winnipeg, right up to the last year, and the whole of it was sold last year to a company called the Saskatchewan Valley Land Company for a certain figure, and that sale was made by the firm of Osier, Hammond & Smith. Now, I do not know how much that firm realized out of it, but there is a general impression in the west that they made a pretty good thing out of it. AH we object to is that when we propose to give subsidies to build roads, a gentleman connected with this institution gets up in this House and protests against any more subsidies being given to assist in opening up and developing territory. I say, as suggested by my hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Scott), that these gentlemen made a good thing" out of it, and now when other people want to get railways built through that country to open it up, we object to these gentlemen getting up and protesting against subsidies hpingl given for that purpose after they have filled their own pockets.

I quite understand the object of this attack. The member for Assiniboia says, and the member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Davis) supports him in saying, that I have made a false statement when I say that these lands were sold at the time the railway was built and the bonds were sold. I say again, Mr. Speaker, that these lands were sold at the time the bonds were sold, they were sold to an English company.

Might I ask the hon. gentleman a question ? If it is a fact that the lands of the Qu'Appelle, Long Lake and Saskatchewan Company were sold a year ago, how is it that as late as two years ago the company were refusing to accept lands from the government and the government brought suit in the Exchequer Court about the matter ?

Surely any one can understand that. The purchasers bought these lands under the conditions that they were granted to the railwa3r company, and they considered that the lands offered by the government did not come up to those conditions, and they employed solicitors to enforce the bargain. Many of the lands have not passed from the government and have not been accepted. 1 make the statement that the lands were sold at the time, they were sold with the bonds in both cases, and the whole of the money that was raised from the sale of these lands and bonds went into the road and paid interest on the bonds. There was no money made except the ordinary profit made by the contractor-
I do not know how much Mr. James Ross made out of his contract. The Englishman supplied the funds and he got part of the land, $12,000 or $13,000 a mile, for building the road. I do not know how much he made out of it, and it is not my business.
I was acting simply as an agent. Let me refer to the attack which the hon. gentleman made gratuitously upon me in connection with the town sites. I, with Lord Strathcona and Mr. Angus, have been trustees for the town sites, partly on government land, for nearly twenty years. A commission was appointed to make an investigation and they brought in a report stating that we owed the government so much money. That is some years ago. The trustees disputed absolutely and entirely that report. We have been the trustees from that time to this, and have endeavoured to get the government to come to a settlement by sueing us, and the government refused to do it. but they keep the question open in order that gentlemen like these may make attacks upon me in the House. Let them make an attack upon Lord Strathcona and upon Mr. Angus, who were trustees with me. The Prime Minister, I think, won't get up and make such an assertion, but it is men of that character-
Order, order.

I apologize-members from the west who make that accusation. I say that to-day my solicitor and the solicitors of the Canadian Pacific Railway are pressing the government, and have been pressing the government for four years past, to bring this dispute to a conclusion regarding these town sites, and the government are delaying to do so for a purpose.

I do not know whether the right hon. gentleman, the leader of the government, approves of this style of attack made by the member for Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) upon my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Osier) ; I presume he does not. I think I may say that the hon. gentleman from Assiniboia went out of his way in making the charge which he did, and in using the words which
he did the other evening in regard to my hon. friend from West Toronto. My hon. friend from West Toronto needs no certificate of character from me or from any of his colleagues. He is known from one end of the country to the other, and is respected for his honesty and in every way. He has lived all his life in the city of Toronto, and has been twice elected to this House by the riding of West Toronto. His firm to which hon. gentlemen opposite have alluded occupy as high a position in this country as any other firm in a similar business. Therefore, I say the hon. gentleman went out of his way in using the language he did in regard to my hon. friend. You must remember, Sir. that this hon. gentleman employed tactics similar to these in regard to the hon. member for Peel when he brought affidavits into this House to discredit the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) and he was entirely out of order in reading these affidavits.
Order.
The hon. gentleman is referring to a previous debate.

Yes, I will not say anything further then with regard to that. However, my hon. friend from West Toronto, in all these transactions, has enjoyed the highest reputation, and his friends have the utmost confidence in him, and it is a surprise to them and a surprise to him, ho doubt, to find that a transaction fourteen years old should have been brought up in this House the other night and discussed in the manner that it has been.
The results of the transaction are still present in the North-west Territories.

The hon. gentleman from West Toronto referred to the reports, and the way the newspapers of this country have taken advantage of the statement made by the member for Assiniboia to throw discredit upon my hon. friend. A report of that day's proceedings in the House was headed in one of the Toronto papers : ' Charges against Mr. Osier, M.P., that he profited by government concessions. Mr. Scott's speech on the Grand Trunk Pacific question.' That was the heading of a discussion covering many columns in the ' Globe.' I do not know whether that was the object of my hon. friend or not ; if it was, I think he was very unfair. I think that tlie members of this House ought to be governed by the same rules that govern gentlemen outside the House, they ought to be governed by rules just as strict. There are certain things that we grant each other as gentlemen outside this House, and inside this House, and I think hon. members ought to be governed by the same rules of etiquette that govern the conduct of gentlemen outside the House. The bom gentleman who preceded me said that per-

haps this report was misunderstood, and that perhaps my hon. friend did not understand it in the way it was intended, and he asked my hon. friend from West Toronto if he had read his remarks. Now, this is what the hon. gentleman said the other night:
I am reminded that my hon. friend from West Elgin (Mr. Robinson), one evening since the commencement of this session, expressed some curiosity to see that individual who is frequently termed a grafter. My hon. friend from West Elgin will remember that one evening here he read a letter from some one in Vancouver, I think, who said he would like to >see one of these individuals spoken of as grafters. It seems to me that if we could put our linger on the gentleman who got away with these $15,000,000, we would find a grafter under our finger. Now, I would advise my hon. friend from West Elgin to cast his eye down to the seat just four rows in front of him, to the seat of the hon. junior member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) and he will see-or he would see, because the seat is vacant at the present moment-he would see, if the seat was filled by its member, one of these grafters who, by himself and his associates, got away with this sum of 15,000,000 odd dollars.
Now, if the hon. gentleman says there is nothing personal in that, I do not understand -what the English language means. I say it is most unjustifiable, and I appeal to the right hon. leader of the government
Does the hon. gentleman deny the truth of It ?

Do I deny the truth of it ? I have every confidence in the statement of my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Osier). I believe every word he has said is true in regard to this matter. I will not take up the time of the House any longer in regard to this. I do not consider that there ever has been a more unjustifiable or a more unfair attack made upon any hon. member of this House than that which the hon. member for West Assiniboia has made upon the hon. member for West Toronto.

Mr. Speaker, I think it is an unfortunate custom that has grown up in this House during the past few years to refer to newspaper reports and to use them in the House, even when I have felt that the hon. members referring to them knew that they could not possibly be true
speakername: The MINISTER OP PUBLIC WORKS (Hon. James Sutherland).

speechtext: I am referring to what appeared in ' Hansard.'

When these newspaper reports involve a personal attack upon an hon. member of this House, the member making use of them could at least ascertain whether there was any foundation for the statements contained in them. It is unfortunate that during the past few years this custom has been so prevalent in this House. I do not occupy Mr. KEMP.
the time of the House very much, but while I sit here I hear one member after another get up and make use of some matter which had appeared in a newspaper, and which apparently had been written for the purpose of being used in such an improper manner. We also hear letters being read in this House for the purpose of making attacks upon members of the House. My hon. friend referred to one which was brought up in this House and which made a dastardly attack upon respectable men who had never made any money out of their connec-tiou with politics. I think we should all be gratified to know that we have in this country enterprising citizens who have had the ability and energy to take up large public enterprises and assist them forward. It is no discredit to a citizen who does so. He should not be singled out as one of the chief sinners against whom insinuations, innuendoes and attacks are to be directed, nor should it be recklessly charged that his motives are Improper. My hon. friend (Mr. Osier) must remember that unless he changes his methods In regard to this matter, he can hardly expect that the circumstances which have given rise to this discussion will not be referred to. I simply rose for the purpose of expressing, as a member of this House, my view that the practice of reading newspaper reports and letters is a most objectionable one.
This Is ' Hansard.' The hon. minister is under a misapprehension. I am reading the very words that the hon. member for West Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) uttered as reported in ' Hansard.'

I was not referring to the hon. member for East Toronto (Mr. Kemp), but I will say frankly, and leave it to the House and to the country whether I am right or not, that the hon. members from Toronto are perhaps the greatest sinners in this respect. When the Orders of the Day are called, or when the Order is reached to go into supply, matters of privilege are brought up based on some rumours that they have seen in newspapers.
What does the hon. minister refer to ?

1 refer to this, that for a great many years, long before my hon. friend (Mr. Kemp) was a member of this House and since, news-pa per reports along the line of the remarks that were made in this House against my hon. friend were constantly quoted, and I think if he would turn up the columns of the ' Mail ' newspaper he would find the most bitter attack on my hon. friend that ever appeared anywhere, or, at least, since he was a member, along those lines, and It is from these newspaper attacks, I suppose, that these statements have originated in this House. I think it is due to the good conduct of this House, as well as in the

public interest, that hon. members should be careful to verify these statements, and that they should at least have respect enough for themselves, for the country and for their colleagues, to be very sure of the facts before they bring forward newspaper reports in this House and make statements that they must know are not true. What have we heard during the last week ? Instead of a dignified and businesslike discussion of the question before the House, we have had most bitter personal attacks made upon a gentleman from Toronto, an enterprising citizen. I doubt very much if hon. members who have attacked this gentleman will get up and say that he is guilty of any dishonourable conduct in respect to his connection with public enterprises. Still, we have one after another getting up and reading newspaper reports referring to this gentleman in the most discreditable manner. I say it is not in keeping with the dignity of the House or the public interest that this should be done. I am quite willing to admit that if a member of this House, or if any citizen, has committed an act that is improper he should be criticised, but no respectable citizen should be unfairly attacked because he is connected with a public enterprise, the prosecution of which is in the public interest. It may be that it is quite within the right of any hon. member to do so, but for one hon. gentleman after another to get up and attack Senator Cox without any justification, is a most unreasonable and discreditable proceeding on the part of those hon. members. I think we should be proud to know that we have citizens who take a part in large public enterprises, and we ought to be careful before we make insinuations and innuendoes against those men, who are amongst our best citizens. There ought to be some reason before such attacks as these can be made, and I hope that my hon. friend (Mr. Osier), who no doubt feels aggrieved at the statements which have been made in regard to himself, will realize how unfortunate it is that this custom has grown up to such an extent on both sides of the House. I think hon. gentlemen will agree with me that it is a custom which should not be continued.

Mr. Speaker, that very nice little bit of a scold may be interesting to the House, but I cannot see that it will answer any good purpose. As to the propriety of the conduct of hon. members of this House, each one individually will try to govern himself according to the rules of the House and according to his own judgment ; but it seems to me that the hon. gentleman's statement is specially inapplicable in this case when you come to consider it. If it were a question of newspaper rumour that had no foundation in fact being used as the basis of an attack upon an bon. member of this House, then there might be some justification for the advice gratuitously given the
House by the hon. Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Sutherland). Does the hon. gentleman deny the right or privilege of any hon. member here to defend his own character or conduct when it is improperly, untruthfully and unjustly assailed ? If this particular case happened to be one based only upon newspaper rumour, then there might be some justification for his remarks, but the very fact that the newspaper rumour is founded upon a statement made in this House, and which is recorded in ' Hansard,' and which deliberately declares that the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) had profited by the swag with others to the extent of $15,000,000, gives an entirely different complexion to the matter. My hon. friend from West Toronto availed himself of the undoubted right and privilege which every hon. member of this House has to set that matter straight, and to do that he was necessarily obliged to make an explanation of the whole transaction. I thought he put it so clearly to the House that every hon. member would at once accept it, but the hon. member for West As-siniboia (Mr. Scott) did not accept it, but rather endeavoured, as I think, to justify the unfair charge that he had made. Does the hon. minister who has just taken his seat say that the hon. member for West Toronto was wrong in trying to defend his own character, reputation and veracity ? If he does, then his scold may be in point.
I made no charge except such as can be based upon the records of the Railways and Canals Department. Every figure I quoted is on record there.

The hon. gentleman says he made no charge, but is it not a charge to talk about swag as follows ?
My hon. friend from West Elgin will remember that one evening here he read a letter from some one in Vancouver, I think, who said he would like to see one of the individuals spoken of as grafters. It seems to me that if we could put our finger on the gentleman who got away With this $15,000,000- '	'
Was that not a charge ?
-we would find a grafter under our finger.
Then he goes on to explain who that gentleman was.
I would advise my hon. friend from West Elgin to cast his eye down' to the seat just four rows in front of him, to the seat of the hon. the junior member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) and he will see-or he would see, because the seat is vacant at the present moment -he would see if the seat was filled by its member one of these grafters, who by himself and his associates fot away with this $15,000,000.
If that is not a charge, I do not understand the meaning of the English language.
Read on.

Is that not a charge against which any hon. member, on a ques-
10515 '

tion of privilege, has a right to defend himself ? And when the hon. member has done so, the hon. member for West Assiniboia has not the courtesy in him to accept it, and to say no more about it, but on the contrary lie' makes an effort to justify his language. Then the hon. Minister of Public Works (Hon, Mr. Sutherland) refers to it as a frivolous matter and as a mere newspaper rumour outside of this House.
Why do you misrepresent what I said ? I did not say anything of the kind.

Why did the Minister of Public Works get up to read a lecture to the hon. member for West Toronto and to this House, and when the hon. member (Mr. Osier) referred to what was not a mere newspaper rumour, but a statement made by a member of this House with all the responsibility that attaches to his position, and recorded in ' Hansard,' and a matter of history as to what took place in this House
The hon. gentleman knows that I did not read him a lecture. What I did was to express my regret that these newspaper articles should be used in the House.
The Minister of Public Works said that we were wasting the time of -the Hfouse because this matter was brought up.
I never said a word about wasting the time of the House.

If it was proper for the member for West Toronto to defend his character, why should the hon. gentleman and the House be read a lecture by the Minister of Public Works? If the hon. member (Mr. Osier) neglected to call attention to the matter, lie would be neglecting his duty to himself and to his constituents. Here we have a statement recorded in ' Hansard ' as made by a member of this House, and every word in that statement is just as strong as every word in the newspapers including the headings. The hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Osier) has done what was eminently proper. He would fail in his duty if he did not set himself right and give the member for West Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) an opportunity to withdraw the assertion he has made.

I think it is about time that this unfortunate incident should come to a conclusion, and it ought to come to a conclusion in a manner which should be accepted by members of both sides of the House. Sly hon. friend from West Assiniboia (Mr. Scott), some few days ago, made a statement, comparing the contract which is now before the House with the contract which was made by a former government, and he brought in as a matter

of comparison the Long Lake, Qu'Appelle and Saskatchewan Railway, as to which he showed by the records of the government that funds bad been provided to the amount of $4,000,000, whereas only $2,500,000 had been expended ; $1,500,000 going into somebody's pockets. He said that he thought that these profits had gone to the promoters, and my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Osier) very properly vindicated himself, and stated that lie was not one of the promoters and that not one dollar of that money had gone into his pockets. That statement is conclusive. There is nothing more to say upon that. My hon. friend (Mr. Osier) is exonerated from the charge of unduly profiting from the system that then prevailed, but some one else did profit by it. Therefore the argument of my hon. friend (Mr. Scott) holds good, that the method formerly followed is not as good as the method followed by this government. My hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Osier) is a respectable citizen, he is a respectable member of the community and the moment that he has given his word, even if he were not a member of this House, that is enough, and the matter should not go further. But so far as the argument of my hon. friend (Mr. Scott) is concerned, it still remains the same. The only thing he had in view was to compare the present contract

No, no.
The 1 xvIME MINISTER. Yes, I cannot see that my hon. friend (Mr. Scott) had anything else in view than to say with regard to the contract before the House :	here is
a contract under which nothing goes to the promoters, while in former times under other governments there were contracts in which undue profits went to the promoters. No one can deny that in this matter of the Qu'Appelle, Long Lake and Saskatchewan Railway, one and a half million dollars of profits went into somebody's hands which did not go into the road.

Would my right hon. friend allow me to interrupt him. I thought I had made myself quite clear to every one in this House, and I am sure the Prime Minister would be the last man in this House to make a statement which is not correct. What I said and what I repeat is: That the difference between that two and a half million dollars, the contract price, and the amount of the bonds, was paid into the bankers in London to meet the interest on these bonds for six years. That money did not go into the hands of promoters or into the hands of contractors, but it went into the hands of bankers in London and it was held in trust, and for six years thereafter the Qu'Appelle and Long Lake bond holders were paid six per cent. It was exhausted in six years, and from that time to this the bondholders have got nothing except the interest paid by the government. The same applies to the Calgary and

Edmonton. I know the Prime Minister will accept my statement and I can assure him that it can be verified by the trustees at any moment. Not one dollar of that money, the capital, went into the hands of promoters or any one connected with it. It was all paid out for the construction of the road and deposited for the interest for six years.

I accept without any reservation the statement of my bon. friend (Mr. Osier) that he did not profit in any way, but when it comes to a question as to whether or not some one else did not profit, I must take issue with my hon. friend. However, that is not a matter personal to him ; it is a matter outside of this House. I do not think any person in this House profited, but if my hon. friend (Mr. Osier) takes that ground that no undue profits were taken out of the transaction, I cannot agree with him. However, that is not the matter at issue. The matter at issue is simply a personal matter as to the honour of my hon. friend (Mr. Osier), and as to that, his statement is enough and there should not be one word more to say upon it.

I was not in the House the other day when this matter was brought up, and I can only depend upon the record which ' Hansard ' presents to us of the proceedings which then took place. I would not have risen now were it not for the lecture that the Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) felt it his duty to deliver to the members for Toronto. If we make any unfair statement in this House, we are responsible for it, and we are also responsible to the constituents whom we represent. So far as we are concerned we have endeavoured to represent our constituents to the very best of our ability, and in doing so we have avoided any breach of the rules of the House. If in matters affecting the interests of our constituents, we were not to bring to the attention of the House, reports printed in Toronto papers, in order to see if there is any foundation for them, we would be derelict in discharging the duties we are sent here to discharge.
Written for the purpose of being brought up to slander some one.

The hon. gentleman says these articles are written on purpose.
The MINISTER OF PUBmC WORKS. So they are.
Hear, hear.

Of course, as the Minister of Public Works would not make a statement of that kind unless he knew he was speaking the truth, and if he knows that these articles were written purposely to be brought up in this House, he is not discharging his duty as a member of this House, if lie does not state by whom these articles
were written and by whom they were printed. So far as I am concerned I have never suggested the printing of any article, and I have never written any article for the purpose of having it brought up in this House, nor do I know of any article ever having been written for such a purpose.

You are not the only member for Toronto.
Mr. CLARKE, I admit that, but speaking for myself I repel the insinuation that I ever did in any shape or form what the Minister of Public Works has suggested. But, Mr. Speaker, I wish to draw your attention and the attention of the House to the fact that this is the second or third time that my hon. colleague from West Toronto has been attacked in this House because of his connection with the Calgary and Edmonton and the Qu'Appelle, Long Lake and Saskatchewan Railways. Attacks have been made upon him on two occasions in his absence, one of them several years ago; and he has acted within his right in giving an emphatic denial to the statements made. What lias he asserted to be the fact with regard to his connection with these railways ? In the first place, he has said-and no hon. gentleman has contradicted the statement-that he had no connection whatever with those who obtained these charters from parliament. Will any hon. gentleman deny the accuracy of that statement ? He says further that he had no connection with those who obtained the land grants in connection with the building of these roads. No hon. gentleman has denied the accuracy of that statement. He says further that after many futile attempts had been made by those who had obtained the charters and the land grants to secure the construction of these railways, he was asked by those parties to undertake the floating of these enterprises. He was asked, because of his high reputation and the high reputation of his firm as financial agents, to undertake the work of raising the necessary funds to enable these roads to be built. He went to the old country, and through the influence which he possessed there, and through the confidence which capitalists had in him. he made the necessary financial arrangements by which both of these roads were built. He has declared that in making these financial arrangements and in disposing of the bonds necessary for building the roads, the land grants were sold at the same time. He has further declared that every dollar raised by him was put into the construction of the roads or was set apart to provide for the payment of interest. He has also said that his firm received only a very small commission on the work performed from those who desired to get these roads constructed. As these statements have not been denied, as they cannot be denied-because any person who knows my hon. colleague knows that he would not

make a misstatement in a matter of this kind-surely this ouglit to be the last of these scandals to be brought up in this House against him. There has been another charge made, supplemental to those to which I have referred, that is, that the firm of my hon. colleague is selling the lands referred to. Is there any crime in that ? Has that firm not a right to engage in business pursuits in the North-west or in any other part of Canada ? Is there any charge that that firm is selling these lands under false pretenses ? I think my hon. friend has only done his full duty in calling attention to these charges, and asking that they be withdrawn. He has given them an emphatic denial, and I hope that the hon. member for West Assiniboia will withdraw every accusation that would tend to impeach the honour and integrity of my hon. friend.

Does my hon. friend insinuate that any crime has been charged against his colleague ? I took pains to state the other evening that I cast no aspersion upon him and charged no crime against him, except his connection with these matters of improper legislation, for which the Conservative government and not my hon. friend is responsible.

With the permission of the House, I will just read what the hon. gentleman is reported to have said, and then leave it to the judgment of the House whether he made any charge or not:
My hon. friend from West Elgin will remember that one evening here he read a letter from some one in Vancouver, I think, who said he would like to see one of these individuals spoken of as grafters. It seems to me that if we could put our finger on the gentleman who got away with these $15,000,000 we would find a grafter under our finger.
Read further.

I will. I must, however, read as I go-read each line at it presents itself :
Now, I would advise my hon. friend from West Elgin to cast his eye down to the seat lust four rows in front of him, to the seat of the hon. junior member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) and he will see-or he would see, because the seat is vacant at the present moment-he would see, il the seat was filleu by its member, one of these grafters who, by himself and his associates, got away with this sum of 15,000,000 odd dollars.
If the hon. gentleman says that is no charge, then, Mr. Speaker, I have nothing more to say.
Would my hon. friend read further? Read my whole statement with respect to that matter.
I will, with pleasure. I will read the whole speech if the House will listen. The discussion follows :
I rise to a point of order. Is It in order for an hon. gentleman to call another hon. gentleman in this House a grafter?

Mr. Speaker, if you will permit me, before you give your- ruling, I make haste to withdraw the appellation, and I leave it to my hon. friend to apply the term that he thinks will best suit to any man who, with his associates in the railway business, manages to get away with a matter of $15,000,000.

Quite apart from the rules of the House, it strikes me that, instead of insinuating charges that are very grave indeed if true the hon, member should come out straight and fair and charge my hon. friend from West Toronto with what he insinuates.

I cannot imagine that there is any ambiguity in my words. I have stated here that somebody, some person in this country, got into their pockets, through Conservative railway legislation, a matter of $15,303,891, which would not have got into their pockets under proper legislation.
What has that to do with the particular gentleman he picked out ? He might as well refer to me or any other gentleman.

I will make a further statement, and make it upon my responsibility, that the hon. member fori Centre Toronto-I do not want to make any mistake, I will name him-Mr. Osier, is one of the gentlemen who is implicated in this matter.
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that I need not take up the time of the House reading any more.

Mr. Speaker, this discussion lias shown one thing pretty clearly with reference to the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier), that is, that if he expects to escape criticism in this House in future, he himself will have to be a little more guarded in the statements he makes. The other evening he made the statement in this House that this government had granted a subsidy to the Lake Erie and Detroit River Railway to purchase the support of the Walkerville distillery.

Then, I will not refer to a past debate. The hon. member has made the statement that this government purchased the support of the Walkerville distillery by granting a subsidy in aid of the Lake Erie and Detroit River Railway. That statement I characterize as utterly without foundation, and asi casting an improper reflection on a most reputable firm in my constituency.
