Mr. Speaker, 1 have listened with a great deal of care and attention to the remarks made by the right hon. leader of the House. I think hon. gentlemen on both sides of this House will give our leaders the credit of never employing language of the kind referred to to-day; and while I partly agreed with the right hon. gentleman's remarks as to the right of the hon. member for West Assiniboia to use any argument or figures he chose, I was sorry that he closed his remarks without disapproving of the word used by that hon. gentleman, namely, that the hon. member for West Toronto was a g(rafter. Had the right hon. gentleman called upon his followers to withdraw the objectionable word probably this debate would have closed. I, therefore, think that the right hon. gentleman in allowing the opportunity to pass for expressing his disapproval of the language used, has not shown to-day that courtesy which usually distinguishes him. As a rule, when any hon. member has anything to say reflecting on the personal character of any other hon. member on either side, he does not take advantage of the latters absence to make a personal charge. The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) however chose to take that course, and I would point out to my young friend, who has not been many years in this House, that he will not find tactics of that kind will gain him any advancement in the estimation of hon. members on either side. Such conduct might be left to older members who have some reputation to lose, and who stake that reputation when they adopt such procedure. I have nothing to say against the hon. member for Assiniboia, as regards his ability; but in my judgment it takes a number of years for a man to arrive at that stage when he can afford to take the course which the hon. gentleman has seen fit to follow. No man can afford to use language of the kind the hon. gentleman has indulged in. I might point to one of the best parliamentarians in this House, the hon. member for South Oxford (Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright)-whom I consider one of the best parliamentarians in the matter of language-and while I have heard that right hon. gentleman go very far, I never heard him go so far as to use language similar to that in which the hon. member for West Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) has indulged. The hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) has stated here to-day, on his honour as a gentleman, that he was not one of the promoters, but simply an agent in this matter. Why should he be charged with having made money out of it ? Even if he did make a million dollars or more out of it, is that an argument in connection with the subject before us ? As an agent, he was not a promoter, and should not be charged with having been a promoter. But the hon. gentleman persisted in disputing the statement of the hon. member for West Toronto. 1 have not heard the
hon. member for West Assiniboia withdraw the offensive word ' grafter,' and until he does that he will not have made the amends which this House has a right to exact, if it has any regard for its own dignity.

I had not intended to say anything, but it does seem to me that if the matter should close in the condition in which it is at present, the end will be worse than the beginning. The rules of parliament are the result of years of experience in the motherland crystallized into law and practice. Unless courtesy be maintained in debate, not only will the personal feelings of members, but the public business suffer. I have always understood that the word of a member of parliament, given in the House, must be taken in any matter reflecting upon himself personally. There is no one who will not admit that the charge made against the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) was most offensive and oiie which should not have been made. And when tile lion, member for West Toronto rose in his place and denied the charge, the hon. member for West Assiniboia, who made it, was bound, by all parliamentary usuage and practice, to withdraw it. But instead we find him justifying the language he used and we find other hon. members supporting him. We even find that the right hon. the First Minister-and perhaps it is more noticeable in his case because he is recognized on both sides as the soul of courtesy-we find that even he, although not saying a single word to which anybody could take exception, omitted to touch the very point before the House.
Quite the reverse. I said that the statement of the hon. member for West Toronto should be accepted without a word, and I say so now.

But the point I make is that the right hon. gentleman failed to advise his follower to withdraw the objectionable expression. If language of this kind is not to be withdrawn, we will be establishing a precedent in debate.
It was withdrawn the other day.

The whole discussion is on that point. My hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Osier) rightly demands a withdrawal of the term used, and the hon. member for West Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) seeks to justify his language. We even find a Minister of the Crown, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Sutherland), attempting to excuse it by a reference to statements made on this side against a prominent senator. I have heard that senator's name mentioned at different times in this debate, but I never heard any epithet applied to him at all equivalent to that of ' grafter.' Insinuations were made as to the hopes and aspirations of that gentleman, but no specific

charge. The only time I heard any charge made against him was when the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) addressed the House. But as I am mot at liberty to refer to a previous debate, I cannot repeat what was said. In fact the only specific charges I have heard made in this debate, apart from the present incident, against any member of this House, either from the government or the opposition benches, were the charges hurled again and again at a gentleman who, not long ago, was a colleague of the First Minister. But the charges against that hon. gentleman were not made from this side. I would point out that if this matter is to close at its present stage, if an hon. member can charge another with being a grafter, and not be compelled to withdraw' the objectionable expression, it is hard to say what will be the result during the next few weeks when passions may be excited and hon. gentlemen may be tempted to follow the precedent now laid down.

As the hon. member for West Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) I understand, will not have the opportunity of speaking again, I would like to refer to this debate. As I understood the hon. member, he described a certain condition of affairs regarding the Regina and Long Lake Railway.' He pointed out that it had cost $4,000,000, between bonds and land grants, and that $2,500,000 only had gone into the building of the road. The other $1,500,000 had gone into the pockets of somebody.
That has been denied.

We have then the statement of the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier)-a most remarkable statement coming from a gentleman of such high financial standing. He has told us that he paid $1,500,000 to the bondholders, being six years interest in advance on the $2,500,000 which he had borrowed. And in addition he pledged the land grant. That is the most remarkable financial transaction I have ever heard of. What rate per cent that would bring on the amount borrowed, 1 leave to an actuary to calculate. It is equivalent to borrowing $100 and paying $75 as interest in advance, which could not be considered a very profitable financial transaction, yet the hon. gentleman asks us to believe that he paid the $1,500,000 to the bondholders in advance for the interest, on $2,500,000, and not only that but the amount of the land grant, which he sold at $2 per acre, was pledged also, besides the $80,000 per year the company received from the government for carrying the mails.
I rise to a point of order. The hon. member for West Toronto has given a most unqualified denial to these statements and the hon. gentleman has to accept them.
I am not saying that the hon. gentleman was in it.
Order, sit down.
I am in order.
My point of order is that the hon. member for West Toronto has given a most explicit and definite denial, and his word is now being questioned by the hon. gentleman who has the floor.

I am not questioning his word. I am taking his own statement, fie said that the $1,500,000 did not go to anybody's pocket except the pockets of the bondholders, being six years' interest in advance on the $2,500,000. Is that not correct?
No.
That is the statement in ' Hansard.'

I do not think that, as a rule, I am very dense in these financial explanations. I have already explained several times what the cost of the road was, and 1 have shown that the money, in addition to the cost of the road, was deposited with Morton, Rose & Company in trust to meet the interest on the bonds for six years, while the road was earning nothing. I have not the figures with me, but the cost of the road was about two million and seven or eight hundred thousand dollars. The money that was deposited was the exact amount required to meet the interest on the bonds for that sum for six years. I have not the figures now, but I tell the hon. gentleman that is absolutely the fact, and that the two figures will agree. Every dollar that was raised by the issue of those bonds was put into the road or deposited to make up the amount that with accumulated interest would pay 6 per cent interest on the cost of construction for six years.

With the explanations that have been given by my hon. friend it is evident that this was a rather peculiar financial transaction, that the land grant was pledged and also a sum of money was deposited with Morton, Rose & Company to pay interest on these bonds for six years. Let us leave that phase of the question- and I may say that we accept the hon. gentleman's statement that the firm of Osier Hammond & Nanton had nothing to do with it, although we in the west know very well that that firm have been looking after the land grant of that railway for years, they have been looking after the town sites and handling the land grants, and that Mr. Nanton came down here and brought an action against the government in the Exchequer Court to compel them to exchange for that land grant better lands, lands that were cultivable. Yet we accept the hon. gentleman's statement that he had nothing to do with it, although his firm had the

entire management of the Calgary and Edmonton Road. Wliat do we find ? We find a state of affairs that has made the blood boil in the heart of every member from the west, and of every settler in Alberta in years gone by. Hon. gentlemen opposite spent millions of dollars to settle Alberta, and yet, while that expenditure was being made this very road did more than anything else to drive people out of this country. What did they do ? They not only obtained large sums of money for the construction of that road, but when it was completed they never operated the road at all. They never ran a train on it. The Canadian Pacific ran it and have had to run it until this day. They took the money and the land grant and never gave the people any railway accommodation. The Canadian Pacific Railway had to run the road, but not owning the road-bed and the track, they naturally did not run it as well as they should.
I submit that this is not relevant to this debate.
I am talking directly on the subject of the Calgary and Edmonton Road, which has been the subject of discussion for the last two hours.
It is the hon. junior member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) that is being discussed.

It is the connection of the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) with that road.
At one o'clock, House took recess.
House resumed at three o'clock.

When the House rose at one o'clock, I was dealing with the alleged connection of the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) with the Calgary and Edmonton road. I had dealt partially with his alleged connection with the Regina and Long Lake Road. For the Calgary and Edmonton road, a company was formed, some years ago, to build 105 miles south from Calgary to MacLeod, and 192 miles from Calgary to Edmonton.
Mr. Speaker, 1 desire to renew my objection that the remarks of the hon. gentleman are^ not relevant to the question before the House.

There are two questions raised, first, the connection of the hon. member for West Toronto with the railway, and, secondly, the formation of the company itself. These two questions are the subject of discussion now. I am very sorry that the discussion has taken so wide a range, and I would urge hon. gentlemen to shorten their remarks.

I shall not allude to any other road but the two roads I have mentioned. As I say, the Calgary and Edmonton Company was formed, and some millions of dollars were raised over and above the actual cost of construction. Notwithstanding that fact, the road was never operated by the company ;whicli got this land grant and this large subsidy. Not only was it not operated by that company, but it was handed over to the Canadian Pacific Railway, who have operated the road for the last two years, but in such a way as to do great injustice to the settlers who went In there, and many people have left that country, to my certain knowledge, because of the insufficient railway service afforded them. Now, in the construction of this road I want to refer to one or two incidents. In the first place, when they ran that road south to Macleod, what did they do ? Instead of going to that town, which had been established some 20 or 25 years before by a number of ranchers and had made considerable progress, men who had built up a number of large business places-instead of going into that town of Macleod, they established the station four miles from that town, cutting it out entirely. The town was almost wiped out of existence until the Crow's Nest road went in a couple of years ago, and gave them some relief. What did they do at the town of Edmonton ?	-
I am afraid the hon. gentleman is wandering from the question. The hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) discussed the financial side of the question.

I am going to show exactly the financial aspect now. They came to Edmonton, a town established on the north bank of the Saskatchewan river. Did they go across that town ? No, they built a town, of their own-and I now am coming to the financial aspect of this question. They built a town on the south side of the Saskatchewan, which they called South Edmonton, but it is now called Stratheona. They would not build over to a town already established, with some 2,000 people, built by men who had been there for 25 or 30 years, who had taken their lives in their hands, going across the trails where no other persons had ever settled. No, they would not give these people railway facilities, they built a town of their own south of the river, and they had sufficient influence with the government of the day to take away the Dominion Lands Office from Edmonton and try to bring it over to South Edmonton. They went so far as to have the safe and the books of the Dominion Lands Office loaded on to carts to be hauled down to the river, and the people of Edmonton, who had no confidence that they would get justice from the government, took the law into their own hands. It is just one of these instances that caused the rebellion of 1885, instances

of misgovernment by tbe government then in power. The people said to them, You may think that you are strong enough to move this land office from this town, but we say you are not. And they went anil took the carts, and took off the wheels of the carts, punished the men who were driving the carts, and took the books back to the land office at Edmonton, and the land office is there to-day. That shows, Mr. Speaker, the efforts these gentlemen were making to build up the town of South Edmonton and make a lot of capital out of it. That is one of the grievances under which the people of the North-west have laboured for years.
Now, the hon. gentleman says he bad no connection with this road, in no way was he interested. Well, we know very well that the firm of Osier, Hammond & Nanton, of which the hon. gentleman was senior member, have still control of that land grant and of that road. They make all tbe arrangements with the Canadian Pacific Railway office-I won't say that the hon. gentleman is interested himself, but there is strong confirmative evidence that he must be aware of his firm's connection with the transaction. He also said this morning that he knew nothing about the Regina and Long Lake road, that he was not interested in it. He further stated that two million and a half dollars of bonds had been placed in England, that a million and a half dollars had been placed in the hands of Morton, Rose & Co. to pay six years interest. Now, I have in my hands the ' Hansard ' of 1898, and I find that this subject was discussed at that time in this House. The hon. gentleman complains of my hon. friend from West Assiniboia being privileged by his position of member of parliament to bring such a question before the House. But I find that the hon. member for West Toronto had an opportunity away back in 1898 of taking action at law, if he desired, by reason of statements made by a gentleman who is not now in this House; I refer to Mr. Hugh Sutherland, now executive agent of the Canadian Northern road, at one time a member of this House, a man who is a supporter of the Conservative party, a man who has considerable financial standing and is well acquainted with the financial and railway affairs of the west. I find that some time before 1898, Mr. Sutherland went to England and endeavoured to float certain bonds to build the Winnipeg and Hudson's bay road. The hon. member for West Toronto wrote a letter in the * Globe ' at that time, reflecting upon that work, and saying it should be given no assistance. That letter was replied to by Mr. Sutherland, and with the permission of the House. I will read it, because it deals directly with the point that is the subject of this discussion. He says :
In the first place the company was conceived in deception. It professed to he an independent Mr. McCREARf.	.
company here as in truth it was a mere Canadian Pacific snare to catch the guileless investor. Look at the names of the directors :- H. C. Hammond, partner of Mr. Osier, president ; E. B. Osier, director of the Canadian Pacific Railway ; Senator Mclnnis, director of the Canadian Pacific Railway ; R. B. Angus, director of the Canadian Pacific Railway ; J. G. Ogden, comptroller of the Canadian Pacific Railway ; W. Sutherland Taylor, treasurer of the Canadian Pacific Railway ; and Charles Drinkwater, secretary of the Canadian Pacific Railway This company issued a prospectus through Morton, Rose & Co., of London, on July 18, 1889, asking the public to subscribe for $3,809,140 of its bonds at fi per cent. The following misleading paragraph appears in the prospectus :-
On February 1, 1896, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company will, on giving six months notice, have the power of calling in and paying off the above bonds at 110.
The ' Canada Gazette ' edited by Mr. Thomas Skinner, a London director of the Canadian Pacific Railway, a supposed authority on Canadian investments, published the prospectus, with tbe following editorial note (see page 376): 'It is taken for granted that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company will, at the end of six years, exercise its power to absorb the road, and in that case the payment of the bonds at 110 would, as a matter of course, follow.'
Mark you, 6 per cent at par, redeemable .by the Canadian Pacific Railway in six years at 110, took the investing public by storm. The bonds were readily sold, and were soon quoted on the London market at an advanced price. The prospectus also stated that the company had obtained from the government a cash subsidy of $80,000 a year for twenty years, and a land grant of 14,000,000 acres, to show that, independent of the railway, the company possessed large substantial assets.
It leaked .out some time afterwards that the Canadian Pacific Railway did not intend to redeem the bonds at 110, and therefore ' would not exercise its power to absorb the road'; that the Qu'Appelle, Long Lake and Saskatchewan Company had disposed of its land grant to another company, represented by Mr. Osier, under another corporate name ; that, in fact, the bondholders had nothing to fall back upon for their investment of $15,000 a mile but the road itself, without rolling stock or terminals: that the actual cost of constructing the road was about $1,500,000 less than the bondholders had advanced upon it, and down went the bonds on the London market from 110 to 30.
What about the poor widows and orphans who had purchased these bonds over in London? What about the financial standing of the hon. member for West Toronto, who now tells us -that subsidies to railways are a fruitful source of political corruption, and that no subsidies should Be given to any other road? A man who lives in a glass house should not throw stones.
Does the Canadian Pacific Railway now intend, or did it ever intend, ' to exercise its power to absorb the bonds at 110 ' ? It has a lease of the road from this generous Qu'Appelle Railway Company for six years without rental. If it never intended to redeem at 110, it could afford to run the road in such a manner for that period that net earnings would be nil. As a matter of fact, the service was so bad and rates so high that in some cases the people of Prince Albert have had to re-

sort to the old time ' ox-cart ' method of transportation. The settlement of the Prince Albert district has been seriously retarded in consequence, and the present settlers disheartened. The fact is, this roundabout road should never have been built, but instead thereof sufficient aid should have been given the Manitoba and North-western Railway to extend its line to Prince Albert. This, however, would not have suited the ' stock-jobbing ' propensities of Mr. Osier and his associates. No, the idea appears to be to wreck the Qu'Appelle Railway at the end of the six years' lease by ceasing operation, followed, in all probability, by default in payment of interest on the bonds, and the difference between ' exercising its power to absorb the road at 110 ' and what the road might bring under the hammer, which would probably be 10 minus the 100.
For fear it may be said that there is no authority for the assumption that it is proposed to cease operation of the road next year, I may say that I am credibly informed that the government has already received such an intimation, and I believe it is the first case of the kind on record in Canada. In view of the foregoing it is not refreshing to listen to the virtuous indignation of Mr. Osier, when he says :-
' I say without any hesitation that I consider tho result of the operation of this road for the last five or six years should of itself be a sufficient reason why the government should make no such grant to the Hudson's Bay Railway Company.
Is it not refreshing now for this lion, gentleman to get up and say no grant should be made to any future railway ? If this is not a stock-jobbing scheme let the kon. gentleman bring suit against Mr. Sutherland in the courts, as Mr. Sutherland is a responsible individual.
May I ask the kon. gentleman what he is reading from ?

I know the rule, Mr. Speaker, but It is in order to give the hon. member for West Toronto another opportunity of explaining this peculiar transaction that I was reading this letter. If this letter is not true the hon. gentleman ought to take action against Mr. Sutherland, the writer of this letter. I think I have read sufficient of it to show that Mr. Sutherland has made some peculiar statements, and if I were to go on and read the whole letter through as I might do, I would find that even stronger statements had been made. I do not know whether the term ' grafter ' should have been used or not, but it has been proven that there was a graft by somebody or that an enormous sum of money was made illegitimately out of this transaction. What could you call a man who participated in a transaction like that ? I have seen it stated in the press that if a poor devil steals a coat to keep himself warm he is called a thief, but if he steals $3,000,000 or $4,000,000 he is called a Napoleon of finance. Probably the word ' grafter ' is supposed to come in there. However, there is no doubt about it that there was a large amount of money received from the people for a consideration that never was given, for a railway that



never turned a wheel, for a streak of rust across the prairie, one line to Prince Albert and another to Edmonton. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that this discussion has taken a very considerable range and that it might have been a great deal shorter. What strikes me particularly is the extreme indulgence of the right lion, leader of the government (Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier). He is the most indulgent man I ever saw in connection with the rules of debate in this House, and all I can say is that if he were a father confessor he would enjoy in our church a very great reputation. As a matter of fact it narrows itself down to this : What were the words used by my hon. friend (Mr. Scott) and why is it that these words have not been withdrawn, or why is it that it was not suggested by the right hon. leader of the House that the hon. gentleman should purely and simply withdraw them ? It is quite easy to understand that in the heat of debate when advancing an argument such as my hon. friend was advancing he should go a little beyond the bounds. That is natural but what seems a little strange is that after the statements, most unwarrantable and I should say insulting, made by the hon. gentleman have been denied and which he made in the absence of my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Osier) he should not simply have withdrawn the improper expressions used. I ha.ve no doubt that if your honour at the present moment suggests to my hon. friend the propriety of withdrawing these expressions he would willingly do so. What was it that my hon.| friend said ?
Is it not perfectly fair, Mr. Speaker, that in considering this proposition we should compare it with the legislation placed upon the statute-books of this country in years gone by by the Conservative government ? Now, as I pointed out, on these two little deals, these two little railways, comprising about 550 miles, somebody was allowed to get away improperly with $15,303,891. My hon. friend from West Elgin will remember that one evening here he read a letter from1 some one in Vancouver, I think, who said he would like to see one of these individuals spoken of as grafters. It seems to me that if we could put our finger on the gentleman who got away with these $15,000,000 we would find a grafter under our finger' Now,
I would advise my hon. friend from West Elgin to cast his eye down to the seat just four rows in front of him, to the seat of the hon. junior member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) and he will see-or he would see, because the seat is vacant at the present moment-he would see, if the seat was filled by its member, one of Ihese grafters who, by himself and his associates, got away with this sum of 15,000,000 odd dollars.
Mr. McCreary.
After tlie attention of my hon. friend had been called by some bon. members of this House to the gravity of these charges, be went on as follows :
I will make a further statement, and make it upon my responsibility, that the hon. member for Centre Toronto-I do not want to make any mistake, I will name him-Mr. Osier, is one of the gentlemen who is implicated in this matter. I do not blame him at all. The individuals in this company are not expected to work for their health. When they go into railway enterprises they are going to make all the money they can out of them. I am not throwing any aspersion upon the hon. member for West Toronto ; but I am calling to the attention of this parliament and the people of this country the kind of legislation that the Conservative party put through when they were in power, and the kind of legislation which enabled their friends to get away with an amount of money like this.
As I understand getting away with and improperly taking away money are expressions which cast very severe aspersions and when added to that is the term 'grafter,' as far as I understand that term, the aspersions become an absolute insult. My bon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Osier) contradicted that statement this morning. He gave an explanation as to what part he took in carrying out this transaction, and he denied absolutely that he was one of the promoters of this company. Then my hon. friend from Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis), whose interference in the debate is the cause of its prolongation ; he called attention to the land deals, and we found that my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Osier) had merely acted as trustee for the sale of that land, and that he was associated in that trust with Lord Strathcona, a man whose reputation is world-wide, and with Mr. Richard B. Angus, one of the most honourable public men and honest citizens of Montreal. Any aspersion cast upon my hon. friend (Mr. Osier) falls equally upon those who acted as co-trustees with him in the transaction, which is here denounced as a piece of scoundrelism by the hon. gentleman from Saskatchewan. Under these circumstances, it seems to me that the summing up of the right hon. Prime Minister was scarcely calculated to give that high tone to the debate, which according to the statement of the Minister of Public Works, has been abandoned in this House for some time. of the people's money ; if we are allowed to apply these expressions to men occupying the position of the hon. gentleman from West Toronto (Mr. Osier) and to such men as Lord Strathcona, who at present occupies a high position in official life under this government, and to men of the high standing of Mr. R. B. Angus ; if we are allowed to do that without any check from those in authority, then what is to be the limit of decent discussion here ? The Minister of Public Works stated that the well-known rules of debate have been departed from, and he instanced the case of Senator Cox. I have heard no man in this House on either side, make any such charge against Senator Cox, as was made by the member for Assiniboia against my hon. friend (Mr. Osier). It is true that the saying has been invented and has become popularized that ' Cox can't wait,' but I submit there is nothing in that expression as it has been used-and I do not know it has been used by any member of this House-which conveys anything like the aspersion that was contained in the words of the hon. member (Mr. Scott). If these expressions of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Scott) were used in the heat of debate,, that might be pardonable, and it will be sufficient for you, Mr. Speaker, to insist on the hon. gentleman withdrawing them in order that an end may be put to this discussion.

Mr. Speaker, before the Orders of the Day are called, I would like to ask the right hon. leader of the government if he can give me any information with respect to a matter to which my attention has been called. A despatch from Toronto advises me :

Might I ask the right hon. gentleman if it is the intention of this government to adopt a similar course to that which has been adopted by the United States government, and to send a summary of the Canadian case to the Associated Press for distribution among the newspapers of this country ?

Our case has been before the public for four or five weeks

already. I have myself seen, and my hon. friend cannot have failed also to have seen, several articles on the Canadian case as presented to the commissioners. 1 am not aware that anybody has taken the trouble up to this time of having a summary of it made. That is a matter that has not been referred to ns. It has been left to the enterprise of the Canadian newspapers.

Before the Orders of the Day are called, Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask you if it is in accordance with the rules of this House to declare a motion carried when an hon. gentleman is on his feet to address the House ?
I suppose I am not obliged to give an answer to a categorical question like that.	_
It is a small piece of business.

Mr. Speaker, before the Orders of the Day are called, I would like to ask my right hon. friend for information on a matter of some importance. It has been stated throughout the country, and mentioned with some show of authority in newspapers which at first approved of the government's transcontinental railway scheme, that a modification had taken place in the views of the government, and that a portion of that scheme would be withdrawn. Some said that the eastern section would be withdrawn, and others that other portions would be withdrawn, at any rate for the present. In view of these statements, and in view of the fact that we are at present occupied with the study of that important measure, I think it is proper to ask if the government intend to abandon or divert any part of the scheme, or in any way to modify the measure which is now under our consideration. Some parties have stated that the Quebec-Moncton section would be abandoned. My right hon. friend will also have noticed that elsewhere it has been stated that the Quebec-Winnipeg section would be abandoned. It is proper under these circumstances that we should seek information from the government on these important matters.

Mr. Speaker, I have had occasion before to remark to my
hon. friend that he is altogether too credulous of newspaper reports. I am sure it does not require from me any derogation of such rumours; but since the hon. gentleman has put the question, I have only to tell him now that the ' government understand their duty better than to abandon any part of their scheme. They would be recreant to their duty if they did so, and the whole scheme will have to be dealt with as it has been put before the House.

Mr. Speaker, I am recorded in the Votes and Proceedings of Tuesday as having voted for and against the amendment of Mr. Puttee. I would like that to be corrected. I voted for the amendment, but not against it.

My attention was called to that mistake yesterday. If the hon. gentleman will look at the Votes and Proceedings of this day, he will see that it has been corrected in an erratum. The hon. gentleman is mentioned as having voted for the amendment.

On section 2,

When the House rose yesterday, we were discussing the question of the cost of carrying the produce of the North-west to the sea-board. The speech of the First Minister has been printed and I understand it is ready for circulation. In that speech I notice this reference to the cost of transportation :
'We consider that it is the duty of all those who sit within these walls by the will of the people, to provide immediate means whereby the products of these new settlers may find an exit to the ocean.
And then come these words which are capitalized :
At the least possible cost.
He said in another place :
For one or two or three generations at least, perhaps more, these new settlers will grow cereals probably and nothing else.
Evidently the Prime Minister was of the opinion that the chief freight which would go to the sea-board over this route would be cereals, the wheat of the North-west. We have had some discussion regarding the cost of carrying wheat. I have taken the stand that wheat cannot be carried over that long rail route to compete with the roads now in existence, and I take it for granted that had the government been convinced of that fact, it would not have gone into the eastern part of this scheme. There is no evidence to show that grain can be carried over this proposed road-which practically parallels the water route for a considerable distance, although many miles away-in competition with the water route,

and the combined rail and water route. The general opinion of shippers in this country and in the United States is that our great St. Lawrence system, beginning at the Straits of Belle Isle and ending at the head of the great lakes, is a wonderful one. Grain can be carried from the head of the lakes to Buffalo at one cent a bushel. It can be carried in vessels capable of holding 250,000 bushels ; and there are at Buffalo excellent means of loading and unloading. It can then be carried through the canals, now that they are fourteen feet deep for two cents per bushel. I believe that it can be carried to Quebec at from 3 to 31 cents per bushel profitably. Something was said by the hoD. member for Missisquoi (Mr. Meigs) about the canals being out of date. Well, there are canals and canals. There are canals which are not in operation, and there is a vast difference between canals connecting two great bodies of water like the two canals at Sault Ste. Marie, or the Welland, or the St. Lawrence canals, connecting these great stretches of inland water, and a shallow canal through a country in which there are no such natural water-ways as our great lakes, so that we must consider the existing conditions ; we must not lose sight of the great lakes, in discussing this question. I would like to impress upon the First Minister that one of the most important questions in connection with this projected road is the question of carrying the products of the North-west at a cheap rate. If this new road will carry grain and pay 3 per cent, it is going to do something that is entirely contradicted by present statistics, and we ought to have some information to show how it is going to do it. Reference has been made to a statement of Sir William Van Horne, and a certain amount of prejudice is attached to what he says, because he is the head of the Canadian Pacific Railway. At the same time we must admit that he made a straight statement ; and I believe it to be true. At any rate the government thought highly enough of his opinion to try and secure his services as chairman of the transportation commission. What Sir Wiliam Van Horne said is this :
Sir William Van Horne, in an interview today regarding the Grand Trunk Pacific scheme, said that in his opinion the solution of the transportation problem, as affecting the chief products of the North-west to the sea-board was the betterment.and cheapening of the cheapest route, the lake and rail-route, with which no railway, neither the Canadian Pacific nor any railway north of the great lakes could hop? to compete in cost, for rail lines could only compete with water lines where they have the advantage in distance and where working conditions are most favourable.
He made another statement very similar.
It is not my intention to offer any obstruction to this Bill, but yesterday we spent the whole day without profit because there Mr. KEMP.
were questions asked of the government, and somehow or other the discussion ran wild and before the questions were answered hon. gentlemen on both sides brought up other issues, and the point on which information was demanded was lost sight of. The question I desire to put has regard to the cost of carrying grain. The Order in Council of the 27th of May clearly makes this point:
The conditions with regard to the navigation of the St. Lawrence route, and, generally, any Improvements, enlargements or other matters affecting the more economical and satisfactory uses of any Canadian channel of transportation by land or water.
The minister further states that in making such investigation attention should net he confined to routes and facilities which are at present utilized, but, if necessary, new surveys should be made to determine whether any more economical and satisfactory channels of transportation by land or water can be opened up.
Then the Order in Council points out that among the forces operating against the attainment of all-Canadian transportation are :
Competition by United States vessels from Lake Superior ports ;
Diversion of Canadian products through eastern outlets to Boston, Portland and other United States ports, should he investigated, and the best and most economical methods used by our competitors should he carefully studied and reported upon.
I take it- that by this Minute it was intended to determine what is the most economical means of transporting the products of the west to the sea-board, and what I ask is what information the government have on this point. There are mountains of information, we are told, but this is the essential point. Will the hon. minister say that this road will be able to earn 3 per cent on the investment and carry grain in competition with existing railways.
We have been debating this measure for three weeks. The point brought up by the hon. gentleman has been brought up and discussed time and again.
Fifty times.

At least, and we have not been able to convince my hon. friend, and I am afraid that anything I can say will not convince him.
Mr.. KEMP. Oh, yes.

I am afraid he is past conviction. This is one of the questions on which we cannot agree, and the only way of solving it is a vote. Perhaps we are in the wrong, but I believe that we are in the right. Let me tell my hon. friend something which, I think, will convince him that he is in the wrong, and it is this. Comparing always water transportation with railway transportation and suggesting that

railway transportation is an alternative to water transportation. It is nothing of the kind. Because we propose this measure, because we intend to implement it and to put it into operation, we do not do so with a view to doing away with the system of water transportation. Water transportation will have to go on in the future, happily for the country, as it has in the past. The thing which we wish to impress on the country is this-and I would like also to impress this on my hon. friend (Mr. Kemp) who has just spoken and on all those who think with him on that subject-that water transportation as it exists to-day is not sufficient for the needs of the country and that it must be supplemented by other transportation, by railway transportation. What have we to-day under the existing system ? As soon as the crop is harvested, from this month, September, until the crop is harvested and threshed, until the close of navigation there will be a rush to take the wheat from the wheat fields to the head of Lake Superior in order to store it there to ship it as soon as possible to the sea-board. This rush will last for one, two or three months, September, October and November ; then the farmers will have to wait from December. when navigation is closed, until next spring, before they can again resume their shipments. That is an abnormal position for the people of the west, it is an abnormal position for the people of the east. It is abnormal for the people of the west in this, that the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian Northern Railway, which has just come into operation, are not able to secure enough rolling stock to accommodate the shipments of wheat. It is obnoxious to the people of the east because for these three months they are starved of rolling stock and are told by the railway companies :	We
have transferred all our rolling stock to the west in order to transfer the crop to the head of Lake Superior. Therefore we have a condition which is abnormal and which is not satisfactory to the country, and we want, as far as we can, to relieve that condition of things and to make possible the transportation of wheat not only in the summer, but in winter as well. My hon. friend from North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton), who I claim is an expert in these matters-
Some lion. MEMBERS. Oh, oh.

Yes. My hon. friend is an expert and I do not know a greater authority either in this House or outside of it. If there is one man in this House who can speak with authority on this question of transportation, it is my hon. friend from North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) and I make no exception.
Would my right lion, friend permit me

If we want to make any progress we must adhere to the
rules of debate. I have been told to-day that I have been too lax as leader of the government to enforce the rules of debate ;
I have profited by the lesson and therefore I will apply them to my hon. friend (Mr. Clancy).
My hon. friend from North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) told us yesterday that we have not seen the last of the development of railway transportation. My hon. friend has told us that perhaps at no distant date it will be possible for railway transportation not only to compete with water transportation but to overcome and overtake it. This to me, whatever it may be to gentlemen on the other side of the House, is not an improbable contingency. When we look upon the record of railway development during the last twenty years, and especially during the last ten years we must come to the conclusion that the statement made yesterday by my hon. friend from North Norfolk is not at all over-sanguine. It is not impossible to hope and suppose that at no distant date railways will be able to compete with water-ways in the transportation of products. At the present time in the transportation of wheat water-ways have an advantage. Why ? On account of the facilities for elevating the wheat from the railways to the barges and from the barges to the railways again. But so far, for instance, as packing freight is concerned I believe that there is reason to state that at this moment the railways can compete successfully with water routes and this will not be denied. Twenty years ago this would not have been possible, but, it is true at this moment on account of the great improvements that have been made in railway operation. My hon. friend (Mr. Charlton) claims that with the improvement of grades, with the improvement of rails, with the improvement of engines, the time will come when railway transportation will overtake and overcome water transportation. We look forward to this time ; I cannot say we are certain of it, but we hope and believe it will come. We cannot be content to allow the present condition of things to continue. I have described the position as it is to-day. The wheat grower of the west who has not disposed of his crop before the 1st of December, before the 15th of December at the latest, will have to wait until next spring before lie can take advantage of the market.
Oh, oh.

My hon. friend could not do otherwise. He could ship a part of his crop to Lake Superior but he could not get it further. Railway transportation will come to his rescue. Even today it is possible for the Canadian Pacific Railway, not to a large extent, but to some extent, to carry wheat around Lake Superior. I would ask hon. gentlemen on the other side how long is it since the Canadian

Pacific Railway lias been able to carry wlieat from Winnipeg around the north shore of Lake Superior ? It is less than five years, if I am correctly informed and I think I am, since they commenced to carry wheat from the wheat fields all-rail to St. John. They are doing that now to some extent although not to as great an extent as they would like, because the condition of their line is such that they cannot do it to advantage. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) some days ago advanced a scheme to buy the Canadian Pacific Railway from North Bay to Fort William in order to make it a common highway for transportation. He did not propose to use it as it is, but to improve it and to make it possible to use it as a highway to carry grain from the head of Lake Superior to the maritime provinces. That is the plan of the hon. leader of the opposition, a plan approved of as I understand by my hon. friend from Toronto to buy the Canadian Pacific Railway from North Bay to Fort William and even to improve this line, to blast the rocks along the rocky shore of Lake Superior and to improve the road-bed of the Canadian Pacific Railway line, to overcome the gradients, to straighten the curves and thus to make it a grain road.
So far so good. But then I have an answer to my hon. friend from Toronto. If it was a good plan of the leader of the opposition to (suggest the propriety of buying the Canadian Pacific Railway's line from North Bay to Fort William and then to improve it, it is a better plan, I think, by far to build a line over a better section of country to do the very same thing and to make it a grain route. My boil, friend (Mr. Kemp) wants to know if we are able to fix the rate which will be charged on the new line to-day. I am sorry to say we cannot fix the rate to-day, that is too much to expect from us, and I do not think his question is serious. The fixing of the rates will depend largely on the economy of construction, the gradients and curves we will be able to obtain and the character of the road that will lie built.
ill1. BROCK. Why commit yourself until you do know ?

Mr. Speaker, because we know of the character to come to a conclusion. My hon. friend is not open to conviction upon that. I told my hon. friend the other day that there were mountains of information on this subject. I do not think I do him an injury-and if I do I will be willing to apologize-by saying that I do not think he has approached any of these mountains to obtain information. I do not think he wants to be informed and he believes that the character of this country is such as not to afford us a good route. But we have information which will suffice to enable us to publish in Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
a few days a pamphlet based upon official reports and upon nothing else in which it will be shown that for two-thirds or three-fourths of the distance between Quebec and the west the country is a plateau as level as the valley of the St. Lawrence from Quebec to Montreal. So, I say, we have there the character of road that we desire to have. When we have done that we will have relieved the farmers of the North-west to a large extent. It is not only wheat that will be carried over this road. I will tell my hon. friend one thing as a manufacturer-and I hope that we shall carry a good deal of his own goods over that railway-I believe that we shall be able to do a great deal for the manufacturers of Canada by the construction of that road. My hon. friend represents the class of manufacturers, a very worthy class, and I believe that if there is one class who ought to be in favour of this railway it is the manufacturers, because it will afford them a competing line with an existing road to take their goods to the west. The west will be in need of all their goods, and as return freight it will be possible for that railway to take wheat from the North-west to the harbour of St. John. This is the information which I have to give to my hon. friend, and I think it will commend itself to the judgment and the sound sense of every member of this House.
Mr. Chairman
I would like to hear from my hon. friend from Toronto Centre (Mr. Brock).

I will be glad to let the Premier hear from me. We have had, what is for him, a long speech on this question, every word of which condemns his own scheme. If he has information-and I have no doubt he would not say so if he had not-if he has information upon which contractors and engineers can build a road from Moncton to Winnipeg, with the grades insisted upon by the gentleman who he says is the greatest transportation authority in this country, if he has information that a road with those grades can be built, then I think lie condemns himself and his whole scheme, because one of the great features of his scheme is that it cannot wait, it cannot wait even for information. With the information which he says he has now, he feels that he is justified in forcing this road upon the country and in forcing this contract upon the company. If he has the information which he says he has, he should have gone back to that Minute in Council, and should have been willing to submit this question to those commissioners whom he has appointed for this very purpose. Blit before he commits this country to an immense expenditure of money, particularly under the circumstances that he has stated just now, if he has information that that

plateau at tlie north side of the height of land is of such a level nature and of such a character that he can huild a road such as has been described as absolutely necessary by that gentleman whom he quotes as the greatest authority in this country-if he has got that information, I say that he can afford to wait, X say that this country will be willing to wait. What I would urge upon the government at the present time is that they should wait ; and that they should submit this contract to the tribunal which they have appointed for the very purpose of forming a judgment upon the information that the Premier says he has got. Now I would be diffident to set up my opinion against that of the distinguished gentleman whom he relies upon. I have made a statement in this House, and I am prepared to stand by it, that I have Information regarding the building of a road north of the old line from Toronto to James bay, to the effect that that country over the height of land where their road is going to run is of such a nature that there is no intention at the present time of building that road, either by the city of Toronto, or by any company, or by anybody else. They are anxious of course to meet the Canadian Pacific Railway road, they are anxious to build to that point.
But where is the company going to get its business from, where is it going to get any local business, that is the life-blood of 'any road either in Canada or in the United States ? Does my hon. friend mean to say that any prudent railway men expect to make money and to pay dividends without doing any local business at all ? Why are they so anxious to fill up the intervening country with population ? It is because it will furnish local business out of which the railroad company may make their dividends. It may be said that in this case, there is probably no thought of dividends. I think the company may abandon all thought of dividends and the government may abandon all thought of interest out of this road, because if I understand this matter aright this road has been forced upon the Grand Trunk Pacific people. It was not contemplated by them in the first place. The best judgment of the managers of that company was to build the road from North Bay through to the Pacific ocean. That was their intention, that was their first thought, and we often find in many other matters besides railroading that first thoughts are the best. But these things that came afterwards forced the new scheme upon them. B,ut I do not believe the Grand Trunk Pacific are going to lose anything by agreeing to do what they have agreed to do. I have this much faith in the intelligence of the directors of that company, that they would rather throw this road up and throw it upon the government, than have to work it when the government insist upon their 3 per cent interest being
paid-I am speaking of that portion of the road from Winnipeg to Moncton. Now let me tell the Premier wtyat 1 think would be a business-like thing to do at the present time. I know it means the pocketing of a good deal of pride, I know it will mean taking a certain amount of back water, but I contend that if we should be actuated by patriotic motives, and I contend that our hon. Premier is actuated by what he thinks to be the best interests of the country, although he is too liable sometimes to lean upon dangerous reeds. He refers to a state-men made yesterday by an hon. gentleman that wheat could be drawn by that road in competition with water or any other means. But that gentleman has made a variety of statements on this subject, and we do not know to which one he wishes to adhere. But judging from that hon. gentleman's reed'd for the last eight or ten years, if I was going to build a railroad or anything else that was going to cost millions of dollars and was going to take several years to build, I would hesitate very much before relying upon that hon. gentleman's opinion given at any particular time, because he would change his mind at least once or more during the period. I think the Premier, instead of taking the advice of so great an authority as the member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton), would do better to take the great railroad men into his confidence. I would prefer, speaking for myself, to leave the decision of this question in the hands of the Railway Commission that the Premier has nominated, I would turn the matter over to them even now, even though some of them may be committed to the present scheme. Because I believe in the honesty of these gentlemen, and when they have the evidence before them that the Premier speaks of, and the other evidence that they will collect, if they should recommend this road, the Premier will find just as strong supporters of that scheme on this side of the House as there is on the other side. But I think, the Premier is wrong. He must not venture to think for a moment that all the patriotism is on the other side of the House. That has not been the opinion of the people of this country, who entrusted the Conservative party with the duty of building the Canadian Pacific Railway, and they did build it. Fault may be found, fault has been found, and will continue to be found with the Canadian Pacific Railway. But will the road that the right hon. gentleman is shoving through this House with railroad speed, escape fault being found with it after it is built ? That road has got to be run after it is built. What about the snowfall, wbat about filling up the puttings in that part of the road hundreds of miles away from civilization ? It will not be in the same position as the Grand Trunk Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway, in the midst of a large population. That road

has got to be run many hundreds of miles through a country without a vestige of habitation. This is a very serious matter. Then you may have accidents on that road, and a number of passengers may be killed or injured. Look at the position you will be in. Where are you going to have your central stations ? Look at the expense of maintaining stations in that country. Why, Sir, it will cost double to run and maintain that road through that country after It is built, than it will to build it.
Your chance of getting 3 per cent has vanished into thin air. I contend that the road is absolutely discredited in the minds of people who are best able to judge. If this is going to be forced through at the present time, if you are going to force it just as you are going to force the grain afterwards up hill, you will have as much difficulty in one case as you will in the other. I want to allude to my bon. friend on my left (Mr. Meigs), who made a most businesslike and straightforward appeal. I saw that it took with the right hon. gentleman, and it was to him very convincing. My hon. friend had run a canal boat somewhere on Lake Champlain thirty years ago, and the moment a railway was built through the country that gentleman sold out, or may be he gave his boat away. I would suppose that he would give it away for nothing if it was of so very little value. However, whether he gave it away or whether he sold it, he got out of the business land ran away. I was brought up on the banks of a river which had a navigation system -the Grand river. There was the Grand river navigation system, which my hon. friend the Minister of Customs (Hon. Mr. Paterson) will know about. The railway was built and the company went out of business, and why ? Because the people interested in it did as a lot of men do, instead of, in a manly way, standing up and trying to compete with the railway by improving their canals and works, they closed up the business and ran. Is that an example for this' great Dominion ? Is that something that this country should do ?
What would you have done if you had been losing money ?
I would have made a great deal better attempt than they made to meet the opposition.
You would have sold out like any one else.

This country has invested in a great many enterprises. This is not the only one. We have several enterprises on our hands at the present time and the *government are paying $500,000 a year over and above working expenses to carry on one of these enterprises. The Pacific cable. I suppose, was a patriotic institution-
Order, order.

Mr. BROCK-which was forced upon this country. The right hon. gentleman, I see, does not like to hear about it. Ways'and means have to be found to build this railway that we are talking about. We have to get the money. I do not think we can get it in this country. We will have to go to England or some other country for it. We will have to raise an enormous amount of money in the next few years, necessary to replace the money that we have already borrowed at very high rate and the money that we require to build this railway. We are going to the money market very much discredited, after having gone with this scheme which falls short of paying its operating expenses by $500,000 a year, a scheme which was forced upon this country with so much enthusiasm, and we are now showing our patriotism by sending a message a day over the cable. Let us be careful that this present scheme is not going to get a black eye as that has done. We are not a wealthy people. We are a poor struggling people, making our way by economy and care, making our way because we meet business requirements as they occur. lret, here is an attempt being made to force a scheme upon the country that cannot pretend to give the relief that hon. gentlemen opposite claim it will give for at least six or seven years. Hon. gentlemen opposite are in a great hurry to have the scheme forced upon the country and to get a snap verdict, largely upon the great and deserved popularity of the right hon. Prime Minister. But from popularity we have to come down to business, because this money has to be raised in the old country. I do not think of going to the old country, or of writing letters in the ' North American Review,' or of doing anything of that kind to injure this country, but I contend that the action we are taking in this matter will injure the credit of the country in the markets of Europe. It has been so ill-advised and it has been so hurried, taking into account the minute of council that was issued with the knowledge of the right hon. leader of the government, laying down certain platforms and making certain statement entirely different from the arrangement which .it is now sought to force through parliament, that it will not be a surprise to us if our credit is destroyed or injured so that to the amount of money that this road is supposed to cost us will have to be added one-thiru.
I did make the statement that the money will cost us 4 per cent, and I should not be surprised if it does cost us that, thereby entailing a serious loss upon this country. Why should not the government be perfectly willing to leave this matter in the hands of the commission they have appointed for the purpose of dealing with such business and let them ascertain the facts and place them before the House ? I can assure the right hon. leader of the government that if they report in favour of the scheme the

members on this side of the House will give it careful consideration.

I would like to ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Brock) if he has ever expressed himself as being in favour of what was the Grand Trunk Railway's original scheme of building a road from North Bay to Winnipeg?
That was not the original scheme. The original scheme was to build a road from North Bay to north of Lake Winnipeg and Port Simpson. Winnipeg was not mentioned in the original scheme.

Would the hon. gentleman tell us the towns, cities and inhabited portions of the territory between North Bay and Port Simpson to be traversed by this line, and would he say how long the road is between North Bay and Winnipeg ? He has talked about the line being 1,800 miles from Moncton. Would that uot be about 1,100 miles of that same road that he is in favour of and that he has spoken in favour of?

The hon. gentleman is very anxious to make out a case. He is taking a great deal for granted. I did not express approval of the road from North Bay to Winnipeg. The statement came out in the ' Gloibe ' from Mr. Hays and Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson that it was the intention of the Grand Trunk Railway people to build that road, and I said it would be a great advantage if they would do it because it would open up a new country, but would the hon. gentleman name the cities and towns between Quebec and Winnipeg this this line is going to touch ? He asks me to name the towns along the line that I expressed my approbation of and which was to be built by the old Grand Trunk Railway Company. Would he name the towns between Quebec and Winnipeg that this line is going to serve? There is the w'hole case. I can appeal to hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House. I say the time will come, if hon. gentlemen persist in pushing this scheme through, when they will rue it very much indeed. I only intended to make a few remarks, but the right hon. gentleman was kind enough to suggest that I should make a few remarks and I have briefly done so.

I was speaking in all kindness to the hon. gentleman. He says that the railway from Quebec to Winnipeg goes through an uninhabited country. He says there is no trade for it, and he asked me what towns and cities it would pass through, which at present are existing. We say that towns and cities would spring up as a result of this. If that be the objection to our scheme,
I want to know why the hon. gentleman (Mr. Brock) said that the Grand Trunk scheme from North Bay to Winnipeg
I beg pardon.
Well, to Port Simpson-but the hon. gentleman understood it was going to Winnipeg.

No, they spoke of building a branch north of Lake Winnipeg to Port Simpson. Do not lose sight of the fact, that I did not understand then that the government of the country were going to finance the scheme. I understood it was to be done by the Grand Trunk Pacific themselves. I am very much afraid that the Prime Minister is being seriously misled by just such statements as that made by the Minister of Customs. I am objecting to rushing into this country until we have absolute knowledge of the engineering difficulties, and as to whether it is possible to get these grades which the hon. member for North Norfolk speaks of. This country will demand that information and it will get that information yet, and it may be a surprise-I won't say to every gentleman opposite-but it will be certainly a surprise to the leader of the government.
We will have to put up with it.

I again ask the question. Has not the hon. member (Mr. Brock) said, that the Grand Trunk should receive a bonus for building the road from North Bay to Winnipeg, but not over the prairie section ? Now, then, having said that, he objects to the government's scheme because there is no traffic at present on the route between, we will say, North Bay and Quebec. It is about 1,100 miles from North Bay to Winnipeg, and it has only three or four hundred miles further to go to Quebec, therefore the hon. gentleman (Mr. Brock) is approving of building 1,100 miles of this road.
He approved of the building of it by the Grand Trunk Railway Company.

These gentlemen opposite are changing their ground again. What has it got to do with the location of the line, who builds it ? There were no more towns and cities on that line under the scheme proposed by the Grand Trunk than under our scheme. The best railway men we have in the country, tiie Grand Trunk Railway, proposed to build the 1,100 miles between North Bay and Winnipeg out of the 1.400 between Quebec and Winnipeg, and yet the hon. gentleman is afraid of this whole scheme, although he has only refused to sanction the 300 miles from North Bay to Quebec.
Three hundred miles from North Bay to Quebec.
Three hundred or four hundred miles.
I am bound to think that the Minister of Customs is making it a point to misrepresent me.
I have no (iesire to do that whatever.

I never stated that I was in favour of the government lending aid to build the Grand Trunk system of railway between North Bay and Winnipeg. But when I was told they were going north of Lake Winnipeg, I said that entering as they were a new country, it was a matter of consideration whether the government would not be justified in assisting them over that portion of the road, which was not on the prairies. I do not require to go very far to condemn this scheme. The Minister of the Interior probably knows more about it than all the other ministers put together, and he has stated that there are 400 miles of that country even between Winnipeg and Quebec, that will for all time be unfit for agricultural purposes.
That is the portion the Grand Trunk Railway were going through.

Wait now ; you cannot draw any red-herring across the track this time. The company said that with a view of reaching the Pacific they were going to extend their line, not the government line, by the Grand Trunk line. They didn't mention the day they would get to the Pacific, and when I expressed that opinion it was certainly understood that the road was to be financed by the company and not by the government. A great deal of ridicule was attempted to be heaped on the member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) in relation to his statement as to the amount of capitalization that would be represented by that road in the course of fifty years. But the hon. gentleman only gave his own experience, and the experience of other roads in this country. The original capitalization of the Intercolonial Railway was about .$21,000,000, and now it is about $73,000,000, so that it has multiplied by three in twenty-five years. I tell you that somebody is going to lose by this Grand Trunk Pacific road from Winnipeg to Quebec, and somebody has to pay the daily and weekly and yearly loss on the running of that road. Who is going to pay that loss ?
The Grand Trunk.

Do not make any mistake about that. It is the people of this country who will pay that loss. When we want to prove that our country is prosperous we cite the profits made by a railroad and the converse of that proposition is true. *If it can be shown that this road, for even ten years, does not pay for the grease to oil the wheels, what kind of an affect will that have in England when we go to float other loans for public projects in this country ?

Suppose that we should want money to improve our water-ways, and our ports, and our canal system, what will be the effect on the money market when it is known that the government has such a poor opinion of their own railway project, that they don't think it will pay interest for ten years ? I contend that the scheme which they are now propounding will bring discredit on the country, and the discredit that the member for North Norfolk attaches to it in regard to its want of stability, is one of the worst troubles connected with the whole business.

The discussion that has taken place to-day has been so animated that some hon. members have almost got on their muscle. I had the pleasure of listening to the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) and the hon. member for St. Mary's (Hon. Mr. Tarte) discussing the feasibility of transportation by water ns compared with transportation by rail. The hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Brock) tries now to make out that the government is resting its whole case on the cheap transportation of wheat, and other bulky products from Winnipeg to the sea-board. I take issue with the hon. gentleman (Mr. Brock) on that. The Prime Minister has explained the position of the government in that respect, and I also take issue with the right hon. gentleman when he says, that either at this date or at a future date, railways will compete with water transportation. I do not believe they ever will, in our time or in the time of the next generation anyway. It is against nature that they could. I am too practical a business man and have too much experience to believe anything of the kind.
My hon. friend the ex-Minister of Public Works says it can be defended for colonization purposes. So it can ; but still he throws cold water on the scheme. It can be defended. It will open up and develop a country that is now undeveloped. There will be Wheat grown in that country more approximate to the east which can be moved by rail : but when it is said that the Canadian Pacific or any other railway will move bulky freight such as wheat from the North-west to the seaboard to the advantage of the producers, I take no stock in that statement. It will more properly apply to all classes of freight except bulky products of the country, which must be moved by water. I say that the scheme of the Ottawa and Georgian bay canal is a proper scheme. That scheme was approved of by Hon. Alexander Mackenzie and by Sir John Macdonald, and they were sound in their views; and I am surprised at the hon. member for Missisquol (Mr. Meigs) getting up and saying that he had some experience of water transportation, and that because some railway was constructed to parallel the water stretches on which he was doing his boating business, he had forsooth to

throw up the sponge and went out of business. Well, Sir, he had not much pluck. When I had competition in business, I fought it and generally succeeded. Competition is the life of trade. I am sorry my hon. friend takes such little stock in water transportation. He says building canals is money thrown away. That is not the experience of France, Germany, the United States or even Canada. Hon. gentlemen have advocated the St. Lawrence water-route. I am sorry that they appear to have overlooked the great advantages which this Canada of ours is going to derive from the construction of the Ottawa and Georgian bay canal. Sir, I am astonished at such sectionalism, such selfishness. Perhaps that expression is too strong, but I am afraid their leaning is a little in that direction. I am sorry that they do not look at this question in a broad, patriotic way as Canadians. If they did, I think all hands would join me in this scheme. I have not lost faith in the present administration. They move pretty rapidly. The engineers, from Walter Shanly, in 1856, down to McLeod, in 1900, have reported in favour of this scheme. They say there are no insurmountable physical features, and Mr. Wisner, an eminent engineer from the United States, has estimated that it will not cost over $80,000,000. That is based on surveys already made, and is for a depth of 20 feet of water ; and Mr. McLeod, in revising the estimates of Mr. Wisner, says he is $7,000,000 above the mark. The hon. member for St. Mary's (Hon. Mr. Tarte) spoke very enthusiastically in my county in favour of that project, and in favour of improving the French river immediately. But, Sir, in his addresses in this House during the present session, he has not spoken so strongly on that subject, though he says it is well enough to improve the French river as far as North Bay. Some hon. members have said that he was satisfied so long as he could make connection there with the Canadian Pacific Railway. I do not know what they meant by that. Then he tried to alarm the House by saying that the expenditure from North Bay east would be very considerable, and that we could make no proper calculation of the cost. But the hon. gentleman is not an engineer any more than I am. We must pay some regard to the statements of the engineers who have exploi'ed the route and made the estimates ; and I believe that now, with the improved manner of tunnelling and excavating rock, we can construct the Ottawa and Georgian bay canal for less than $80,000,000. Even if we cannot, and if it should cost $40,000,000 more, it would be money well invested by this country for having such a means of transporting the bulky products of the country, and opening up the deposits of wealth which we have along the route. These things cannot be moved by rail; it would cost too much to move them. If wheat were moved by rail
from Winnipeg, the cost of transporting it would eat everything up, so that there would not be much left for the farmer. The Ottawa and Georgian bay canal would solve all these problems. I did not intend to say anything to-day, but when I saw hon. members of this House in rich fighting humour, I thought I should take a hand in.

There are two things which have come out very prominently in this debate to-day. We have had the acknowledgment of the right hon. the First Minister that the shippers of this country would pay for the blunders of the scheme now before us. That is a statement on which we may lay fair emphasis. My hon. friend beside me tells me that it will be the wheat grower, the toiler, who will pay for them. The shipper will pay in the first instance, and the farmer ultimately; that is what it means by a very easy translation. We have also the right hon. First Minister relying on the horn, member for North Norfolk as the authority for that statement. No one doubts the hon. member for North Norfolk's ability. We	are told	that he	isan expert,	which is	a very	apt term.The hon.	gentleman	is an	expert	atturning corners. I would like to ask the right	hon. the	First Minister	if
he has any more assurance that the hon. member for North Norfolk will not change his opinion on this question before the session closes-because it would take some days yet-than he had that he would not change the opinion he expressed last May. Let me call his attention further to that hon. gentleman, in whom he seems to have such implicit confidence. I believe that hon. gentleman expressed some opinion on the right hon. gentleman himself once. I want to know if he has such implicit confidence in that opinion in regard to himself ? We were told by the hon. gentleman not long ago that the province which justly feels pride in the right hon. leader of the government should be garrisoned. I want to know if the right hon. gentleman has implicit confidence in the opinion of the hon. member for North Norfolk on that subject ? We all recognize the ability of the hon. member for North Norfolk, especially when he appears to the best advantage, when he is facing both ways. I would like to know what position he occupies in this House, even if he had been consistent in his past life, that we should accept his opinion on a question of this kind. The hon. gentleman has much skill in manipulating and garbling extracts, and turning them to account; but after giving an opinion one day, he rises the next day and, without a twinge or a blush on his cheek, says that he was quite wrong, and that he has since received new light. We had it from his own lips since this session began that he was opposed to this scheme, until he went into caucus, holding that it would be disastrous for the country.
I beg to deny the assertion of my bon. friend. He is misquoting me and misrepresenting my position.

I should be very sorry to misquote the hon. gentleman. He is very properly jealous of his statements in matters of that kind. I do not know any hon. gentleman whom we should be more accurate in quoting, because it is always to our advantage to do so. Let it go to the country in regard to the hon. member for North Norfolk that there has never been one great question in Canada on which he has not faced both ways.
