I defy any hon. gentleman to point to any great question, on both sides of which the hon. gentleman has not been found, and he has never thought proper to apologize for the contradictory course he has taken on any one of them. We have it clearly set forth by the Prime Minister that he relies solely upon the great ability of the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton), as a railway expert, to justify him in forcing this scheme through the House. Well, I never heard that the hon. member for North Norfolk ever built any railways or even ran one. True he is a large shipper, but only in one particular branch, and that has absolutely nothing to do with the problem of transportation.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: He can turn a short curve.
Yes, he can do that, but that is different to hauling freight.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: He wants favourable curves.

He certainly has a partiality for curves. The First Minister told us a moment ago that the leader of the opposition proposel to purchase a certain portion of the Canadian Pacific Railway and improve the grades for the purpose of making that a road over which grain might be hauled. While that is perfectly true, what the leader of the opposition proposed to do was to utilize that road for the purpose of carrying grain, not during the whole period of the year, but after the close of navigation. Does anybody imagine that the proposed railway will carry grain, if it should carry any, from Winnipeg to Moncton ? No one can close his1 eyes to the fact that you may build as many railways as you like north of the height of land, the grain will go by way of Lake Superior during the navigable season. We are told that a pamphlet is to be published giving all required information about the route and the country to be traversed. We will no doubt have a worthless pamphlet circulated, which will simply give extracts, where they are favourable, and leave out the rest. You can take reports and select here and there favourable portions, but you will find many others of the opposite character, and the former will be given as indicating the nature of the whole country. The favourable portions of the reports will be published, and the others

i
I carefully omitted. The right hon. the First j Minister has repeatedly told us that there j are mountains of information at hand, but he has been unable to designate where they are to be had. He has been unable to point to a single authority except the hon. member for North Norfolk. One would think that by this time the right hon. gentleman would have been able to refer us to the particular authority on which lie relies for the information which we have been unable to find. If we could even find the mole-hills of information, much less the mountains, we would be satisfied. The people of this country, Sir, are not going to be satisfied with the mere wave of the hand of the First Minister. Through that country there have been some surveys made, but all we have is a mere summary of those surveys, and not one survey has been made precisely upon the line proposed by the hon. gentleman. Yet we are told that there are mountains of information. What are the reports to which the right hon. gentleman refers ? Where are they to be found ? Well, I confess my mental blindness

I am not to blame for that.
Mr-. OLANCY. There are a good many things I have ceased to hold the right hon. gentleman responsible for, and that is one of them, but there are some things I cannot acquit him of. I cannot acquit him of having made, in the most deliberate fashion, a most wholesale statement, unwarranted by any facts yet disclosed. We are told that a pamphlet is to be published. I venture to say that it will consist of the extracts given by the Minister of the Interior, and which are utterly valueless. He read extracts from the reports of surveyors, having reference to a particular locality on the river here and there as if they applied to the whole country. Such extracts are worse than valueless ; they are misleading. I venture to predict that this pamphlet will be a mere garbled collection of favourable extracts, intended to delude the people instead of to instruct them.

In desiring to say a few words on the question engaging our attention, I must say at once that I have no justification for so doing, except the wish to consume a little of the time which is being deliberately wasted. If I supposed that by taking up some portion of that time, I was prolonging this debate, I would not rise in my seat, but I am quite satisfied that time is being deliberately dissipated, and we might as well take a hand in the thing as leave our friends opposite to do it all. That is my only justification. AVe wasted all day yesterday and to-day. There has not been an argument advanced in these two days that has not been made fifty times in the course of this discussion. We heard all the transportation arguments of the bon. member for St. Mary's division

(Hon. Mr. Tarte) fifty times before. TUe only new thing he introduced yesterday was that, some way or other, this proposition will interfere with some particular solution of the transportation problem which he himself desires.
We have heard that wheat question discussed over and over and over again and the statement made that we cannot carry wheat from Winnipeg all-rail in competition with water carriage. If that was a new proposition and we had never heard it before we might profitably waste a few hours in listening to it. But I venture to say that in the speeches, almost 100 of them that we have heard in the last six weeks this same wheat question has been trotted out fifty times, and will be trotted out fifty times more before the close of this debate. I understand that owing to the illness, which we all regret, of the hon. leader of the opposition, it is necessary to dissipate time (until he gets well and can again control the situation. Whether that be true or not, there certainly ought to be a disposition on the part of our friends to confine themselves to the question under discussion; and to leave wheat, which has nothing to do with this subject, alone. We have heard the wheat question discussed until we know exactly what it costs to take a bushel of wheat from Winnipeg to Montreal, and it is problematical what it will cost to take it from Winnipeg to Quebec. I heard yesterday my hon. friend from West Toronto state that for years the country has been clamouring for another transcontinental railway. Now we have had that trotted 0)ut, and we have exhausted the newspaper quotations to show the people that we require another transcontinental scheme. Now cannot we drop that for once and take up the matter under discussion ?
Does my hon. friend refer to me ?
No.
You said West Toronto.

I meant East York. You are all so mixed up that it is hard to separate you. I must confess that the hon. member for West Toronto (Mi-. Clarke) does not often fall into the weakness that my hon. friend from East York (Mr. Maclean) does. We have heard it said that this is a good election proposition. That statement has been repeated over and over again. It has been said that it is a good election proposo-tion for New Brunswick and the maritime provinces, for Quebec, for Ontario, for Manitoba and for the North-west Territories, and British Columbia. My hon. friend from East York stated that point as if it was a new argument and as if that was the whole intention, the whole reason for building this railway. If it is true that the construction of that railway is a good election proposition it is the best compliment that can be paid to the gentleman who originated the scheme. My experience in politics is that a good election proposition is good government, and that a bad election proposition is bad government. You cannot put a scheme before the people of Canada as a good election proposition which is not good government unless you take the people of Canada to be fools, and to be easily caught. If this scheme is endorsed by the people and is a good election proposition, it is a good scheme on its own merits. The best endorsation you can have for it is that you believe the people will endorse it. But you say it is a bad scheme in itself, and therefore the people must be either fools or knaves ; that is the only deduction you can make. I can assure the members of the government that if they have a proposition to submit to the people which is a good election scheme for all parts of this country it is a good thing for the country or the electors will not endorse it. Now we are told over and over again that we have not sufficient information to enter upon this scheme. We have quite enough information to enable the Grand Trunk Railway to go into it from Quebec to the coast, we have information enough to justify us in guaranteeing the bonds to an almost unlimited extent for the very same scheme, but not information enough to justify the government going into it. If the government were in possession of sufficient information to show our friends on the other side of the House that this road is going over an absolutely level country with no grades at all, they would still say the scheme was not a good one. It is impossible to get enough information to satisfy you, and if we got information enough to prove that this was likely to be a financially successful proposition the hon. gentlemen opposite would want to know the number of rails or spikes to the mile, the number of curves in a mile, and they would find objections in some way. That is what they think they are here for, not to perfect this scheme, but to find fault with it and to turn the microscope upon its imperfections. They have said over and over again that we have not information enough and if this discussion lasts two weeks longer, we will have the same old problems trotted out what is it going to cost to carry a bushel of wheat from Winnipeg to Quebec ? I would like to ask my hon. friend (Mr. Kemp) what he will sell goods for five years hence, or to say that he will sell a certain article of pressed ware for so much.
Try him with a contract.
I suppose he will make as good a bargain as the government has made with the Grand Trunk.

If he did not make a better bargain he would be in bad shape.

Mr. HE YD,. If he makes a better bargain he is bound to be a rich man, because under this contract, the other party has all the risks and we have all the benefits. You would judge from the opinion expressed by our hon. friends that the Grand Trunk Railway did not know what they are doing. Does any one suppose that Mr. Hays and the gentlemen behind him who are supplying the money, who are willing to put this money into this unproductive scheme and cun the railway for fifty years, do not know what they are doing.
They do not put a dollar into it.

Not a dollar in it, and that is the reason you should pass it. All you have to do is support the scheme, and if the Grand Trunk do not put a dollar in it the whole thing- falls to the ground, and the people's money will not be lost. I assume that the Grand Trunk people know what they are doing, and if they intend to build a railway from North Bay passing north of Winnipeg, and putting a branch line to Winnipeg, and going out to the coast, they have carefully considered this scheme and they believe it will be a good business proposition, and one which will make money for the Grand Trunk Railway. What we are doing is simply adding about 400 miles more from North Bay to Quebec and from Quebec to Moncton. We are not seriously interfering with the original Grand Trunk proposition. They proposed to go from North Bay, but they were forced by the very gentlemen who are now finding fault with the road, to go to Quebec. Not a voice was raised in the Railway Committee room protesting against the extension to Quebec on the ground that we had not information enough. Every man in that committee supported that proposition, and now hon. gentlemen opposite are finding fault and saying that we have not sufficient information. I do not care if we have enough information or not. The Grand Trunk are behind this scheme, they guarantee ,us against loss, and I have a suspicion that they know what they are doing. The very fact that they are guaranteeing to run the road for fifty years is an assurance that the government has not made much of a mistake.
They cannot pay dividends.
How do you know ?

I know by their reports.
Mi-. HEYD. Do you know more than Mr. Hays does ? I am inclined to think that Mr. Hays and Sir Charles Rivers-AVilson and the managers of the railway know better than my hon. friend from down below whether they will be able to pay dividends, sincere and conscientious as he is. Although he has no money in this scheme he is already predicting failure, while the men who are going to put their money in are quite satisfied with It.
Oh, oh.

Our friends laugh. If they do not put the money into the scheme the whole thing falls to the ground. They were satisfied a few weeks ago that the Grand Tr,uuk Railway were going to build a railway from North Bay to the coast, and they were not going to take long. Air. Hays stated in the Railway *Committee that they would build that road in two years and would guarantee to build it in five years, and no one doubted the proposition, because Mr. Hays knew what he was talking about, and we were all anxious to have him go into it. The thing that gratifies me is that the government is going into that part of the scheme which in the future will control to some extent the carrying trade. They are not assisting a railway from Winnipeg to Quebec, and putting it into the hands of a private corporation for their sole advantage. The unearned increment of which we hear so much will come to us at the end of fifty years with all the improvements that will have taken place during that period of time. And then the railway will be handed over to us when it may be expected to be of some use and likely to be a benefit to this country.
They tell us we have not got information enough. Why, for six weeks we have been thundering away over this question, and when our friends opposite want more information they will trot out some newspaper opinion of some three-cent writer, probably hired for $5 or $6 a week, that so and so is going to take place, and in all seriousness is brought to the attention of the First Minister, and he is asked if it is the intention of the government to withdraw from this scheme, and whether they are going to make great changes in this railway. Well, he is answered. It is not the intention of the government to do anything of the kind. Then another gentleman gets up and says that the Atinister of Customs is hostile to this scheme, and that he actually intended to withdraw from the government. That statement is made in all apparent seriousness, and the Alinister of Customs tells him there is nothing in it. Then some newspaper says the Alinister of Finance was almost going out of the cabinet because he was opposed to this scheme, and the Alinister of Finance gets up and makes a magnificent speech endorsing this scheme from end to end. They keep trotting out newspaper quotations when they have not got minds fertile enough to invent some argument against this scheme. Now, I assure the government that the arguments of our friends opposite have not had any weakening influence upon us, that we are still prepared to stand by the Premier in this matter. I would say to the Premier : Don't let those earnest and sincere remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. Broc-k)who is now looking at me, influence you. He will vote for an old canal,

with scows, and tugs, and lose a lot of money on them, but he will not vote for this scheme. Now, I have too high an opinion of the intelligence and business acumen of the hon. gentleman to suppose that he -would have hung on to the canal that runs from Brantford to the Grand river, with the intention of running it against the railways. They have abandoned that enterprise and turned it into electric power, and they are making money. He, Mr. Meigs, sold out as soon as he found, his scows were not going to pay. What would the hon, gentleman do if he had a lot of cotton on hand and knew that the market was going to drop ? He would unload his cotton. So I would advise the ministers not to be too much impressed by his earnestness in this matter. He don't mean what he says. He intends of course to be sincere. I believe he is conscientious, but there is such a thing as being conscientious, and at the same time being absolutely blind to the arguments of one's opponents. We know that some men are afflicted with colour blindness, they are unable to distinguish red from green. They are mentally willing to do it, but from a physical defect of the eye they cannot do it. In the same way, some men are so politically constituted that they cannot see any virtue in an opponent. There are men in this House who cannot see anything good in this railway.
gome hon. MEMBERS. Hear, hear.

Certainly, that is what I say, it is constitutional with them, and they cannot help it. If this railway was planned by the most experienced railway engineers in ^his country, if it was endorsed in its financial aspect by the most capable financiers in this country, if it was propounded by a government with the most earnest and serious intention of doing good to this country, in their minds there would be nothing good in it. During the seven years I have been in this House nothing that was ever propounded by this government had any merit in the eyes of hon. gentlemen opposite. I do not remember one important contribution they have made towards the legislation of this country during the past seven years, and I have never heard any one on the other side lift up his voice to support any legislation this government has proposed. It is a chronic condition with them to oppose everything that the government introduces into the House. But I can assure the Prime Minister that the more we hear our friends on the other side criticising and condemning this scheme, and reading newspaper quotations against it, the more firmly we are convinced that this is a good enterprise, otherwise they would adduce some sound, logical arguments why it should not be gone on with. The argument that we have not got enough information has no weight with me, particularly as we have behind us a reliable 331
and live railway corporation who assumes all the initial responsibility.
Mr. TAYLOIt. The hon. gentleman has made a speech
I was only killing time.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I am glad the hon. gentleman admits the fact that he is killing time. He made a speech of two hours in length on the main question, and now, when the opposition are anxious to criticise the Bill fairly, he gets up and says that he is killing time. We are anxious to get on with the Bill. The hon. gentleman made a speech two hours in length and he gets up to-day and repeats a great deal of that speech, travels all over the country from one end of it to the other, killing time. Now. after being here for five or six months, I do not think the hon. members of the House are anxious to kill time-although the government have spent about five months hatching this scheme before they brought it down to the House. Then the hon. gentleman says : We are willing to go to the country, we have got a business government and we are willing to go to the country on this question. The Prime Minister, when he formed his government, said he had surrounded himself with business men who would do business on business principles. Now my hon. friend from Brantford has been a member of the town council.
Of a city council.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
What would he think of a city council, or a town councillor a village council, or a county council, entering into a contract with contractors to put down a system of waterworks at a cost of half a million or a million dollars without a mandate from their electors, signing a contract with a company to put down a system of waterworks at a cost of half a million or a million dollars, without having a survey made or an estimate of the cost, or anything else ? Would his electors return my hon. friend and his associates to power in such a case ? What is the first thing a business man will do when he is going to build a house ? He will get his plans and specifications, and an estimate of the cost. So will a municipality, if they are going to commence a work. The councillors of that municipality first prepare plans and estimates and then submit them to the people in the form of a by-law, and let the people pronounce whether they will vote a sufficient amount of money to carry on the work or not. What has this government done ? They come down with a proposition to spend $125,000,000 of the people's money, without ever saying, by your leave. Then the ministers of the Crown, the advisers of the Governor General, come to this House and make statements why they are doing this. It is true that one of the ministers, the ex-Minlster of Railways, said the reason



they were doing it was because Senator Cox couldn't wait. But what reasons have the Prime Minister and his colleagues given ? The Prime Minister made a statement that any school boy in the country will contradict, when he goes on the platform to defend his policy. His principal reason was that the British government would be shut off from communication with Canada, and that we could not ship our goods over to England if the American government took it into their wise heads to cancel the bonding privileges; that we were locked in for five or six months in the year by ice, and that we could not ship wheat, nor a carload of cattle, or anything else, to the sea-board. Why, Sir, any little school boy will say to the Prime Minister : I have been looking at the map.
We have our water-ways for seven months in the year, and we have our Intercolonial Railway down through the maritime provinces and we can ship our goods all the year round. The right hon. gentleman thinks he makes out a strong argument when he says that we should build this road because the Americans may take it into their wise heads to abrogate the bonding privilege. It should be beneath the dignity of any cabinet minister to make a statement in this House that he cannot go upon the platform and justify. Any school boy might get up and contradict such a statement as that. What did the Postmaster General (Hon. Sir William Mulock) say ? He made a statement that the proposal of the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) meant buying 57 miles of railway in the United States. Is there a school boy in this country who will not contradict such a statement as that ? There are only three miles in the United States. It is 57 miles from Cotqau to the end of the road, but the road runs through American territory for only three miles to connect with an American road. The youth of this country reading the statements of the hon. Postmaster General and of other hon. ministers which should be beyond question will be justified in saying that our ministers are making statements that are not true. The lion. Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding)) says that they are going to build a road 1,S00 miles long for $30,000 or $40,000 a mile which means an expenditure of $55,000,000 or $60,000,000. Yet, the right hon. Prime Minister says that the road is going to cost the country only $13,000,000. The hon. Minister of Finance says that it is only going to cost the country $11,000,000. He says :	I
called in an actuary and he said give me $8,000,000 and I will buy an annuity and that will pay off the debt. Is there any school boy in the country who -will not see the absurdity of that statement ? Suppose that a farmer buys a farm for $10,000 and he proposes to give a mortgage and pay it off in annual payments but instead of that he is Mr. TAYLOR.
advised not to give a mortgage but to buy an annuity and pay off the debt in that way. These are the statements the hon. ministers are making in this House. There is not a boy growing up who has read the statements of the hon. ministers but will say : We condemn them. And they will condemn these lion, gentlemen not because of the statements they have been making but because of the unbusinesslike way in which they have gone into this contract and in which they are endeavouring to compel the people to go into debt to the extend of $125,-
000.000 to build this road. The debt is there and they are endeavouring to make the people believe that if they buy an annuity for $8,600,000 they will be able to pay the whole thing off. They do not tell the people that they are placing a mortgage on the farm of every farmer in this country to the extent of $35 per head. I am sorry that the hon. Postmaster General (Hon. Sir William Mulock) was not in the House a moment
Say it again.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: When I made the statement that the hon. Postmaster General as a minister of the Crown ought to tell the truth, and that a minister of the Crown Should not make statements in this House which have no foundation in fact. Ministers of the Crown are looked up to and respected by the people and they are expected when they make statements to keep within the truth. The hon. Postmaster General said in his speech the other day that the-hon. leader of the opposition proposed to buy^the Canada Atlantic Railway and that 57 miles of it was in the United States. That is a statement that he made use of against his opponents when he knew that the Canada Atlantic Railway Company had only three miles of line in the United States.
Who said there were 57 miles in the United States ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I have been led to look up to the judges sitting in our courts of justice and to ministers of the Crown as being men to whom young people should look up. We looked upon the judges of this country as being beyond reproach but by this Liberal government dragging them into polities-
Order, order.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: They have appointed a judge
Order.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I am not reflecting upon the judges.

Question.

Mi-. SPROULE. Did the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Heyd) confine Himself to the question ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The hon. member for Brant travelled all over the country.
Question.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I am alluding to the conduct of ministers of the Crown in making statements that any school boy would contradict. The hon. Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) knows that any school boy would contradict the statements he made in his speech.
Question.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, will you please call the hon. Minister of Justice to order for interrupting me ?

I do not think the hon. Minister of Justice is out of order. He is perfectly in order and I would ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) to confine himself to the question under consideration and not travel so far away from it as far as the judges are concerned.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: What is the question under discussion ?
The question under discussion is this clause in the Bill.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I disagree with you, Mr. Chairman, and I will appeal to the House if you have not since this Bill came before you allowed every hon. gentleman who lias spoken to travel away from the Bill. The question is whether the people have a right to be asked to assume an indebtedness of $120,000,000 to pay for this road.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: If I said $560,000,000 1 would not tell a lie fifty-four miles long as the hon. Postmaster General did in the statement that he made in tins House by stating that the Canada Atlantic Railway had fifty-seven miles of line in the United States when there were only three miles
The hon. leader of the opposition stated that.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: What would one of our school boys say of one of the ministers who got up in his place in parliament and made a statement that was not true ? I was drawing some comparison about the judges and the Chairman-I wish the Chairman who is paid for staying here to discharge his duties would remain in liis seat so that it would not be necessary to call in one of the members of the House who does not know the rules of the House at all.

I thought yesterday the discussion took a very wide range. That was mv conviction and I 331}
think the rules of the House will bear me out in saying that the discussion should have been confined to the clause under consideration, but the government allowed considerable latitude. I have allowed the discussion to proceed in this way while I have been in the Chair to-day to a certain extent but I still think they were wrong in doing that. I certainly think that the hon. member (Mr. Taylor) has travelled a good deal farther from the main question than any other hon. member who has spoken to-day.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The hon, gentleman who preceded me travelled a great deal farther from the question.
Not in so far as I understand it.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: And you did not stop him. The railway that we are discussing, the hon. ministers say, will extend from the Atlantic to the Pacific, but as a matter of fact it commences down at Moncton and Moncton is not on the Atlantic at all, as I understand it. We are talking about a great transcontinental line running from the Atlantic to the Pacific. I have not gone over the range of the discussion to-day. I have not even referred to the railway from Moncton.
I do not object to your travelling over the whole line of railway if you desire to do so, but I do object to the hon. gentleman travelling over foreign subjects.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
I am not travelling over foreign subjects, but I am discussing speeches of ministers of the Crown who have made statements which are not in accordance with the facts and which any school boy would contradict. I imagine the right hon. leader of the government going down to one of his constituents. They have appealed to the country and he goes down to one of' his constituents and asks him to support him in the election on this great railway project. The Prime Minister travels on his way from home, and he sees a little boy and he asks him : Is your father at home ? And the boy answers :	No ;
he is away canvassing ; we are going to have an election, and he is trying to bust the government for putting a tax of $25 a head on every man, woman and child in Canada, and as we have ten in the family we have to pay $250. The minister says to him : You have got fifty fine head of cattle there, and what are you doing with them, and the boy answers :	We are going to
send them to England for Easter beef. But the Prime Minister says :	How are you
going to send them there in the winter, because the Americans have abrogated the bonding privilege and you can't ship them to Halifax ; you will have to ship them to Montreal, and you will lose $10 a head on them because you cannot get them to

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Yesterday and to-day lion, gentleman on the other side of the House wasted three-quarters of the time in unprofitable discussion. It is they who are doing the killing of the time. We are trying to make the Bill perfect, and to get through it as speedily as we can in order that we may go home, but they are obstructing the business of the House and talking at random. If they wish to spend hours in useless discussion, we on this side can put up man for man with them. The difference is, that our men will tell the truth, while their men are trying to mislead the people with regard to the whole thing.

This school boy argument has some force no doubt in the mind of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor). Let me read to him what the leader of the opposition said about this 57 miles of the Canada Atlantic Railway :
The Canada Atlantic Railway extends from Depot Harbour on the Georgian bay to Coteau junction a distance of 342 miles. In addition to this, they have a line 57 miles in length between Coteau junction and Alburgh junction in the state of Vermont.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Well now, the Minister of Justice ought to go to school; It is quite true that the leader of the opposition said that, but what the Postmaster General said was that there were 57 miles of the Canada Atlantic Railway in the United States. The Minister of Justice is trying to mislead us, just as all the ministers are trying to deceive the people of this country, by making statements that are not in accordance with the facts. The Canada Atlantic Railway does run to Alburgh Junction but there is only three miles of the Canada Atlantic Railway in the United States. It runs from Coteau Junction through Bouaventure county.
Through what county ?
I am afraid we must both go to school. Bona-venture county is 400 miles away from the Canada Atlantic Railway.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Is there not a portion of the Canada Atlantic Railway in Bouaventure county ?
No.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: It is Beauharnois county I mean. I made a slip in the name. I am not so familiar with these French names as is the Minister of Justice. The Canada Atlantic Railway runs from Coteau Junction for 57 miles, through Beauharnois count}' to Alburgh Springs, to make connection with an American road for Boston ; but as a matter of fact only three miles out of this 57 miles are in the United States. If the Minister of Justice looks that up he will find that my statement is correct.
You didn't get the Postmaster General out of the hole after all.
I tried very hard.
You made it worse.

Iu connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific scheme I spoke this afternoon in reference to freight rates, and the explanation of the First Minister was courteous as it usually is. I think I understood every point he referred to. I was not surprised, however, at the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Murray) who supports the government, stating that he did not believe in the theory propounded by the Prime Minister that the cereals and products of the west, can be carried over this road profitably to compete with existing roads. There are a good many members on the government side wTho hold the same opinion as the hon. member for Pontiac with regard to that. The hon. the leader of the House said that he had much confidence in the judgment of the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) in respect to this matter, and I take it for granted that the right hon. gentleman rested his case on the statements made by that hon. member. If the right hon. gentleman, however, looks into the matter carefully, he will find that the opinion of the member for North Norfolk cannot be borne out by the facts. The leader of the government said that package freight would also find its way over this road as package freight finds it way over other railways. That no doubt will be the ease.
1 would like, however, to draw the attention of the right hon. gentleman to the fact that in the carriage of package freight the railways cannot compete with water transportation any more than for the carriage of grain. In the summer time and during the open season of navigation, package freight in the United States going west to Chicago or anywhere west of the great lakes, finds the water at Buffalo, or as soon as it can, and a great business is done there in transferring that freight from the trains to the vesels, by which it is carried to Chicago or other points on Lake Michigan or Lake Superior, where it is again transferred to trains and so proceeds west. That will be found to exist in many cases. Take another illustration. The Canada Atlantic is carrying large quantities of package freight from New York city. I am told by the authorities of'that railway that last year 25 per cent of the package freight from New York city that was destined to western points on Lake Superior and Lake Michigan was carried as far as Albany by barge or boat, there transferred to Canada Atlantic cars on the Delaware and Hudson River Railway, carried to Parry Sound by rail, there transferred again to water, and
then carried in vessels to Chicago and other points on the western lakes. What is our experience in this country ? My right hon. friend said that the manufacturers would use this road. If it is built, I am sure that they will use it, provided that its rates are as low as those of other roads. But running so far as it does from the industrial centres in the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, I do not think it is going to be of much advantage to the manufacturers for the carriage of package freight. Probably 75 per cent of the manufactured products of Ontario and Quebec find their way to the North-west by all-water or rail-and-water routes to Fort William. This summer a new era has dawned in Canada in water transportation. The circumstances that exist between Buffalo and Chicago also exist to some extent between Montreal and Port Arthur. A new line of steamers has been put on, and is doing a tremendous business in carrying package freight, because its rates are much lower than the rates by rail between eastern points and Fort William ; and more vessels are being built. Package freight in future will be largely carried by water and by rail-and-water to the head of the lakes. The products of Ontario and Quebec are gathered up by the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Grand Trunk Railway, and are taken to Owen Sound, Collingw'ood, Sarnia and Windsor, and are there transferred to vessels, which carry them to the head of the lakes ; and during the season of open navigation they will always find water as soon as possible.
I have not heard the right hon. First Minister state the reason why, after deciding to appoint a commission to investigate this question, he did not wait until that commission reported before introducing this railway project. Was the government afraid that the commission would not report in favour of it ? I say again that tills railway can never compete with the water route in carrying grain from the west to the east. At the same time, I believe that the time has come when the grand old city of Quebec will profit to a great extent by the carrying of grain by the water route.
The right hon. gentleman referred to the system of transferring grain to elevators. Sometimes there is one transfer, sometimes two. But when we remember that it only takes one or two minutes to take the grain out of a car and put it into an elevator, you may see how infinitesimal is the cost of such an operation. The elevators generally produce very good revenue and pay good dividends to their owners. But when the transportation companies own the elevators, they do not charge very much, and do not count very much on that part of the cost.
The Prime Minister also said that in the winter time grain was carried to some extent from the west to St. John, N.B., by the Canadian Pacific Railway. I do not

think there is any very great profit in that business, though it is done at a fairly high rate ; but if the Canadian Pacific Railway or the government railway had elevators on the Georgian bay, they could be filled with grain as late as the 15th of December, up to which date I understand vessels can operate between the western side and the eastern side of the lake; and if these elevators could be filled with grain up to that date, then the Canadian Pacific Railway, which is interested in the port of St. John, and the government railway, which is also interested in maritime ports, would have business in hauling that grain to those ports. But even if the Canadian Pacific Railway had more favourable grades and curvatures than it has, I do not anticipate that it would be able to carry very much more grain in the winter time than it does now.
The right hon. gentleman has this afternoon put forward this argument, that the farmers would be able to get their grain sold during the winter-. My experience is that the farmers do not have to carry over the grain themselves. They deliver it to warehouses and get warehouse receipts, on which they get their money. The grain is stored in that way.
But how much does the farmer lose on it by selling it after navigation is closed ? He loses from six to eight cents on every bushel of wheat.
That is a fair question for discussion. X have heard that question discussed.
You cannot get a farmer in the west to tell you anything else. There is no discussion on it there.

I have heard that question discussed very thoroughly, and X am under the impression that the cost of taking the grain out in the winter would amount to more than the storage charges. That is the impression I have gained from gentlemen who are posted in this business. At any rate, we have the fact before us that in the western states a large proportion of the grain is marketed in the fall, and the balance goes out in the spring. The right hon. gentleman has referred to the fact that the hon. leader of the opposition said something about the Canadian Pacific line north of Lake Superior being improved for the purpose of carrying grain. As I understand what the leader of the opposition said, he prefaced his observations by regretting that the commission had not been appointed, which the government had promised, but as regards water versus rail routes, it seems to me that he was altogether in favour of water competition. He gave the rate on freight from Minneapolis and St. Paul to Boston as 291 cents per hundred pounds, and showed that a similar rate prevailed between other points, from which it could Mr. KEMP.
be easily seen that the argument advanced by the hon. member for North Norfolk cannot be substantiated by the rates of freight existing at present on grain to the seaboard. Something was said about the congestion of traffic in the North-west. No doubt there was congestion last year, and that accounted for the demand for the construction of a new railway. A peculiar condition of affairs existed. The Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian Northern Railway were certainly not in a position to handle the traffic going in or coming out during last year. They had not sufficient rolling stock or motive power, but since last fall they have acquired a tremendous amount of both. Out of the $20,000,000 of extra capital, which the Canadian Pacific Railway have been allowed to issue, I am informed that nearly $15,000,000 was spent upon extra equipment. But it was impossible for any railway, either in the North-west or in the United States, to get delivery of the rolling stock last year which it required. This fall, however, I do not believe that there will be any cause for complaint. I believe that the farmers and shippers of the North-west will be satisfied with the facilities they have; and in any case this railway, even if built at once, could not relieve the congestion in the older settled parts of the country, because it will not go there. I am not discussing whether extra railways are needed in the North-west or not. I think they are, but I am discussing the eastern end of this proposed line, and I do not think that the hon. member for South Brant (Sir. Heyd) was justified in making the rambling speech he did. If we are going to get through we must keep to certain points, and the point I am discussing is the carriage of grain. What I contend is that the government shall not, on the information before ns, commit the country to this extravagant expenditure on a road away to the north, with the idea that it will carry profitably the products of the North-west. It cannot compete with the existing routes, and the carriage will not be reduced one iota.
Are you talking of the products of the North-west or of its wheat ?

I am discussing the argument of the right hon. gentleman. He said :
In one, two or three generations at least, perhaps more, these new settlers will grow cereals and probably nothing else.
That is what I am speaking of. The hon. the Minister of the Interior (Hon. Mr. Sif-ton), before he went away, said that wheat) was carried from Kansas City to Chicago for five cents and that it could consequently) be carried from Winnipeg by this new line to St. John at 101 or 11 cents. I have taken the trouble to inform myself, and I find that wheat is not carried from Kansas City to Chicago at five cents per hundred pounds

but at fourteen cents, and that the average rate is twelve cents. Possibly there may have been some cutting down of rates at a particular period, just as sometimes there are excursion rates, but those are not things on which to build a case. I am therefore strongly of the opinion that the government have not sufficient information to warrant its going on with the eastern end of the road.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
The hon. member for West Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) made the statement that the farmers lost six to eight cents a bushel through having to hold their wheat over through the winter on to the spring. I do not know what authority he lias for making that statement. Everybody knows that the grain buyers all over the country buy wheat in the fall and store it until the spring and sometimes lose eight or ten cents a bushel by storing it. But it all depends on whether the market is higher or lower in the spring than in the fall. If it is lower, they lose money. Then besides there is shrinkage in the grain which amounts to one or two cents a bushel. No matter how dry the wheat may be when it goes into the warehouse, you cannot weigh it out in the spring at what you took it in. I have been in the business some thirty years and have never shipped a carload of wheat to Montreal, St. John or Halifax in the winter, because the difference in the freight rates between rail and water makes it more profitable to ship it in the spring. That is done from the head of the lakes down, and even in those parts of the country, where there is no water communication, they get cheaper freight rates by rail in the spring than in the fall. The other day, in speaking on the proposition of the leader of the opposition, the Postmaster General said :
Of this four hundred miles of railway, fifty-seven miles of it are in the state of Vermont.
He was there referring to the Canada Atlantic Railway, and further on he said :
X am told that the market price of the Canada Atlantic Railway is hot less than $17,000,000, if it can be purchased to-day. At all events between these prices we can put It down as $15,000,000, and that includes the fifty-seven miles of railway in Vermont. What the government of Canada is going to do with fifty-seven miles of railway in the state of Vermont, I am at a loss to know.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: How much has the Grand Trunk Railway in the United States ?

I am speaking of the government buying railways in the United States ; I am not speaking of private citizens doing so. If it is proposed by the hon. leader of the opposition or by the party supporting him, to expend the people's money in the acquisition of railways in the United States then a different proposition is involved.
These are the words of the Postmaster General in dealing with this purchase of the Canada Atlantic Railway. He says to the people of Canada : The opposition propose taking your money and buying 57 miles of railway over in the state of Vermont; you people in Canada are too loyal to support anything of that kind. That is what he, a minister of this country, Postmaster General and Minister of Labour, states to the people of this country. Surely the people of Canada would expect a gentleman with all these titles and a knight besides, he, Sir William Muloclc, Postmaster General, Minister of Labour, the vastest man thei'e is in Canada, before getting up to make a statement of that kind, to look at the map. Any school boy looking at the map of the Canada Atlantic Railway will see that there are only three miles of it on American territory, a little branch running out to connect with the Vermont line. Surely the Postmaster General, now that his words are quoted, will rise and apologize to the school boys of Canada, saying : I did not study the map of this country, I did not look at the new map published by the Department of the Interior showing all the railways of Canada, and among them the Canada Atlantic Railway, all of it on Canadian territory except a little three-mile branch. And then he tries to stir up the loyalty of young men, and he says : Surely you will not support the leader of the opposition when he proposes taking your money and buying a railway a part of which is in Vermont. Surely he will do the leader of the opposition justice and do himself justice by taking back what he must have known to be a misstatement of the facts.
Shall clause 2 be adopted ?
I do not think the Committee is ready or that this clause should be adopted in this way.
We do not want to press it. Do you desire to discuss it further?
Surely.	_
Oh, I understand now.

My hon. friend the member for Toronto has called attention this afternoon to a very important feature of this agreement. Had we not had the assistance of the hon. member for South Brant (Mr. Heyd), who says that he rendered us the service of killing time, we might have advanced the study of this feature of the agreement a little more. My Ron. friend (Mr. Ileydl came into the chamber and vodlc tip at least half an hour in giving us a general appreciation of the agreement, speaking from copious notes. I do not see that my hon. friend justified the statement that lie would help us to kill time and await the return of the leader of the opposition. The discussion which took place yesterday must have convinced the committee that

there is no desire to kill time. We are certainly unfortunate in being deprived of the assistance of the leader of the opposition, who has given this question, from its inception, very careful consideration. He would be the last man, I am sure-and I know it from his own mouth-that would desire to delay in any way the progress of this Bill through the House. We cer-taiuly have no such desire, but we consider it our duty, now that the general principle of this agreement has been discussed, to look into the details very carefully and we intend to perform that duty, even if it does take a little time. My right lion, friend will agree with me that, if the entire morning was taken up with a very useless discussion, that was attributable entirely to the friends of my right lion, friend, because when explanations are given such as were given this morning by the hon. junior member for Toronto (Mr. Osier), an incident of that kind might be terminated in one minute by the hon. gentlemen opposite doing what my right lion, friend's partisan did at the last minute this afternoon. Therefore, if the time has been wasted to-day it lias been wasted by a discussion that might very easily have been terminated much sooner. Is it our duty to give our attention to this* agreement ? I take it that it is, and I have foundation for that line of conduct in my right hon. friend's own course since the beginning of this session, and if the committee will allow me, I intend justifying the exercise of the powers we have, which we have used most moderately and reasonably since yesterday, by quoting from the Order in Council passed by my right hon. friend himself. After hearing the terms of that Order in Council, I think my right lion, friend will admit that in giving the details of this most important agreement the attention we are now giving, we are simply doing what my right hon. friend considered three or four "months ago was the absolute duty of every member of this House.
At six o'clock, committee took recess. After Recess.
Committee resumed at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Section 2 of the Bill is under discussion.

Mr. Chairman, when you left the Chair at six o'clock I was suffering some irritation at the reproaches which the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Heyd) had made to gentlemen in opposition who were criticising the present measure, and I stated that we were following in that criticism the lines laid down by the hon. gentlemen who sit on the treasury benches, particularly the line of conduct which fortunately was laid down by the Prime Minister and his colleagues in the Order in Council of last May, in which the principle was affirmed,

which moreover has been admitted here since yesterday by iny right hon. friend, that having discussed at length, not according to the statement of my hon. friend from Brant, wasting time-because in that waste every member of this House participated on both sides-but having discussed at length the principle of the Bill it would be absurd for us merely to glance over each section of this important agreement, the most important that has been under consideration in this House for over a quarter of a century without examining that agreement in detail. My hon. friends know as well as I do that when a Bill incorporating a railway company, even of the most trifling importance, passes its second reading, it is submitted, in a committee which corresponds to this one, to the most careful scrutiny. We have already seen Bills of comparatively small importance discussed before the Railway Committee in all their details, for two. three, four and five sittings. Why should we not carefully examine the details of this Bill ? I referred to the rule laid down by my right hon. friend himself, in the Order in Council of May last. Let me just quote from that Order in Council, which is incorporated in the motion offered by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition. It is said there that it was the opinion of the government on the 19th of May last, an opinion from which the government in every particular has departed, that:
The questions to be considered are complicated and involved, including among the objects to be sought the transportation of western products from place of production to the markets of the world.
This involves the consideration of their transportation ;
Prom place of production to Canadian seaports.
From place of production to the western ports of Lake Superior.
From the western ports of Lake Superior to Canadian seaports.
From Canadian seaports to Europe.
From place of production through Canadian ports on the Pacific. . . . It is obvious

Says the Order in Council prepared by the government:
-that before any satisfactory conclusion can be reached upon these questions a thorough and comprehensive inquiry should be made regarding :
The conditions of original shipment. . . . The storage requirements of lake, river and
ocean ports. The harbour facilities	
The conditions with regard to the navigation of the St. Lawrence, and generally any improvements, enlargements or other matters affecting the more economical and satisfactory uses of any Canadian channel of transportation by land or water.
Now, these were the views entertained by the government on the 19th of May last, and they contrast singularly with the position taken up even since yesterday, since we have been examining the details of this agreement. Yesterday we took under con-

sideration clause 2 of this Bill, and under that clause, as we are all aware, the whole agreement comes up for consideration. What more natural I ask than that we should, proceeding to discuss this agreement, take up the iirst clause, that is the first which has been under consideration since the House went into committee upon this Bill. Perhaps that clause, the most important of all in regard to the inquiry as to details, might have advanced some stages more had not the discussion supervened this morning, the length of which, it seems to me, was wholly attributable to the conduct of the member for Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) who was called upon to make some explanation of the language he had used in a previous debate. Now, Sir, what is that clause, let me read it to the committee in order that we may know exactly the absolute pertinency of the inquiries we have made since yesterday :
A through line of railway, of the gauge of four feet eight and one-half inches, comprising two divisions, to he called ' eastern division ' and the ' western division,' respectively, shall be constructed, in the manner hereinafter mentioned, between the city of Moncton, in the province of New Brunswick, and the navigable waters of the Pacific ocean, at or near Port Simpson or some other port in British Columbia, as may be agreed upon. The eastern division shall comprise the portion of the said railway to be constructed from its eastern terminus, through the central parts of the province of New Brunswick and through the province of Quebec, by the shortest available line to the city of Quebec ; then westerly through the northern part of the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, and through the province of Manitoba to the city of Winnipeg ; and the western division shall comprise the portion of the said railway between the said city of Winnipeg, or some point on the said eastern division, and the Pacific ocean, extending westerly through the province of Manitoba, the North-west Territories and the province of British Columbia.
That is the clause which we are now examining, and I submit that it is useless to argue that the starting point of this western division is not at Winnipeg and the terminal point on the prairies at or near Edmonton. What we are considering now are the terms of the agreement, whatever may have been contained in the Bill incorporating the Grand Trunk Railway Company, this is a totally different Bill. We are dealing with an agreement made between the government of this country and that company, who will at all times claim that in the laying out of its line it is governed entirely by this agreement. Well, what more natural, in words as vague as these, that an indication of the route to be followed on the western division in these words, that it would ' start from some point at or near Winnipeg and terminate at the Pacific ocean '-what more natural, I say, than that we should ask the government to indicate to us, in a general way at least, where that railway is going to pass ? Here we are called upon to give a guarantee for a very
large amount of money for the construction of a railway, the greater part of which, as a continuous railway, we will have to construct ourselves at a cost- approaching if not exceeding $100,000,000. Now, when we ask the government, these broad and indefinite limits being given in the agreement, where the railway is going to pass, we are told a variety of things in a most unsatisfactory manner.
Now my right hon. friend, at the end of the debate ,upon that point yesterday, in answer to the member for East York (Mr. Maclean) who said that before spending the people's money we were entitled to know where this railway was going to pass, my right hon. friend said that we would know where this railway was going to pass when we had voted the people's money for the construction thereof. That was the ground taken by the right hon. gentleman. Those were his very words, and I submit to this committee that such an explanation as that in regard to the course of this railway upon the western division is not a satisfactory explanation upon which we can dispose of the details of this important measure. My right hon. friend in the earlier part of the debate said that the question of the determination of the location of this road was one that could only be settled after the surveys bad been made. In vain did I ask my right hon. friend not for the precise location of the road, but to give us some points by which we could see what would be the direction taken by the railway in that vast country, a country as large as Siberia. My right hon. friend would go no farther in his explanations and we were left in this position, taking up the details of this agreement and examining them, that, with a railway entering a country at least a thousand miles square, if not more, in which already there are two competing lines starting from some point near Winnipeg, from which at the present moment, as I am informed, there are ten lines of railway going out from the city in different directions, south, south-west, west, northwest, my right hon. friend would not even inform the committee to the extent of telling us whether the railway would go directly north, whether it would move towards the unsettled parts of the North-west, whether it would follow near the line of the Canadian Pacific Railway, or the line of the Canadian Northern Railway, or pass between these two lines, or go to the north of the Canadian Northern Railway. Surely we are entitled, if not to precise information as to the location of the line in that district, at least to some Indication which would enable us to pass with intelligence over this clause of the agreement. The hon. Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) realizes the insufficiency of the Prime Minister's answer to satisfy our minds upon an important detail, and the hon. Minister of Justice thought he would meet the objection

by stating that the railway could not be constructed unless in conformity with the general law. Plans have been made, profiles, drawings, .something to show exactly where the railway would pass, and the hon. Minister of Justice urged that as these plans and the -location had to be submitted to the government and receive the approval of the government we need not be anxious. In other words, the hon. Minister of Justice supposed that for ourselves we could be satisfied to pass over this clause, to be satisfied as to construction of the railway in the North-west Territories in a region which, as I stated, occupies a country a thousand miles square, without knowing in any way whether it would go south, west, or north, with any degree of precision, but that we should have sufficient confidence in the government, who, appreciating that important element, would not decide the question or approve of the construction without knowing exactly where the railway should pass. Even if my hon. friend supposes, which he may for the moment, that we have absolute confidence in the wisdom of the government upon that point, when he states that the government would not approve of the location of the road without having precise information, does lie imagine that we, who are called upon to vote this large guarantee, should vote it without even knowing in what latitude the railway is going to pass ? We have here hon. gentlemen from the North-west. My hon. friend from Selkirk (Mr. McCreary) spoke on this question yesterday. Could he not have given some information as to the settled parts of that region Could lie not have told us where the trend of immigration is moving, whether to the north, to the northwest, or between these two lines at present thrown out, one of them completed and the other in process of construction in the North-west ? Could he not have given us some information upon this point ? We are called upon to approve of this guarantee in reference to that section without knowing in any appreciable degree what we are guaranteeing, or what direction the road is going to take upon which the government guarantee will bear. As to the hon. Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) he did not even take that trouble. The Minister of Finance, as I read this discussion of the inquiry made yesterday, said in answer to the hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean) that the railway was going to be placed in such a position throughout the different provinces that it would by its direction secure the complete support of every province in the Dominion in the coming election. The hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) took, at any rate, a more reasonable ground, and he said that it was a matter of no consequence. My hon. friend who has great experience in parliamentary matters and in transportation questions even, took the ground that it Mr. MONK.
was an unheard of thing in the matter of a project of this kind that we should know even with a degree of approximate precision where this line is going to pass. Is it fair when we are asking a question not requiring an answer of absolute precision, but merely tending to inform the committee as to the direction which this line is going to take from the moment that it is under the control exclusively of the Grand Trunk Pacific when it is called upon, as we are informed, to supply the great need of the North-west Territories in the matter of transportation, that we should be given such answers by those who are specially charged in this House and before this committee to not only defend the Bill, but to place at the disposal of members of this House every piece of information available to enable them to decide intelligently upon the different clauses of this agreement ? We have heard it stated in this House, and the statement has gone uncontradicted, that down in the cellars, in the bowels of this building, there is a pamphlet already prepared, issued under the authority of the right hon. gentleman ready for distribution, a pamphlet that is intended to be circulated as soon as this discussion is terminated, and containing a mass of information, and laying before the public a great quantity of data which has not been placed at our disposal at all, not only the meagre data contained in the mountains of information referred to by the right hon. gentleman, but much in addition. These pamphlets we are told are in this very building. Is there a powder magazine a la Guy Fawkes intended to be exploded after this Bill is disposed of V If that be the case, I would ask my right hon. friend and the gentlemen who sit on the treasury benches why that pamphlet is not placed at our disposal now ?
Are they keeping that for the 5th of November ?
It may be. In the meantime, we might appoint a commission, as they do in England, to examine the cellar of this building, to find out if any such magazine exists now.
Wasn't it the 7th and not the 5th ?

Surely the committee does not think that the gist of the demands which we made yesterday, before we passed one of the most important sections of the Bill, were of an unreasonable nature. I leave it to every member of this committee, as men of business, is it right or proper to ask us to say that the section now under consideration is correct as it is, even admitting the principle of the Bill ? And, as has been stated in a newspaper, the Bill having been adopted in principle, we should all endeavour to see that its provisions are carried out in the best possible way. Does my hon. friend from Selkirk (Mr. Me-

Creary) think it is reasonable for ns to say : There is need of a railway in that vast region of the west, but we will continue to ignore what direction, even in a general way, that railway is going to follow ? We suppose, from the terms of the agreement, that it will go through the Yellow Head pass if it is prolonged to the Pacific ocean; but whether it will go north through a region destined for settlement, or through a. region now settled or south, in the vicinity of the boundary of the United States, or pass in close proximity to the Canadian Pacific Railway or the Canadian Northern Railway, is a matter of indifference to us ; we have not even the curiosity to know what direction that line will take ?	1 do
not think that is a proper attitude to assume towards legislation of this kind. No Bill would be accepted by the Railway Committee under these circumstances. Our lion, friends know that in that committee we invariably require to be informed, not only as to the terminal points of a railway for the construction of which a company is being incorporated, but also the general direction of the line. I, therefore, insist again that our bon. friend should state to us not exactly where that line is going to pass, but in general terms what will be its direction ; and the force of that inquiry will only increase when we come to the eastern division-when we come to sanction the construction of a line absolutely, and entirely at our own expense through the northern part of the province of Ontario, and still more the line in the province of Quebec ; because, as I have maintained already and will maintain again, that line through a very large portion of its route in the province of Quebec passes entirely outside of the present zone of colonization, far removed from the regions at present being settled, and where communication by railway is an absolute necessity, if we wish the work of colonization in that province to continue. It is only at the point where the line will cross the Laurentian range in the province of Quebec, and pass in a southeasterly direction to reach the city of Quebec, that it will begin to reach the first fringe of settlement; and do our lion, friends expect that we are going to sit here -we, whose duty it is to carefully scan every detail of a measure of this kind, we who sit for the province of Quebec-(and not know even approximately where that line is going to pass in that province ; that we are to be content with being simply told that, it passes in the vicinity of Lake Abl-tibi, and nothing more ? Surely, we would be fulfilling in a very indifferent manner our duty as members of the opposition in this House, if, when called on to look into every detail of an agreement of this kind -in making examination which my right hon. friend stated again this morning would require time and should be made with carewe got absolutely no information on this important question.
AVhile we were still discussing that question, another very important point cropped up, and one which necessarily must be considered under this very clause of the agreement ; that was, the question of the transportation of grain ; and what did we find ? We found our hon. friend from North Norfolk (Mr-. Charlton), who, according to the right hon. Prime Minister, is one of the best authorities in this country on grain transportation and transportation in general, maintaining in this House a proposition which is not generally admitted by any means throughout this country, and which I venture to say is contradicted by the most prominent railway men in the country. That proposition was that at the present moment, not in the near future, grain could be transported cheaper by rail than by water.
Under certain conditions.

And my hon. friend stated that there was every prospect of this very railway serving not only as a colonization road, but as the cheapest way of transporting grain from the west to the port of Quebec. That was the proposition of my hon. friend. It was strongly controverted by the hon. member for St. Mary's (Hon. Mr. Tarte) and other members of this House. Not an expert in this matter, but one anxious to obtain information, I may say that that proposition has been denied to me by every man who has any experience of transportation who has spoken to me on the subject since this important question has been under discussion. We in this House who are not experts, who are lawyers, doctors, merchants, are called upon to consider, this most important question of the utility of this road as a grain transporting road, and we have not one jot or tittle of information on this subject. My hon. friends who sit on the treasury benches, although perhaps better informed than I am on this point, would be very much embarrassed indeed if they were asked to answer the very simple question in regard to the rates of freight and in regard itlo' the comparative value of water or rail as methods of transportation. My hon. friend the Minister of Justice or the acting Minister of Railways and Canals would be greatly embarrassed if they were asked a question on this point on which we all require information at this very moment-the rate of freight from the city of Winnipeg to the city of Quebec by rail anl water route. They could not answer. They could not give us the rate of freight per bushel of grain, by the rail and water route, and the rate by the water route solely, from Port Arthur to Quebec. We should have before us tabulated statements giving in
