detail tbe rates of freight on every line at present carrying freight from the west to Canadian ports. The government promised that a commission would be appointed to enlighten parliament before any decisiou was submitted with reference to transportation, and I have no doubt that one of the first reports of that commission will be to place at our disposal complete information with regard to freight rates. Now, Sir, I submit that it is only fair for the government to tell us that they have a policy as to railway development in the North-west, and that they intend to construct their railway on certain definite principles. They should tell us through what kind of country this line will go when it starts out from Winnipeg west, and whether it will go through a country already settled and needing railway facilities, or whether it will go through a country susceptible of settlement and cultivation. They should tell us approximately where the location of this line will be. I cannot be told when I am asking for that information, that I am taking up uselessly the time of the committee. In order to facilitate the work of the committee we should at least have that information.

I am very glad you are in the Chair, Mr. Deputy Speaker, because this afternoon when a gentleman of less experience occupied your position, there was a difficulty in getting him to realize that this measure cannot go through until the government will give us reasonable information upon which to form an opinion. I heard a gentleman on our side say that we were to facilitate its passage. In one sense that is perfectly correct. This Bill is to go through, but it will only go through if we get such information as will facilitate its passage. Although I recognize the power of numbers behind the government, I am not prepared to give up all hope yet that something may arise that will prevent this Bill passing through the House. I feel that as the discussion proceeds from day to day, there is some indication that enough will be elected to prevent the passage of this Bill. With the object of securing what we believe to be in the best interests of the country, we are endeavouring to elicit, even though it be by slow degrees, whatever information the government possesses. What has transpired justifies me in sayng that even if we were in possession of every particle of information which the government has, it would be no very adequate supply. However, that may be, we are entitled to a full and free statement of all the information they have. I resent and repudiate the insinuation frequently indulged in by gentlemen opposite, that we are discussing this Bill in order to delay the House. We are discussing it to elicit information, and it is a serious commentary upon the action of the government, that although we have been Mr. MONK.
discussing the Bill for weeks, not until we got into committee were we able to get any substantial information beyond the meagre quota in a fanciful speech made by the Prime Minister when he introduced the Bill. To-day the Prime Minister told us the one reason for railway transportation in the past being more expensive than water transportation, was, that transhipment could not be effected so rapidly from cars as from boats, and he hoped that in the near future this line would be able to do its transhipment as rapidly as freight is transhipped from boats. Now, that is all imagination and hope on the part of the Prime Minister, and yet that is the kind of thing we have to guide us in coming to a decision on this measure. Let the government give us the facts so that we can exercise our judgment upon them, and then there wTill be no great necessity for serious delay. The right lion, gentleman told us also that he believed there would be so great a saving in the near future by reason of improvement in railways, that carriage on land would be as cheap as carriage on water. He thought that this might be brought about by shipment from some point west of Winnipeg to the Atlantic coast without breaking bulk. Well, such an argument as that shows that the Prime Minister is driven to resort to very feeble arguments indeed, in defence of his project.
They must know perfectly well, if they consider the matter at all, that the question of rapid transhipment is not material when it becomes a question of carriage by rail from ocean to ocean. The right lion, gentleman has told us that in a few days a pamphlet will be published, containing all the information possessed by the government with reference to this transcontinental line, but if the government have valuable information in their possession, should they not have laid it before the committee rather than keep it for publication in a pamphlet ? In what form and under what auspices is this pamphlet to be issued ? Is it to be a campaign sheet or is it not ? I am sorry that the right lion, gentleman is not present, but perhaps the Postmaster General can give the information. When the measure was introduced a month ago, he had no information, and in the speech delivered a few nights ago he showed that he knew very little about it, but perhaps he may be able to tell us something about this pamphlet. Is it the intention to submit it, before publication, to this committee ? If that pamphlet is to be issued as an official document, professing to give a fair synopsis of the information in the possession of the cabinet and which ought to be in the possession of parliament, it ought to be submitted to the committee and be sanctioned by the committee. We have been informed to-day that the government expert is no less a person than the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton). That

will be very reassuring to tlie people of this country, who have been wondering for some time where the government had stored away these mountains of information which they say they possess. It was difficult to understand wliat basis of fact the government had for entering into this bargain, and it will be reassuring .to the public to know that the hon. member for North Norfolk is the expert of the government at this crisis in our affairs. If the government could in any way add to the weight of the pamphlet, it would be by having it published with the imprimatur of the hon. member for North Norfolk as the chief government expert. The hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Heyd) admitted that he spoke solely for the purpose of killing time. It was hardly necessary for him to give that information to the House, for that appears to be the distinctive characteristic of all his speeches on this question. It is quite evident that, for some reason or other, the government are anxious for delay. The hon. gentleman, however, tried to make hon. members on this side his accomplices, but so long as the government refuse to bring down the information we require, which is necessary in order to obtain some idea of what is behind this scheme, the charge made by the hon. gentleman comes with ill-grace from that side of the House. The right hon. gentleman told us last night very emphatically that he has no more information to give as to the route and also that there will be no change or modification in the plan. We are dealing now with the second section, which provides for the ratification of the agreement between the government and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. In what position will we be if we adopt the second section ? The right lion, the First Minister told us, with a considerable degree of satisfaction, that when the Canadian Pacific Railway was projected, the agreement was very indefinite. Even the Pacific port was not agreed upon, but was left to be settled later, and he said that that indefiniteness was in marked contrast with the present Bill. In this contract, he said, we have defined where the Pacific terminus is to be. I want to call attention to the fact that nothing of the kind is provided by the agreement. What it provides is that the Pacific ocean port shall be at or near Port Simpson or such other port in British Columbia, as may be agreed upon. Therefore, when we pass this measure, we leave it entirely in the hands of the government to settle where that terminus shall be. We leave it to the [DOT] government, if they see fit, to log-roll on this question, and make it serve such purposes as they may desire. We have a definite terminus in the east and an indefinite terminus in the west, and we have a line as indefinite and as uncertain as possible between these two points. In the Grand Trunk Bill, while we had certainly no very definite information, we had some
landmarks to guide the way. We had a definite point of commencement at Moncton. The road was to run through the central portion of the province of New Brunswick to the city of Quebec, then within fifty miles of Lake Abitibi, north of Lake Nepigon to Winnipeg, thence on to Edmonton and by the Peace river pass or the Pine river pass to the Pacific coast. Not one of these points.is mentioned in the contract. The line is left perfectly indefinite so that the determination of the route will be left at the discretion of the government and the company. So indefinite is the line that they canot decide the point of separation between the prairie and the mountain sections, and in the event of disagreement this is to be settled by arbitration. So vague and indefinite is the line of this railway that the draughtsman of this contract has seen fit to incorporate in it this brief clause-clause 3-which says :
The said line of railway shall be constructed wholly upon Canadian territory.
This clause has been inserted in order that this railroad, which is so vaguely described, shall not altogether escape from Canadian soil. I do not apprehend that this clause Is put in as buncombe or for the purpose of appealing to the electorate. I am to believe, is put in bona fide, with the honest intention of keeping this line so that it will not escape to the south or the north and slip from Canadian territory.

Yesterday, during the progress of this debate, the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) was good enough to admit that the intention at the outset was that this line should be an American road and should pass from Winnipeg to Minneapolis, where it would! connect with the main line of the Grand Trunk, and that Duluth was to be the point at which the great lakes should be reached. The Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) intimated that it might reach some point about Nepigon bay. I presume they are endeavouring to make a deal for the *charter which Mr. Conmee holds there on account of his pulp and fishing concession. As the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) seems to be put forward to do the wind act in this business, I would like to ask him if be has figured out the questions of distances, freight rates and so on, in reaching Nepigon bay and the relative distances to Minneapolis and Duluth, from the North-west.
Carried.

I was askiug the hon. gentleman a question. He seems a little loath to answer. Let me tell the hon. gentlemen we are going to have more information before this Bill passes. Possibly the Minister of Labour could give us some information on this point or is he still figuring out the mileage of the Canada At-

lantic' Railway? Perhaps the minister can give us some information as to how much money has been speht on the Quebec bridge. Is it true that the bonds of that bridge company have been handed out at 60 cents on the dollar, in order that when the bridge is utilized for this railway the gentlemen may rake in the full 100 cents. All silent, all dumb ! Well, now, I do not know on whom else to call; the Minister of Public Works has nothing to do with this railway. I understand that he, like the Minister of Customs, is on strike. The Minister of Customs I was surprised to hear the other day rise and state that there was no truth in the rumour that he had been opposed to this project. I am inclined *to think, after gazing upon his face day after day, while this discussion was going on, while the ex* Minister of Railways and Canals was taking the stand he did, that in his heart the Minister of Customs would have followed the Minister of Railways and Canals had it not been for the sweets of office. Perhaps he may be able to tell us what is the distance between the point where this road will touch Nepigon bay and the main line of the road north of Lake Nepigon. Can the Postmaster General tell us? Can the chief whip ? Can the first lieutenant of the chief whip ? Can the member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) tell us ?
I cannot.

Has the Minister of Labour given consideration, to this aspect of the case-that in ease the Grand Trunk Railway extend their line from Minneapolis to Winnipeg, the line from Winnipeg east, if under the control of the Grand Trunk, would be practically useless ?
I do not wish to interrupt you.

Then I will turn to the Minister of Finance. In the earlier part of this debate the Minister of Finance made this reference to the eastern section :
I will quote further from Sir Sandford Fleming's report of 1864. I may say that there are three routes described-the southern route near the state of Maine, the central route, which is the subject of the present discussion, and the route along the Baie des Chaleurs which was afterwards adopted for the Intercolonial Railway.
In referring to that part of the Finance Minister's speech I subsequently took the liberty of giving the elevations to show that the road had a series of grades, many of them reaching eighty feet to the mile, and that consequently the road) was an impossibility as a freight route. The member for Bellechasse (Mr. Talbot) interrupted me, and stated that that was not the route at all, that the route they were going to pursue was down close to the main border. 1 [DOT]would like to ask the Minister of Finance Mr. HUGHES (Victoria).
which is the route ? Is it the central route ? Now, no prompting by the Minister of Labour. I know the Minister of Labour is aspiring to be the leader of the party, I know that he lias emissaries out through the length and breadth of the country, trying to undermine the Minister of Finance as leader of the party. But the Minister of Finance is nearly as old as the Minister of Labour, and is as old a parliamentarian, and he does not want any prompting by the Minister of Labour. 1 am quite satisfied he will be able to paddle his own canoe in this matter if the Minister of Labour will be good enough to let him alone. Now, I would like to ask the Minister of Finance which is the route that is to be followed in that part of the country :	Is it the central route as
pointed out by the Minister of Finance in this speech ?
I am glad to tell my hon. friend that the eastern route is to be from the city of Moncton to the city of Quebec by the shortest practicable route, as may be defined and determined by engineers.

The member for Bellechasse pointed out that the member for Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson) showed clearly that Mr. Davey's line, that is the line through the central part of New Brunswick, was a diagonal line and had no relation whatever to the new project. Yet it is within the memory of the members of this House that this is the very line that the Prime Minister, in his opening speech of this debate, pointed out as the line they were going to follow. The Prime Minister pointed out that Mr. Davey's line had been surveyed, and that that was the line they were to follow, and that it was 209 miles from Moncton to Edmundston. Well, the member for Bellechasse says that the member for Westmoreland showed clearly that Mr. Davey's line was a diagonal one and had no relation to the new project. In my address I referred to some things that had been said by the Finance Minister, and I was interrupted by the member for Bellechasse who said :
The hon. gentleman is not at all following this route that this proposed scheme is going to follow.
And he went on to say in his own speech where the line was going to be :
The only explanations and locations to be considered of real value are the ones made by Mr. Tetu in 1889 and 1890, and one made by Mr. Hoare in 1891. That covers the entire territory.
In my remarks I pointed out that from Quebec these gentlemen were claiming that was the shortest line. I pointed out that it was absolutely impossible to get such a line of road as these gentlemen were claiming, and I gave some facts and figures. I find that the hon. member for Bellechasse-

I am sorry he is not in his -place-referring to myself, said :
I notice, however, reading the unrevised edition of ' Hansard ' quoting ills speech, that he has thought prudent to eliminate certain figures which he mentioned in the House in relation to distances from points of the Intercolonial Railway to imaginary points of this new government construction. He said that eight miles from Trois Pistoles was the starting point of the central route described by the hon. Minister of Finance, when in reality Trois Pistoles, by as straight a line as the crow flies, is forty-four miles to the nearest point of the projected railway.
I may point out to that hon. gentleman that the statement is absolutely untrue, not one word of truth in it, that neither directly nor indirectly was one (figure or one word which I uttered in the House elided from the report of my speech by any one with my knowledge or consent. I may point out further that when I was speaking of the central route, I was taking it as propounded by the Finance Minister, and that central route starts eight miles south of Trois Pistoles. The hon. member for Bellechasse undertook to point out that we were objecting to the route when any one knows who heard my remarks that I was very distinct in saying that X did not object to the construction of a road through that region because I had previously supported a I.iberal subsidy to a road through that country, but that my object was to -point out that the statement of those hon. gentlemen who claimed that they were going to effect a saving of 200 or 240 miles in distance was groundless. The hon. member for Bellechasse himself gives the whole matter away in his speech. He points out that:
Although the surveyed line may not have the advantages a-s a through route, by its position i-t is admirably adapted to colonization purposes and it would get a share of foreign business without a doubt.
Then he goes on to quote the report of Mr. Tetu in regard to the location of the line, as follows :
The line follows the valley of the Cabano to the head of Long lake, then along the St. Francis valley to the foot of Lake Pohenego-mook, passing at a point close to the United States boundary line. The line so far proved to be very good for grades and alignment, the country along this course rises so gradually that no grade need exceed fifty-three feet per mile.
That is the line to connect with the line from Three Rivers by way of Temiscouata lake to Edmundston, and I was surprised to find the hon. member for Bellechasse does not know the rivers and lakes of the region which he has the honour to represent in this House. . Then he goes on to point out the routes that the government instructed these engineers to follow. To quote further, the engineers' instructions were :
The main object of the exploration with which you have been entrusted by letter of the
31st of August last, should be to discover an easy line for a railway and to prepare a sketch of the level from St. Anselme to Lake Etche-min, and from Lake Etehemin to the frontier, passing through St. Justine. You should also explore from Lake Etehemin, taking a northeasterly direction to the frontier of New Brunswick.
I spoke of the grades. The hon. gentleman goes on to quote :
Grade.-Although, owing to the proximity of the mountains, I was sometimes obliged to go round. I always maintained an easy grade never exceeding one foot in a hundred, with the exception of one-half mile, where I was obliged to allow 18 inches to the hundred feet.
The hon, member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton), the authority put up by the government in this matter, says that no roadi can be a through route that has grades of more thau four-tenths of a foot to the mile, while this has grades of one foot to the hundred. Then, between the 85th and 100th mile the report of the engineer goes on to say :
At this point, I am at the height of 1,450 feet above the level of the sea, in a region of mountains, but the line which I have followed is in a fertile valley, well wooded with maple, birch, &c., through which run numbers of small streams, tributaries to the lake.
I want to point out here, Mr. Chairman, that this line that he is following starts from Levis, which is in latitude 46*50 north, that it runs in a southerly direction to Lake Etehemin, where it reaches latitude 46:20. In other words, the air line distance is away over 30 miles. Thence, it turns northeasterly till it reaches the corner of Maine at latitude 47*25 north, or in other words, it runs south 30 miles and then twists north 70 miles. After leaving LSvis it zig-zags up and down before it reaches Edmundston until it covers a distance of 120 miles, running south, thence running away north, and thence running south again. I afn not taking into consideration the direct air line at all. Now, we will take the figures of the mileage. The hon. member for Bellechasse admits that there is one pass between the 85th and 100th mile, 1,450 feet high. Then he goes on :	*
The summit is reached at the head of Lake Etehemin, 3S1 miles from St. Anselme, at an elevation of 762 feet above the Quebec Central Railway at St. Anselme, or 962 feet above the Intercolonial Railway at St. Henri.
In the remarks which I had the honour to address to the House, I clearly pointed out that we could not get through any pass from Lake Etehemin to the River Ouelle at a less height than 1,306 feet. I think that the hon. gentleman goes me one better, because, according to him, this road will be away up in the air, about 100 feet above the point I gave. According to the figures of the hon. member for Bellechasse himself, I find that there are two points on* that route where the road will reach an altitude

of from 1,300 to 1,500 feet before it can get through.
What is the grade to the mile ?

There is no instrumental survey, despite the statements made by bon. gentlemen in the House. I have searched the records in Quebec and 1 have searched the records of the Railway Department here, and I find that there is no instrumental survey of this route either directly or indirectly, and when these lion, gentlemen stand up and pretend that there is an instrumental survey they are either deliberately or unintentionally misrepresenting the facts to this House and to the country. After starting at sea level at Quebec you must climb up over two grades nearly 1,500 feet.
You can not get four-tenths per cent grades there ?

No, 1 to 11 per cent grades would be the very lowest grades that could be got by taking longer mileages. As I pointed out a year or two ago, it is important that a road in this district should be constructed for colonization purposes, and I said that the Liberal-Conservative members from Ontario were prepared to give it a bonus of $6,400 per mile. I said that we were willing to assist our French Canadian fellow-countrymen in the development of this territory by a bonus to the extent of $6,400 per mile, so that the people could get their crops out, but when it comes to a road that will cost. _$50,000 per mile with grades so great that it will be impossible to haul trains over them we should pause and ask for more information. I would ask the hon. Minister of Justice if he has any data as to surveys of this route. I would like to ask the right hon. Prime Minister, who is always courteous, if he has any data in his. possession	in	relation to a survey.
Was there ever an instrumental survey made, and if so is it possible to obtain a report on the route from Levis passing through the Etchemin pass or through the St. Anselme pass to New Brunswick ? My hon. friend has no information. Then I want to know where are the mountains of information that were available ? I am afraid they were largely in the air. I regret - that the hon. member for Victoria, N.B. (Hon. Mr. Costigan), is not in his place. I regret also that the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Russell) is not in his place. However, before this debate is over, I trust that we shall have the opportunity of seeing these gentlemen here. We find the hon. member for Victoria, N.B., speaking of this route as if it were practically a level one. These gentlemen are seemingly like the Minister of Finance; they know nothing about the route. The Minister of Justice is simply interested in the part that concerns him, Mr. HUGHES (Vlotorfa).
about the city of Quebec ; he knows nothing of it after it crosses the river to Levis. The Minister of Customs is on strike ; and the fountain of information, the hon. member for North Norfolk, has been given the tip to keep his mouth shut. They have closed down on him, and he is not to be allowed to speak any mere in this debate. But we have the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Wade) locating the line. This is about the seventieth location that has been given through New Brunswick :	He
says :
The line will start at ChaudiSre junction and go to Connors station, from Connors to Ed-muudston, from Edmundston to St. Leonard, from St. Leonard to Plaster Rook, from Plaster Rock to Boiestown, from Boiestown to Chip-man, and from Chipman to Barry's Mills, on the Intercolonial Railway.
Suppose we examine that. We will take the figures given by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Talbot), who stated that from Cliaudiere Junction to Connor's station, by the St. Anselme route, the distance is 209* miles. You can easily add ten or fifteen" miles before you get any proper grade. But I will take his figures. Take 209 miles from Cliaudibre Junction to Edmundston ; then, from Edmundston to Moncton via Berry's Mills, 260 miles, by the only available route short of climbing up mountain sides. That makes the distance from Cliaudiere Junction to the city of Moncton 469 miles-less than twenty miles short of the present Intercolonial Railway. I am taking their own figures, given by the hull, member for Bellechasse for the province of Quebec and the hon. member for Annapolis for the province of New Brunswick.
Surely they will not go on with it.

I think they are proposing to withdraw the Bill. I have here the official report of the Geological Survey of that part of New Brunswick to be traversed by this road. This is the Fredericton and Andover quarter sheet map of New Brunswick for 1902 ; and by the route laid down by the hon. member for Annapolis, between the Little Salmon river and the Tobique river, the elevations are shown to be 320 feet; and on the St. John river, before the Little Salmon flows into it, the elevation is about 355 feet. Between these two points, in less than five miles, you have to climb an elevation of 355 feet over a mountain ridge more than 1,000 feet in height; then down into the valley again to 320 feet. Then at Plaster Rock the elevation is about 365 feet. That-is at the present ter-miuus of the Tobique valley branch of the Canadian Pacific Railway. Now, our friend Mr. Wade says they are going to run from there to Boiestown. I want to point out that in that district in less than ten miles from Plaster Rock the land rises from 365

feet to 1,200 feet, and the rise is not by any means gradual, but is over a series of ridges running at right angles to the line of the proposed railway. That means a rise in less than ten miles of very nearly 000 feet, or upwards of eighty feet on the average to the mile ; and our lion, friend from North Norfolk said that anything over twenty feet to the mile is impossible for a transcontinental or through road over which we can haul grain. All one has to do is to take the figures given by the hon. member for Bellechasse as to the mountain ridges in tlie province of Quebec, and you find that the figures I gave when I had the honour of addressing the House on this subject were far within the mark ; because unwittingly the hon. member for Bellechasse has proven conclusively that you have to. cross two mountain ridges, the lowest 1,306 feet and the highest nearly 500 feet higher than that, before you can get into the corner of New Brunswick. Now, I would like to ask the Postmaster General or the Minister of Public Works or the Minister of Commerce or the Minister of Justice, is it their intention to continue this road from Levis on to Moncton ? What does the Minister of Public Works say about it ?
The Premier answered that this afternoon.
I have not heard it. Does the Minister of Public Works say that the Prime Minister still persists in running this road over these mountain ridges V
You had his answer to-day.
I would be very much pleased if the minister would repeat it again.
He said yes.
He did not say that he was going to build it over the mountain ridges.

The hon. member for Victoria, N.B., takes a different route still. He says :
It will avoid the height of land by following up the valleys of the streams which fall into the St. Lawrence. Passing by that range of mountains, it will cross one or two small tributaries which flow into the St. John, it will reach the south side of that range of mountains and follow down until it comes to that point near the boundary lake, where it joins the River St. Francis.
Then he goes on :
You go down that valley, you strike the valley of the St. John in Canadian territory, and go on to Edmundston and Grand Falls, and thence strike across the country to Moncton.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I have pointed out in a rather imperfect manner this evening, what I pointed out in greater detail on a former occasion, that to cross the mountain 332
ridges where these hon. gentlemen claim they are going to run that road in New Brunswick, they will have to attain an elevation of from 1,500 feet to 1,700 feet, and then run down to 300 or 400 feet in the valley in less than ten miles. They will either have to do that or take the more circuitous route through the valley of the St. John.
And save twenty miles.

They will save less than twenty miles. They might save twenty miles if they could take a one and a half or one per cent grade, but if they take the grade of twenty feet in the mile spoken of by the member for North Norfolk their road from Levis to Moncton by the route proposed by these gentlemen, will be from five to fifteen miles longer than the Intercolonial Railway. There is no point on the Intercolonial Railway between Levis and Moncton higher than seven hundred feet, except at the Matapedia heights, but on this route proposed by these gentlemen opposite acc< rding to the engineers, there is an elevation of ],30G feet in one pass and 1,806 in another, which the member for Bellechasse states to be correct.
And he was supporting tlie-project.

Oh, certainly. I see the member for North Norfolk is reflecting, and perhaps he could now give us the mileage between Nepigon bay and where this road would pass along the north shore of Lake Superior.

I was reflecting on the point referred to by my hon. friend in re-i gard to the Wisconsin Central, and I would be glad if he could give me the mileage of that road and the southern and northern termini, and the principal points it passes through.
Certainly. The *Wisconsin Central runs from the 'city of Chicago via Waukesha, which is eighteen miles west of Milwaukee, to Fond du Lac and to Neenali, with a braucli running on to Manitowoe.
It doesn't go near Norfolk ?

It doesn't go near Norfolk, although Norfolk might come to it. It has two branches to Lake Michigan. and Mr. Charles M. Hays being an astute railway man in selecting that road knew his business. Of these two branches one to Milwaukee and the other to Manitowoe, on the west shore of Lake Michigan. These are points that are already controlled by the Grand Trunk ; the harbour of Grand Haven and others. Then the Wisconsin Central runs westerly. I trust the hon



member (Mr. Charlton) will remember this -I beg his pardon he is only a commissioner.

Oh, no, they dangle the commissionersbip in front of him when they want him to vote all right. You can always tell when the member for North Norfolk is going to fall back into line. This is the way it is done. Take up your newspaper some morning, and you will find a telegram dated Washington, stating, ' It is current rumour that the joint commission will meet at an early date next fall.' See the member for North Norfolk walk up the street that morning with an altogether different bearing. His hat stands a little straighter on his head and before a day or two rolls around the hon. member (Mr. Charlton) will be hobnobbing with the Prime Minister, and then he is put up to do some job the same as he was put up to do the other day.
I rise to a point of order. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Hughes) commenced to answer my question about the Wisconsin Central and he branched off,

I apologize for the digression. We get up as far as Abbotsford and then a branch line runs to Ashland on the southern shore of Luke Superior, and from that point the Wisconsin Central has running rights over the Northern Pacific Railway to the city of Duluth. They have that leased for 99 years to the city of Duluth. Then they come down to the main line which runs to the cities of Minneapolis and St. Paul or a very few miles from them, and they have a 99 years' running lease into these two places.

I am very much obliged to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hughes) for the very definite information he has given, and his detailed knowledge of the question leads me to wonder whether he may not have been employed by Mr. Charles 51. Hays in connection with that road, and In that capacity may have acquired this information which surprises me as to its definiteness.
5Ir. HUGHES (Victoria). I can tell the hon. gentleman (Mr. Charlton) that Charles M. Hays has not done me the honour of employing me. I was not aware until now that Mr. Hays was employing members of parliament. I thank the hon. gentleman (Mr. Charlton) for the suggestion. I regret to have to apply it, but it lends further colour to the ardour with which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Charlton) threw himself into the defence of this abominable scheme. However, the hon. gentleman (air. Charlton) must not measure other people's corn in his own bushel. I have never been purchased yet. Like the old darkey who was brought up for stealing water melons : He

thanked the Lord in his infinite mercy that he never was caught before.

Mr. Chairman, there seems to have been a lack of sincere and businesslike argument during this debate on the government side of the House. It is true that this afternoon the hon. member for South Brant (Mr. Heyd) avowed that he was talking against time. It seems to me that a great many others on the government side of the House have been talking against time instead of meeting this question fairly. The leader of the government announced that this railway was to be built for two purposes-to get free of the necessity of depending upon the bonding privilege, and to obtain a cheap outlet for the products of the west. But, instead of that, as the hon. member for York (Mr. Maclean) put it, the whole intent of the scheme seems to be a vote-catcher for political purposes in each of the provinces. Whether it may have any effect in some of the provinces I cannot say, but I do not think it will have such effect in the province of Prince Edward Island. We have in that province an independent paper, so-called, though for the past ten or twelve years it has been a strong supporter of the Liberal party. Speaking of this paper the other day, the hon. member for King's P.E.I. (Mr. Hughes), made some disparaging remarks concerning it, and intimated that it did not really understand the situation. Now, as regards this railway being a vote-catcher, let me read an extract from this paper to show what effect it will have in that province. This is what the Charlottetown ' Guardian ' says :
Following closely the discussion upon the railway agreemnt we have failed to find so far any argument or hint that Prince Edward Island can in any way be profited by it. The ' Patriot ' and the ' Pioneer,' the organs of the government in this province, content themselves with reciting the arguments addressed to the people of the west showing how they may be favourably affected. But surely we have a right to consider how our own people are to he affected. If we do not look out for our own interests we cannot expect the people of the west to look out for us. Eighteen hundred miles of railway are to be constructed by the government and the cost added to the public debt. The average cost of Canadian railways good and bad has been over $56,000 per mile. From what we know of the country between Moncton and Winnipeg it is vastly more difficult than that through which most Canadian railways have been built, and must in all human probability prove more costly. The cost may therefore be 100 to 110 millions for the government portion, exclusive of the guarantee given for the western portion. In proportion to population one fiftieth part of this debt must
be saddled upon Prince Edward Island, a matter of two millions of dollars or upwards. This means approximately $100 per family in Prince Edward Island. Are we to incur this new and heavy obligation without any compensating advantage, absolutely without any return? Surely this is a point worth considering.
But if we come to federal affairs we find the same incongruity prevailing. The time was when Canadian Liberalism stood for something. In the early days of confederation It stood for the abolition of dual representation, for the introduction of the ballot in elections, for the trial of election petitions by the judges for the reform of the Senate and various other reforms many of which were in time adopted. Later it stood for a low tariff as against protection, for the closest economy in administration and against any increase of the public debt. To-day the tariff has ceased to be an issue in our politics, the Liberal party haring adopted what was essentially the policy of their predecessors in office,.a protective tariff with attendant bounties and bonuses. As for the rest we have the Liberal party In power, spending many millions more year by year than the Conservatives ever expended and now proposing to add directly and indirectly a hundred millions of dollars to the obligations and liabilities of the country. In fact we have come to the time when the one great issue between our two political parties is whether we shall or shall not immdiately set about the construction of a second transcontinental railway.
The absurdity of facing such an issue oil Liberal or Conservative party grounds must be apparent to every intelligent citizen. Why should Liberals as such, or Conservatives, because they are Conservatives, be asked to support or condemn this proposal ? It is a vast proposition in railway construction, a huge enterprise to be entered upon or rejected, a proposition to he considered by practical business men on business principles, but what on earth has it to do with party, or party principles ? Ought not every man with his own good and that of his posterity at heart, seeking the true welfare of his country, to approach this question with an open and an independent mind ? What can party do for a man in aiding him to come to a right judgment on this momentous question ? In the face of such an issue are we to be told that we ought to support it because it is put forward by Sir Wilfrid Laurier, or that we ought to oppose it because Mr. Borden and his lieutenants tell us that we ought to do so ? What can partyism do for us in such a crisis but to confuse our minds, darken our undertaking and present the entire issue under a misleading light ?
Especially is this view of the case applicable to readers of the ' Guardian ' and to the people of Prince Edward Island. We are an isolated community and our reason is convinced that in many respects, no doubt because of our isolation and the smallness of our numbers, our just requirements and urgent needs have been overlooked. The Dominion has not kept its compact with us in regard to our winter service. it has been most unjust in the matter of our telegraph service, it has been regardless of our interests in the matter of through rates for freight, passengers and express goods. Suddenly we have this vast proposition of spending a hundred millions on a new transcontinental railway thrust upon us, and we are told the country cannot wait because time does not wait. Instant acceptance is demanded of us for this vast and most important enterprise

instant acceptance is demanded of us who have waited so long for the same rates and the same rights in regard to various public services as are enjoyed by the people of other provinces. Why should we become suddenly enchanted with the prospect of a second Intercolonial laid alongside of the first, a Grand Trunk Pacific alongside of the Canadian Pacific? Is it not a time for island people to preserve an open mind, an independent judgment and attitude ?
Now, this is a fair way of looking at the question. The people of Prince Edward. Island, you will find, are not very strongly in favour of the scheme which, while apparently catching on to the voters of every other province, entirely ignores the transportation facilities which we have been asking for since confederation. I think that, contrary to the ideas of the hon. member for King's, the people of Prince Edward Island, when the time comes, will not look with favour upon a proposition of this kind, entered into and pushed through which such haste. But the proposition made by the leader of the opposition was not that this line should be the main outlet for the grain and other products of the west, but that, during the winter season when the lakes were frozen up, this would serve for an outlet and also for an inlet for the products of the east and west. The leader of the government pointed out that in railway transportation smaller packages do not stand in the same class as grain, and in order to have complete control of the system straight through, we should have this connecting link from North Bay to Porth Arthur; so, while the navigation of the lakes is closed up, the smaller packages of freight would stand more tariff and could be taken in and brought out in that manner. Now, the minister says that we will develop our lake traffic. But the lake route, as has been acknowledged from the other side of the House, is the cheapest way to bring out the products. Thefi; you have got to develop the resources at either end of the lake by erecting elevators, and by the development of canals at the eastern end of the lake. That is one method by which you can get a cheaper transportation. But you cannot force the products of the west, as I pointed out some time ago, out of their natural course, the course of easiest resistance; and you cannot force the products of the west to come out over an all rail route when there is a cheaper route that can and will be developed, but that cheaper route will only be retarded by expending millions of money on a project that the country does not need for years.

great transportation problem of getting the grain of the west out by the cheapest route in order to compete with the transportation facilities of our neighbours to the south of us. While they were operated during the early stages they were far in advance of the railways, but the railways have become so strong .in the United States that for years they have been retarding the development of water-ways because they feared them as competitors. I pointed out in the House a few days ago that in several states they have influenced the laws to such an extent that they have been able to secure the restriction that only three miles of canals can be constructed within one year and that a canal cannot pass through a borough or town. The history of the Erie canal will prove the feasibility of water-ways and it proves that the canal system is the cheapest transporter of heavy products. I propose to point out some of those reasons for the benefit of the House. In the first place, these boats go through to Quebec with a cargo of grain at three cents per bushel. On their return, they load with pulp wood at different points 'on the St. Lawrence, which they take to the cities and towns on the shores of Lake Erie. After they discharge their cargoes of pulp wood, they load with coal for Duluth, Port Arthur and Fort William. So that these boats have three freights-the grain freight to Quebec, and the pulp wood and coal on their

way back. Assuming that this railway is ever built-and most people believe it never will be-and assuming it will carry grain to Quebec and Moncton, what return freight Will it get. Any hon. gentleman who has ever travelled over the Canadian Pacific Railway knows that after leaving Sudbury and passing along to the head of Lake Superior, you see train after train of empty box cars going from the east to the west. That is due to the fact-and I am referring particularly to the summer months-that the Canadian Pacific Railway bring their return freight to the town of Owen Sound, where they load it on their boats and then transfer it to their trains at Fort William. This railway will be in the same position as the Canadian Pacific Railway in going from east to west. It will haul nothing back but empty box cars. The trade has developed to an abnormal extent at Buffalo, according to the reports, which gives the figures from year to year, and which are much more reliable than statements given by an hon. gentleman in this House and taken from some gentleman outside of the House. There is only 900 miles of distance between Chicago and New York city, and these reports show that no grain is carried by rail between those points except what may be carried in the winter months. In the summer the whole trade goes by way of Chicago to Buffalo in vessels. From Chicago to Buffalo is about 900 miles and from Buffalo to New York some 400 miles. The grain is carried in vessels from Chicago to Buffalo where it is transferred into elevators and from the elevators into the cars and taken out to New York, and the whole cost so carried is cheaper than it costs to haul it 900 miles by train. That statement was made by the hon. member for St. Mary's division'(Hon. Mr. Tarte), and no hon. gentleman can produce any report to the contrary. The grain is carried 900 miles in vessels, the elevator charges are paid, and it is then carried 400 miles by train, cheaper than it could be carried from Chicago to Buffalo by rail, and the port of Buffalo handles 325.000.000 bushels of grain in a single season. I think, therefore, that the government should have more substantial reasons to place before the public than the fact that a gentleman named Scott, in the city of Quebec, has had attributed to him a statement, which I am bound to say, he will not shoulder, that grain can be carried 1,400 miles over this proposed system of railway at five and a half cents per bushel. At the beginning the Prime Minister urged several reasons why this scheme should be undertaken at once. One was on account of the congestion of traffic in the North-west, which, we are told, rendered action immediately, necessary. But the facts which have since come to light have exploded that reason entirely. It has been shown that the construction of the proposed transcontinental road would afford very little relief to any congestion of traffic that might exist in the North-west. Another reason given was that by this proposed line we would be able to transport all the traffic from the west to the east upon Canadian soil. Yet the policy of the government may have the very opposite effect in directing the traffic of the North-west into American channels. Another reas n given was that we required cheaper transportation ; yet the government have failed to give a single fact to show that this road will afford cheaper transportation of grain from the North-west to the Atlantic ocean. It is true that a new prophet has arisen among them in the last day or two in Hie person of the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton), one of whose claims is the right to change his opinion upon any great question from day to day as it may suit the party he is supporting for the time being. He has made a remarkable statement, one which I am sure will not be endorsed by any practical railway man on the continent of America, that grain can be transported from Winnipeg to the Atlantic ocean for the small sum of five and a half cents a bushel. He intimated that in some mysterious way some great improvements were to be introduced on this new road, something hitherto unheard of, that would enable the road to cut the rates exactly in two. Now the rates for carrying products on railways are based, not upon guess work, but upon wages, on the consumption of coal, on the capital invested-all these things are taken into consideration in making an estimate of the cost of transportation. So I think the prophecy of the hon. member for North Norfolk will not find any believers among practical railway men.
Another reason advanced for pushing forward this scheme was the possibility that the bonding privilege might be withdrawn. Now, Mr. Chairman, the word ' privilege ' itself is a misnomer in this connection, because the bonding privilege was simply an agreement between two parties for their mutual benefit. In this case, if there is any difference, it is in favour of the United States, it is a privilege for them rather than to Canada. But that reason has also been exploded, and now we hear nothing more of it. Then wre are told that this is to be an all-Canadian route, and we are urged to support it on that ground, as though we had not already an all-Canadian route. I say that the whole scheme is a wild and reckless one, and the statements that have been made in its support are of a most misleading character, indeed one would think that they were made with the intention to deceive. The distance between Winnipeg ai d Moncton is stated to be 1,800 miles, but all we know of the territory through which that road is to pass leads us to believe that it is of such a character that it will be most expensive to build a road through it. Why, Sir, the statement that this road could be built at a cost to Canada of only $13,000,000 was ridiculous in the extreme, and that contention also has been abandoned. The ministers are responsible for these misleading statements, they know very well that they are hollow, and we know that they are entirely fictitious.
Now, this enormous expenditure will be barren of results as compared with the advantages we might obtain by utilizing the natural means of communication which nature has placed in our power. Several hon. gentlemen have dwelt upon the advantage the country would derive from making connection between our water-ways and existing rail communication, and yet if the country undertakes this huge expenditure for a useless transcontinental railway, the work of making these connections between the waters of the Georgian bay and the St. Lawrence will have to be delayed for a generation. The development of our natural facilities would be ten times more advantageous to the country than the construction of this transcontinental railway. Any statements made by the member for North Norfolk that grain can be carried for five and a half cents a bushel from Winnipeg to Quebec, will not be supported by any practical railway man on this continent, and yet he is referred to by the Prime Minister as a railway expert whose ipse dixit should be taken without question. This House has a right to have from the government all the information that they possess in regard to the location of the proposed road. It should be borne in mind that the undertaking of a scheme like this may tie the hands of this country from going into something that would be far more advantageous to the country. The time may



come when we shall find that the increase in the debt as a result of this eutopian project may be a damage and an injury to the credit of the country. There may yet be time for delay, yet time to take into consideration whether it is wise to carry out this wild, extravagant project of building a line from Winnipeg to Moncton through an apparently unknown country at such a cost. To talk about $13,000,000 or to attempt to reduce it by any conjuring of an actuary to $8,000,000 or $9,000,000 is so ridiculously absurd that it is not believed by any hon. gentleman in this House and much less will it be believed in the country. However, there is one reason that may be put forward for haste and it is that the longer this matter is held up before the electors the more will it be discredited throughout the whole Dominion of Canada. We had on a former occasion the argument used that a crisis existed in connection witli the Yukon railway. There was no time for delay. There could not be sufficient delay to bring the scheme down to parliament but they must begin work before parliament met. What did the crisis amount to ? Simply nothing. It was a bugbear held up to promote a railway which was no good and which was fortunately defeated by the Senate. There is a possible chance of salvation from a similar means in connection with this road.

I have here a book edited by Mr. J. Cas-jell Hopkins and dedicated to the right hon. Prime Minister. It contains a record of the principal events of last year. According to this work, it was only on the 24th of November last that the announcement
