When Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson and Mr. Hays appeared before the Railway Committee, all that they asked was the right to go on and build this line, they only asked for an Act of incorporation. While this parliament had been in session from the 12th of March to the 30tli of July, no intimation was given to this House that the government intended to assist this great scheme, but on the 30th of July the contract was laid on the Table of this House, binding the government and people of Canada to expend $150,000,000 in aid of this work. Now, Sir, are those Liberal principles ? Are those the principles advocated by these hon. gentlemen when they occupied a seat on this side of the House ? On every platform where they had addressed the people they insisted that no bonuses should be given to assist railways. But now we find that they are going to assist this Grand Trunk Pacific Company, not only by guaranteeing their bonds on the western section, but by building a line for them from Winnipeg to Moncton, without surveys, without explorations, taking this plunge in "the dark, and building a line that will cost from $100,000,000 to $125,000,000.	.
Now, Sir under these circumstances how and when are we to have government ownership of railways in this country '! There is to be no government ownership here. This road is to be operated by the company to whom it is to be handed over, and who, if they do not feel like doing so, will not be obliged to pay one cent to the government as interest or rent.
Now, Sir, I desire to turn your attention for a moment to the province of Prince Edward Island. This railway is called a national transcontinental railway. The Postmaster General as well as the Prime Minister stated that this railway was to open up every province in Canada. I desire now to say that it is not going to be of any advantage to the province of Prince Edward Island. My hon. friend and colleague from King's in that province (Mr. Hughes), a few evenings ago, stated that this railway would develop great coal mines which would be at once opened up through the province of New Brunswick. Now, I would like to ask any hon. gentleman in this House, where are the coal mines existing between Riviere

du Loup and Moncton ? The coal mines are lying east of Moncton, principally, therefore this railway will not in any way develop the coal mines lying east of Moncton. We have now the Intercolonial running from Moncton to Sydney, traversing the country where these great mines of coal and iron exist. This railway is to be built to Moncton, and I presume that the government intend, notwithstanding the efforts that we are making, to build this line of railway, and they will be backed up by their supporters. When that railway goes to Moncton, I have endeavoured to suggest a means by which it can be connected with the province of Prince Edward Island, and I moved an amendment that this company should acquire the railway now in existence between Sackville and Cape Tormentine, and place steamships on the route between Cape Tormentine and Carleton Point in Prince Edward Island, or any other convenient point, and maintain efficient communication winter and summer between Prince Edward Island and the mainland. That amendment was voted down by the government, and they are doing nothing, while asking the people of Prince Edward Island to contribute their full share to build and maintain this railway. They are not doing anything to assist them with regard to their winter communication. In the summer season we have good communication between Prince Edward Island and the mainland, but the great difficulty is in the winter season when the ice forms in the Gulf of St, Lawrence and the straits of Northumberland. The government of Canada agreed with the people of Prince Edward Island at the time of confederation in 1873 that they would maintain an efficient steam communication service winter and summer between Prince Edward Island and the mainland. That compact has not been carried out and the people of the island last year were labouring under as great difficulties almost as those under which they laboured thirty years ago. I, myself, in crossing about the 5tli of March from Prince Edward Island to the mainland on my way to Ottawa to attend to my duties as a representative of the people, was obliged to work my passage over on a little ice boat, and this, notwithstanding the fact that the government bound itself to maintain sufficient steam communication between the island and the mainland. Although we have been in session for 25 or 26 hours, the hon. gentlemen occupying the treasury benches and their supporters behind them have refused to stand up and explain the meaning of this proposition or to give any information in regard to it. If they have no information let them withdraw the measure and let them appeal to the people. There is no mandate from the people to go on with this proposition. I challenge them to appeal to the people and let them have an opportunity of deciding this question. We on the opposition side

of the House are endeavouring to do our duty to our constituents. We desire to have full information before we make a pledge of this kind involving such a large expenditure of public money. We are only doing our duty when we remain 25 or 26 hours in session with no intermission. Although I am not as young as I once was, I am still possessed of sufficient vitality to remain for a whole week and contend in the interests of my constituents and the people of Canada, to stand up for their rights, to see that the information in connection with this matter is brought down and that this government shall not sit quietly on the treasury benches having their relays, they going off one at a time taking their sleep or their comfort while we who are working in the interests of the people are not allowed the means of comfort which they enjoy. Notwithstanding all that we feel it our duty to contend for the people of this country and to stop if possible this large expenditure of public money uselessly thrown away for the purpose of assisting the Grand Trunk Pacific. Now, we have the alternate proposition introduced by the bon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax). Hon. gentlemen opposite say that the railway which extends for 1,800 miles between Winnipeg and Moncton is going to cost $13,000,000 while the proposition of the leader of the opposition to build about 400 miles of railway is going to cost between $60,000,000 and $70,000,000. That is the kind of argument these hon. gentlemen use on the other side of the House. The proposition made by the hon. leader of the opposition is one that will commend itself to the people because it is a measure which will enable us to utilize the resources which we have at our disposal and obviate a reckless expenditure of public money by building a railway through an almost unknown land.

Mr. Chairman, as a young member of this House, I feel it my duty to make a few remarks in regard to this railway proposition before this clause is passed. I would like, before proceeding with that subject, to ask the Minister of Customs (Hon. Mr. Paterson) what caused the reporters of this House to stop taking the speeches made from about three o'clock up to eleven or twelve.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: To discuss the duties of the reporters is certainly out of order altogether, because that is not within our jurisdiction at all. The House has already settled that question.

I will not disobey the rules of the House, but my opinion is that none of the ministers want to answer that question. I have been here since the 12th of March and I took a deep interest in the proceedings of the Railway Committee during the time that they considered this transcontinental railway project.

I notice that the Grand Trunk Railway Company asked for a charter for nothing but the western division, the portion which they are to undertake under the present proposition. The question was threshed out for a long time, and a great many lion, members wanted to know whether this government were going to grant a subsidy to the railway, but we could not get that out of the ministers who attended the meetings of the Railway Committee. All the time that this committee was sitting some one or two of the ministers were hatching a scheme. I think this hatching started with Mr. Hays, tlie person who is trying to run this thing through, and I understand that he was assisted by the right bon. Prime Minister (Rt. Hon. Sir AVilfrid Laurier). It seems to me that they have been able to hatch out the whole scheme, but they have not been able to secure the adherence to it of the hon. exMinister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair).
' The great argument used in the Railway Committee was the need of improved transportation facilities in the west for the carrying out the grain crop. It was generally agreed in the committee that if the Grand Trunk were going to build this road from North Bay to the Pacific they should get some assistance. Some of the members from the maritime provinces got their heads together and compelled Mr. Hays to say in the committee that he was willing to go to Moncton instead of to an Atlantic port. He was willing to do anything, knowing that the government were to build this road so that it did not matter to him. To my mind, the way to relieve the congestion in the west would be to have started the western section first, and, if necessary, assist the Grand Trunk Railway in building an outlet to the lakes. If that had been done, I am sure that the people of Ontario and the older provinces would have endorsed such a proposition. As to the argument that this road will open up the northern parts of Ontario and Quebec for settlement, and will develop the timber resources of that country,
I am inclined to think that the people of Ontario would prefer to have that timber left for the next generation instead of running railways through it. AVhy should we set out to settle this country when we have to-day millions of acres of land in the North-west that we have not yet colonized, although the government are spending vast amounts of money in the attempt to colonize it. AVliy should we be asked to open up this new territory when we are compelled to bring in at $5 a head Doukliobors and people of that kind, and even to settle that western country, which should be settled with good British subjects.
Then look at the indefiniteness of the route. AVliat would be said if any township council should propose to open a new road, a blind road for instance without having proper surveys made. It seems to me that
the government do not care where they run this railway so long as they are able to spend $100,000,000 or $125,000,000 of the people's money. The Minister of Finance came before this House and said it would cost $80,000,000 to build this eastern section. But he said that we should not have to pay more than $13,000,000. Suppose the minister had gone to his wife.
Is that the Minister of Agriculture ?

No, the Minister of Finance ; if it had been the Minister of Agriculture I could forgive him. Fancy the Minister of Finance of this great Dominion of ours going to his wife and saying :	' Margaret '-or whatever her name
is-' I have $300 and I am going to buv a farm for $10,000.'	' AVell,' she says, 'Minister, you cannot do that, you have only got $300.' * ' But I will borrow the $10,000.'
AA^ell, he buys the farm and pays the $300 of interest. After he has spent his $300 he lias to pay the $10,000 for the farm, as he has only paid the interest on that money. So far as I can see, the Minister of Finance was informing the people of this country of the amount of money they would lose, not the amount they would put into this railway. From what has been said by western members it would appear that there is nothing in the argument advanced that this road will be able to carry lumber from Quebec to the North-west Territories, for it has been stated positively that lumber can be brought from British Columbia and sold in the North-west Territories for less than it would cost to haul that lumber west from Quebec. In the past the government when railway matters were under discussion, have always put forward the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) to speak for them as being the one man on whom they depended. Now, because he has left the government owing to his refusal to obey the party whip, he is abused by them and he has been abused by the hon. member for AVestmoreland whom I believe is a creature of the hon. exminister. That gentleman (Mr. Emmerson) went to tlie committee room and opposed this Bill for six or eight hours but now. as soon as the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals resigned his place he changed his front and is strongly supporting the Bill. Surely he was either not in earnest at the time that he opposed this Bill for six hours in the committee or else he is not in earnest now. I believe that his real opinion was expressed in the committee room when there was no prospect of a vacancy in the cabinet. A change came over the spirit of his dream. As soon as the Minister of Railways and Canals resigned his portfolio the hon. member (Mr. Emmerson) hied him home aud came back here robed in white, honestly expecting that he was going to get the reward of an honest man

who had thrown up the portfolio of Railways and Canals.	[DOT]
All that I can gather as to the route of the proposed line is that there is a starting point and a quitting point. There will be a transcontinental line, if not now, some time in the future, but this country should own the line, other-wise what benefit will it be to the people of the North-west in keeping down rates ? If the line is in the hands of a private company, that company can arrange with others to keep up rates. The hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Fraser) told us in the Railway Committee that the Intercolonial was most useful to the maritime provinces, because it'gave them cheap rates. But that meant that the people of the Dominion had to pay the deficit on running that road, in order to give this benefit to the people of the maritime provinces. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Fraser-) opposed that road in the Railway Committee unless the government were to own it.
I made no such statement.
The hon. gentleman stated in the Committee that he was opposed to giving bonuses to railroads, but w-ould not object to a road if the company built it on its own capital.

I could hardly have said that, seeing that I am seeking a public grant for a railroad in my own county. I do not object to railroad bonuses if the country gets good value for them. In the Committee, on the Grand Trunk Pacific charter, the attempt was made to discuss what was to be given to the company by the government, and I joined with others in saying that that was not the time for that discussion.
Did the hon. gentleman, or did he not, oppose the road to Moncton ?

Certainly not. I was one of the maritime province members who insisted on that. This is my final answer to the hon. gentleman. If he thinks to draw me into a discussion to help him in taking up the time of the House, he will fail.
I think my recollection is as good as the hon. gentleman's (Mr. Fraser's), and I say that, in the first place, he opposed the road going to Moncton.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The statement of an hon. gentleman upon such a matter must be accepted.

I have stated my recollection, and if it is not the same as that of the hon. gentleman and yourself, Mr. Chairman, I cannot help it. I was pleased to hear the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton), when he told us, in May last, that we were to have a board of railway commissioners. Hon. gentlemen opposite are very fond of running things by Mr. JOHNSTON (Cardwell).
commission. They told us, ljefore they came into office, that they knew how to run the country, but the first thing they did was to appoint a commission to advise them as to what they should do. It cost .several thousand dollars, but it was a good thing, for on the strength of that commission's report some part of the national policy has been retained. The hon. member for North Norfolk has told us that for eighteen years he believed in the national policy, though supporting the party that opposed it. And he told us that before that he and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) had done all they could to induce the Prime Minister of that time, Hon. Alexander Mackenzie, to adopt the national policy before Sir John Macdonald did.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Johnston, Cardwell) is making a most absurd statement.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE (Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright).

speechtext:
This matter has often been referred to in the presence of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Charlton), and he has never denied it, and I believe it is a true statement. And I have heard him say in conversation-not in the House- that the party in power had used him ridiculously mean, though he had worked for* them against his own judgment for years and years.
At one o'clock, House took recess.
House resumed at three o'clock.

At one o'clock we took a well deserved rest, because I noticed last night that up to the hour .of three o'clock, while the ministers of the Crown appeared to be asleep in their seats, there appeared to be no one in the House in the interest of the present government, with the exception of the Chairman, who was wide awake enough to pay any attention to the proceedings. I thought that the railway scheme before the House must have been considered a very frivolous thing on the government side, when none of the ministers or their supporters were wide enough awake to listen to the debate. When you left the Chair, Sir, I w-as drawing attention to the amount of confidence that we have learned to place in the hon. member for North Norfolk. It is within the memory of this House, I think it was about tw-o sessions ago, that there was a dinner in the rooms below this chamber, on which occasion the Prime Minister lauded the Minister of Trade and Commerce for having suppressed his views in favour of free trade in the interest of harmony in the present government. Now- I ask myself what must have been the feeling of the hon. member for North Norfolk when he saw that the Minister of Trade and Commerce was rewarded with a portfolio in the cabinet for having suppressed his views in free trade,

and I thought that the member for North Norfolk himself was probably also moved with a hope of obtaining a portfolio when he argued against his own convictions and claimed that this railway would be superior to the water-ways of this country for the transportation of the grain products of the west to the Atlantic ports. Let me also refer to the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan). He likened himself to Sir Charles Topper. The member for Cumberland said that he had put a motion on the Order Paper declaring that all goods coming in under the British preference should land at Canadian ports. He could do that, hut he did not dare to make a motion to that effect in this House where he would be obliged to vote for it. Nevertheless he likened himself to Sir Charles Topper, the great man in the successful launching of the Canadian Pacific Railway. The only way in which he resembles Sir Charles Tupper is in size, but insofar as the qualities of statesmanship are concerned, the resemblance ceases altogether. He gave his reasons for not bringing the subject of his motion on the Order Paper to a vote in the House, saying, I think, that he got a letter, or that some one had whispered to him that he had better not bring this matter to a vote for fear the Americans might take away the bonding privileges now enjoyed by this country.
An impression has been sought to be made by lion, gentlemen opposite that the opposition was trying to hold up this government, that they were killing time. Now we know for a dead fact that the House was in session for three or four weeks when the government had nothing ready to bring down but the estimates. We found out afterwards that the reason they had nothing to bring down before the House was that they were quarrelling among themselves over this railroad. It may not have been such a quarrel as the ex-Minister of Public Works referred to when he said ' they were fighting like blazes.' Still, there must have been a good deal of fighting going on in the cabinet, when the ex-Minister of Railways, who, we are told, is not fit to unloose the shoes of the Prime Minister, felt it his duty to withdraw from the cabinet. I think there must have been other members of the government who were pretty deeply engaged in the quarrels.
Now, Sir, I am opposed to this scheme for a great many reasons, some of which I have already given on a previous occasion, and I will now give another one. I am opposed to committing the country to this enormous expenditure for building this road when the government do not know anything about -where it is going to pass, they know nothing about the route except where it is to start and where it is to stop. Perhaps they have a vague idea of the country through which it will pass, and that is all. I notice that members on the government
side admit that the Grand Trunk Pacific will not be in running order for four, five .six or eight years, but that the western portion may be in running order very soon. We know that there is a certain portion of the Canadian Pacific Railway that does not pay even now, and has not paid. Now if that is the case with a portion of the Canadian Pacific Railway through an uninhabited region of a comparatively small extent, how can we expect this Grand Trunk Pacific will ever pay over nearly the whole extent of the route between Quebec and Winnipeg ? I would like to know how many more immigrant agents the government will need to bring in the people to open up the new country on the line of this proposed road.
1 was perfectly willing that the Grand Trunk Pacific should get a charter to build a railway from the west to some point on the Georgian Bay or Lake Superior, but I am not willing and I do not think the country would he willing to sanction the proposal which is now before the House. My opinion is that if the question were put before the province of Ontario at least whether that road Should be built there would be ten to one voting against it. I would not balk at a large expenditure to improve the water-ways of this country. They belong to us, they are a natural heritage and if the improvement of our system of water-ways were completed we would not require anything but boats to carry the produce from the west. The hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) undertook to paint the banners of the two parties. He said that when we go to the country for re-election, let it be this year or next year hon. gentlemen opposite would go with the banner, ' Laurier, prosperity and victory,' and we would go with the banner, ' Borden, blue ruin and Gainey.' I am surprised that the hon. gentleman should attempt to charge the Liberal-Conservative party with raising the cry of blue ruin w'hen everybody knows that it was the party in power that raised that cry. I think that the least the government can do is to give the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Itt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) a leather medal hallooing blue ruin. This party is not open to the charge of having made use of that cry. I remember that these lion, gentlemen hallooed all over the country for commercial union. I am pleased to know it seems now we are all loyal Canadians. From this side of the House we have never said anything which was not in accordance with the spirit of true loyalty to Canada and the old flag. I remember a time, when in the township that I live in and where there used to be 300 of a Reform majority, we were laughed at if we talked about the old flag. Now nobody laughs at any man who proclaims his loyalty to the old flag. The majority was reduced in the last election to nineteen, but wre hope to make it twenty-

five in our favour in the next election and we may make it one hundred against this railway scheme. Since the hon. member for Cumberland who Is an older member of this House than I am has ivailed himself of the privilege of painting a banner for his party and for ours, I think it is not out of place for me to attempt 1o paint a banner for the (two parties as well. I would say that the two parties, when they go to the country, let it be this fail, or next year, or whenever we do go, will have these words inscribed upon their banners : ' The Liberal-Conservative party-E. L. Borden, Canada for the Canadians, protect the industries needing protection, grant no bounties, no bonuses-and victory,' and the Liberal party

'Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, Cob-den medal, Stratton and defeat.' I venture to say that when we go to the country on the issue now before the House my banner will be found to have been painted right and his will have been found to have been painted wrong. Hon. gentlemen opposite for years kept telling the country what they were going to do for the farriers when they got into power. They got into power and what have they done ?
Nothing.

Yes, they have destroyed our hinder twine industry. They let the American binder twine in to displace the Canadian hinder twine. They have taken the duty off and granted a bounty of about $7 a ton on last year's production- of binder twine. The fanners have a great deal of that to pay but there is one part they have not to pay, and while everybody pays according to his consumption of products he is also obliged to pay a share of the binder twine bounty that is given in -this country although he may not require to use that article. Then, hon. gentlemen said that we were bled white by the national policy.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I am afraid the hon. member is getting on the national policy instead of the Grand Trunk Pacific.
Mr. JOHNSTON (Cardwell. This is a national railway. Hon. gentlemen opposite told us that they were going to give us an American market for our barley, but instead of doing that they gave the Americans free access to our market with their corn and thus destroyed the growing of barley in Ontario at least to the extent of the number of bushels of Indian corn that is brought in for feeding purposes. I have been looking over the schedule of the redistribution or gerrymander Bill and I find that

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman must not take up the gerrymander Bill so soon. We will be into that next week and an opportunity will -then be afforded.

I was just saying what the government was professing to do for the farmers In the building of this railway and then I was going on to illustrate it by showing the representation that the farmers will have in this House if this Redistribution Bill is passed. Now I notice that there are seven farmers in this House who cannot possibly he here after another election on account of farmers' constituencies being abolished and handed over to professional men of one kind or another. That is another thing which hon. gentlemen have done for the farmers notwithstanding the fact that the greater part of the taxes required for the building of this Grand Trunk Pacific and the greater part of the moneys contributed by the government towards the building of other railways have been paid by the farmers. This line is placed away back out of reach of the farmers of the old settled provinces and, as the government say, it is going -to open up new territory and thus will give the new men a better chance than the settlers have now in Ontario, Quebec and the maritime provinces.

Mr. Chairman, I do not know that I have much chance of getting any information on this subject. The questions that have been put to the ministers have been systematically ignored and no information has been -given to us, notwithstanding that the Prime Minister said that we have mountains of information. As the Minister of Justice is in the House, and as I have noticed his unvarying courtesy in setting members of the opposition right in their misconstruction of points of law in which he was interested, I shall direct iny remarks to him. I wish to refer particularly to section 17 of the contract. I think it will be found that the explanation given to the hon. junior member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) does not touch everything in connection with this section, which says :
No addition shall be made to the cost of construction or to -the capital of construction account in respect of customs duties in cases where there -is direct importation of material or supplies by the government.
In connection with section 17, we must read section 8 of the Act and section 5 of the contract. Section 5 of the contract- and after all it is the contract that should govern in this case as far as the estimate of the cost of construction is concerned, because that is the one that lias been signed by the government-says :
Th-e said eastern division shall be constructed by, and at the expense of, -the government, upon such location and according to such plans and specifications as it shall determine, having due regard to directness, -easy gradients and favourable curves.
And now it will be noticed that the wording of the section is almost but not identi-

cal with tlie wording of section 5. Section 8, tile clause of the Act affecting this matter, differs in one little point from section 5 of tlie contract. Section 8 says :
The eastern division of the said Transcontinental Railway extending from the city of Moncton to the city of Winnipeg, shall be constructed by or for the government in the manner hereinafter provided and subject to the terms and provisions of the said agreement of the 29th July, 1903.
Now, the section of the Act says ' by or for tlie government ' ; the agreement says it must he constructed ' by the government.' I am not contending for a moment that that would not permit the government to make contracts for that work, divide that whole mileage into certain sections and give out contracts for them, but I am contending that having it stated that it is to he constructed for the government makes tlie contractors intermediate agents whom tlie Grand Trunk will not need to recognize in any way. If the contractors do it for the government they are merely agents for the government for their part of the work, and as a consequence any importation made by the contractor of material or supplies, as has been well pointed out by tlie lion, junior member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier), will be an importation by the government. I do not believe the government would contend in a court of law that any duty paid by a contractor or an importation made by him could possibly be added to tlie cost of construction. I would like to ask tlie Minister of Justice whether, under these circumstances, in view of the wording of paragraph 5 as distinguished) from section 8 of the contract, it does not follow as a matter of course that even if duties were paid by contractors on any materials or supplies imported the duties so paid will have to be deducted from the cost of construction.

The question that has been asked is a perfectly legitimate one and I may say as a question that necessarily very seriously engaged the attention of those responsible for the drafting of this contract. The object was that materials imported by the government would be treated in exactly the same way as materials now imported by the government in connection with the Intercolonial.
You do not say for the purposes of the road.

That is the view we had. Of course lawyers may differ, but I submitted this matter to the Deputy Minister of Justice who, under the Order in Council and the statutes regulating the Department of Justice, is the legal adviser to the department. And his opinion was that this exemption would apply only to materials imported directly by the government to be used by the government, and not to materials imported by the contractors. But if there be any doubt, It can be set at rest at any time by any amendment which will make the meaning more clear.
That being the case, I presume, when we come to the clause, tlie Minister of Justice will strike it out.
I cannot strike out a clause which is intended to protect the government.

I am glad to hear this clear expression of opinion from the Minister of Justice. I would suggest that in view of the difference between paragraph five of the contract and section eight of the Bill, an amendment is required. In section fi ve the words used are ' shall be constructed by and at the expense of the government. Section eight says, * shall be constructed by or for the government.' This may sound like hair splitting, but great troubles have arisen before now out of the omission of a few words. We will have to take up the agreement in connection with section two of the Bill.
The better plan would, be to take up the agreement clause by clause in connection with this section. If we had done that in the beginning, we would have made more progress.
I was just about to suggest that.
I made the suggestion, but it was not accepted.
When ?
On the first day we were in committee. I said that the best way would be to consider the agreement clause by clause.
That suggestion was not contradicted by the First Minister.
It was not accepted.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: There is a consensus of opinion in favour of discussing the various clauses of the agreement before passing this section. It might be well at present to adopt that method.

The contract may be perfectly clear, but it does not seem clear to me. The Minister of Justice has a faculty of expressing himself in such fashion that those who hear him at least imagine that they do not misunderstand him. I do not think there is a man in the House more capable of putting the meaning he attaches to a clause in such shape that it cannot be misunderstood. I am glad to know that the intention of the contract is clear, that only the importation made direct by the government itself, not through an agent ahd hot through a contractor

Not only those things imported by the government

direct, but those used by the government iu connection with the road. If the government made an importation and handed it over to a contractor that importation would not escape the payment of customs duty.
In view of what the hon. minister has said, I do not think he will consider me hypercritical if
I do not complain.

I do not think he will consider me hypercritical if I suggest that this clause does not convey that meaning to me. And, even at the cost of some repetition, I wish to say that it is most misleading to have the wording of the Act and the wording of the contract different. I think it would be well, before the contract is ratified that it should be made clear. As I say, I do not doubt the ability of the Minister of Justice so to draw a contract that its meaning will be quite clear. I understand the hon. gentleman to say that direct importation applies only to material actually used by the government. Of course, the government could enter into a contract with a contractor to supply a certain article.
It does not need to do so.

No. In this way they could supply materials needed in the original building of the road. But I understand the minister to say that that clause applies only to such material as might be brought in for tlie betterment of the road. 1 submit that one would need inside information in order to interpret the clause in that way. But we ought to keep within the four corners of the contract

we cannot refer to the statute or to anything else. I think it would be a very simple matter for the hon. minister without a suggestion from this side to make that thoroughly clear. There can be no harm done, if the Grand Trunk Pacific so understand it now. It seems to me that more progress would have been made had the government seen fit to let this second clause stand until the different clauses in the contract were discussed. But as that course has not been taken, we are compelled, in considering this second clause, to discuss the entire contract. There are several objections to the contract. There are objections which go to the root and others which merely apply to details. We on this side object to any contract being made by the government for the construction of so important a work without first consulting the electorate. The proper course for the government would be to delay the passage of this measure until the people are consulted. If the people then choose to give a mandate to the government to make a contract, nothing would be left for us except to determine whether the government have made the best contract possible in order to carry out the will of the people as expressed at the polls. It has been said that the opposition are committed to an alternative scheme in the same sense that the government are committed to this scheme. We deny that. The opposition are in a different position. We are unable to crystallize into law the beneficent measures which we would be prepared to urge forward if we were in

office. When we go before the people with an alternative scheme, our scheme is one which has not become binding by Act of parliament but simply one to which we ash the approval of the electorate; but should the measure before the House_ pass through parliament, the government will appeal to the country on a scheme to which they have irrevocably committed the people. When one looks at the circumstances under which this contract was made, one cannot help being convinced that the principle of responsible government has been utterly ignored by this administration. While admitting "the great abilities of the right lion, the leader of the government, he has not that experience in railway matters which would lead people to entrust him with the task of negotiating a contract with one of the most astute railway managers on this continent. One would naturally expect that iu such a transaction, the right boil, gentleman would have consulted that particular colleague of his who, from his experience as head of the Railway Department, might be considered an expert in railway matters. When we find the hon. gentle-mu n thus neglecting to take the most ordinary precautions, are we to blame if we are strongly inclined to believe that the probabilities are against the interest of the people being safeguarded by this contract ? With whom was the contract made ? We find that it was made with a number of gentlemen who are described as representing the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway-a company not yet incorporated. When the Bill to incorporate that company was before the Railway Committee, we were dealing with certain individuals.
I think the Minister of Justice will not contradict me when I say that, while we all recognize the difference between individuals and corporations, and that the moment the Grand Trunk Pacific Company is incorporated, the position of the individual corporators is merged in the company, yet, until the company is incorporated, the gentlemen who ask for the charter are the only oues we can deal with. We find that, this branch of the legislature incorporated certain gentlemen and tlieir associates as the Grand Trunk Pacific Company. Yet, when the Bill had passed to the Senate, we find that an agreement has been made by the government with some other gentlemen who profess to be the Grand Trunk Pacific Company. I think it is not out of place for the government to explain the extraordinary circumstance that this bargain as made with gentlemen who, so far as we know, have no power to bind the

company they profess to bind. We find, among the names of those given as corporators in the Bill to incorporate that Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, names that are well known in Ontario ; Hon. George A. Cox, H. M. Pellatt, and E. R. Wood, all of Toronto ; Hon. William Gibson, of Beamsville ; J. R. Booth, of Ottawa ; the Honourable H. B. Rainville, Charles M. Hays, Frank W. Morse and William Wainwright, all of Montreal, and John Bell, of Belleville. X 'think every hou. member will bear me out iu saying that vast wealth is represented by the gentlemen whose names appear in this charter ; and I have always understood in the Railway Committee that it is considered desirable that men who are strong financially should be incorporators of a company, as giving a guarantee of the strength of the concern. When we look at the contract, almost the first line suggests questions which should be answered. We find that this is an agreement bearing date the 29th day of July. Now, so voluminous a contract as this must have been the result of long negotiations between the government and the company. As we recollect the discussion in the Railway Committee over the incorporation of the company, we see that the circumstances ns we supposed them were entirely different from those which existed. I think we are justified in saying that the government hardly treated the members of the Railway Committee who are of their own party, as well as those who sit on this side of the House, with perfect fairness, when we were allowed to discuss week after week, what we considered a private charter, when the manager of the company and the leader

of the government were, at night, making the effective arrangements which we were only as a matter of courtesy, allowed to discuss by day. These are the points fairly to be considered in connection with so extraordinary a contract submitted to the House at so extraordinary a time. When a measure so important as this is brought before us after we have been in session four and a half months, during what, under ordinary circumstances would be the dying hours of a long session, surely, as representatives of the people, and as called upon to perform the important function of legislation for this country, we have a right to complain. These things all call upon us to regard the contract with the utmost care and to scrutinize it, I was almost going to say with suspicion, but I will not use so strong a term, in order that, if so extraordinary a contract must be made, at least in the interest of the country, it shall be made with the best terms possible.	4
When we look at the second clause of the contract providing the route of this proposed line of railway, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, as it is called, we find that that route is wholly uncertain. Probably no other railway company in this country was ever given a charter with such a choice of routes as is given to this favoured company. It is called a transcontinental line, and that is the title of the Bill, ' An Act respecting the construction of a national transcontinental railway.' Yet, even in so small a matter as the name the Bill is deceptive, for this is not a transcontinental railway. A ' transcontinental ' railway, as ordinarily understood, is one running from ocean to ocean. Yet Moncton, which is one terminus of this line is not one of the seaports which our maritime province friends are prone to boast of. The line is no more a transcontinental line than if it ran from Quebec to Winnipeg. So we are put upon suspicion at once as to the bargain and the terms of the bargain. No member of the Railway Committee can have failed to learn why Moncton was chosen rather than some seaport. If the government had the courage of their convictions and were acting in a patriotic apart from a political sense, it would decide which Atlantic port should be the terminus of this transcontinental railway, we should have a proposal to run from ocean to ocean and could 'discuss fairly and intelligently the line projected. The line which stops at Moncton, as it is understood, will have an extension to some port on the Atlantic. We can understand, perhaps, that Halifax would support a Bill that would end the line at Moncton with the understanding that the true terminus would be at Halifax, while they would oppose it if the true terminus were St. John. So the converse is true, that St. John would not oppose the passage of such a Bill if they thought for a moment that the terminus would be in St. John instead of Halifax.

So I repeat that if hon. gentlemen opposite wish to bring a measure before the people which they can submit on national grounds, apart from party grounds, they would be justified in making it a truly transcontinental line, and in naming the seaport be it Halifax, or St. John, or any other, which they propose to make the terminus of the eastern end of the line.
Then, when we come to the portion of the line running through New Brunswick, Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba, the North-west Territories and British Columbia, we find an absolute uncertainty as to where it is to be located. Those of us who are members of the Railway Committee remember that the question of whether there should be a distance of 30 miles or 40 miles between, railways in the North-west, was threshed out in that committee this year. The government at one time was supposed to have the idea that 40* miles should be the minimum distance between the railways; later on, 30 miles was considered the proper distance. But here we have an Act incorporating the most important of all our railways, in which no limit whatever is stated. Therefore, the members of this House are called on to vote for a transcontinental line that, so far as we know, may not be two miles distant from the Canadian Pacific Railway or the Canadian Northern. Now, if we are to have a system of intelligent representation, if members of this House have any responsibilities or any power, surely it is unjust, as well to supporters of hon. gentlemen opposite as to hon. gentlemen on this side of the House, to ask them to vote blindly in support of a line which, I venture to say, there is not a single man behind the government would vote for if it were located where it could be located under the terms of this Bill. When we come to the North-west Territories, probably even more than the other parts of the country, hon. gentlemen should see the necessity of having the route, at all events, approximately located. I can understand that hon. gentlemen opposite will say that it is absurd, in advance of the surveys, to insist on knowing within a few miles where the line is to be located. I agree that it would be absurd and unfair if we were to assume that the railway is to be located without surveys. At the same time, we have a right to ask for an approximate intimation of the locality where the road will be placed. We ought to be told, within 100 miles of it, we ought to have some general idea as to the part of the country this railroad is to traverse. The matter will come up later on on another clause, but how can we vote intelligently to give this grant to assist the railway, when we do not know where it is to be located ? If you located that road within a few miles of the Canadian Northern or the Canadian Pacific Railway, there is no hon. gentleman who would be willing to give the assistance that is

promised by tbis Bill. At the same time, if the road is to be located in parts of the country that require to be developed, then all the members of the House might be willing to give a degree of assistance that, under other circumstances, they would be justified in refusing to give.
Now, if It were thoroughly understood that for ail time to come we never would require another transcontinental line, then perhaps this question would not be so important. But I am sure we all recognize that this is a growing country, we recognize the possibility that other lines may be required, and that it may not be long before other lines are required. That being the case, I think we should know now where this line is to be located, because it is conceivable that if the principle were laid down that the three transcontinental lines now under way, including this one, were to be all that ever could* be built, then a( certain fixed route might be justifiable for this one. If lion, members had more confidence in this country, and thought that in a short time four or five transcontinental lines might be required, then a route that might be a proper route for it, if there were to be but three, might be very objectionable if there were to be four or five. That consideration is another reason why we should know where this road is to be located.

The government in drawing the contract 'have made a certain provision in clause 7, and I confess from reading it that I am unable to determine what the object of the government was in doing so. In clause 7 the government have provided that:
In order to insure, for the protection of the company as lessees of the eastern division of the said railway, the economical construction thereof in such a manner that it can be operated to the best advantage, it is hereby agreed that the specifications for the construction of the eastern division shall be submitted to, and approved of, by the company before the commencement of the work.
It goes on to provide that the work is to be done in accordance with the specifications. When we come to construct the western division there is a similar proviso that the specifications are to be approved by the government's engineer before the construction is proceeded with. On the face of it the clause seems very reasonable, very fair and very effective, but whether or not it will be effective, of course, must depend on what object the government had in placing it in the contract. If the intention of the government was to secure a cheap and honest construction of the road, if the intention was to secure to the company that on the eastern part on which they are to pay a rental there shall be cheap and' honest construction, I have no hesitation in saying that the clause absolutely fails of the intent that the government had in view. If the government wishes to control the expenditure on the western division on the ground that the government has guaranteed three-quarters of the expense and is therefore interested in keeping down the expenditure as much as possible, practically no assistance whatever would be given to the government by allowing their engineer to supervise the specifications. It is to be assumed that the government on their end of the road will attempt to build a good road witli as low grades and as good curves ns possible and the same assumption is to be made for the company in building their end of the line. Therefore, as far as the specifications are concerned, their supervision will he of no practical benefit to the government on the one hand or to the company on the other. I would suggest that if we wish to control the construction of these different sections of the road in the interests of the company and of the government, respectively, it is the tenders and the contracts to which we should give our attention, as they are the means by which the
expenditure is made. It is not necessary to charge that money will he spent dishonestly, but inasmuch as the government by their very provision made the assumption, that it is in the public interest that the expenditure should be supervised, and inasmuch as they have assumed that the company has the right to supervise any expenditure, on the other hand, surely I am justified in asking tlie government to make that an effective instead of a nominal clause, so that not merely the specifications but the plans, tenders and contracts shall be confirmed and ratified by either party to this bargain. I think in view of some of the loose clauses to which I will refer later, that it is particularly necessary that there should be such a provision as this. I am sure that hon. gentlemen opposite who are prepared to vote for this Bill will do so with a lighter heart and defend their course more successfully before their constituents if they show that they have done everything in their power to secure as economical and effective a construction of the road as possible. The construction of the said eastern division shall be commenced so soon as the government has made the surveys and plans and determined upon the location thereof, and shall be completed with all reasonable despatch.

This naturally strikes us as a clause calling for scrutiny. We find in the Bill, section- 21, that:
The Governor in Council shall have the power at any time to suspend the progress of the work upon the said eastern division until the then next session of parliament.

That, perhaps, should have taught us a lesson. We found in that case, that, where there was no legal liability, because no lawyer in this House would contend that there was a shadow of liability on the part of this country to Mackenzie & Mann for the work they had done on the Yukon Railway, because, it was said, they had gone on relying on the signature of a minister, this country should pay them damages, and the country did pay them damages to the extent of $300,000. With that precedent in view- and I am not contending that this company would have a legal claim or that it could bring an action for damages and compel the country to pay-is it not quite clear that there will be a much stronger claim equitably and morally for damages on the part of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company than in that case ? If the government are not certain that they can find a route, if they say they are not certain by providing in their Bill that if they cannot go ahead they can suspend the work, they should make it clear, and inasmuch as they do not know anything about the country or about the route, and inasmuch as the Grand Trunk Railway Company do not know anything about them, if the government found itself unable to complete the work the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company should understand that they could not hold the country liable for damages. If a claim were presented by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company for damages for the nonconstruction of the line from Winnipeg to

Moncton, we, on this side of the House, might go into the box and contend that the damages to which they were entitled would be absolutely nothing, inasmuch as we had very little respect for the prospects of the road which it is proposed to construct between Winnipeg and Moncton, but if such a claim were presented, surely the utterances of lion, gentlemen opposite would rise up against them, because we find from the right hon. leader of the government down to the humblest member of the party that they have been vieing with one another in extolling the marvellous beauties of its unrivalled scenery and the great wealth of its resources. The company shall lay out, construct and equip the said western division of the said railway to a standard not inferior to the main line of the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada between Montreal and Toronto, so far as may be practicable in the case of a newly constructed line of railway, hut this section shall not be held to oblige the company to construct a double track railway.

struct that road the law of the land was that articles imported by or for the use of the government, or any department thereof, come in free under section 450 of the tariff. The question has been raised as to bow far rail traffic is overtaking rail and lake traffic as regards cheapness. Between Chicago and New York there are from six to ten railways, running through a well settled country, a country that is, in so far as I know, comparatively a level country compared with the country between Winnipeg and Quebec. These railways between Chicago and New York, so far as I know, have all the advantages of low gradients and every other facility that will enable a railway to carry grain cheaply. Let us see how they are progressing and overtaking tlie water and rail routes in securing the traffic. I will go back for tbirty-tliree years to the year 1870. In that year it cost 25-20 cents per bushel to carry grain by lake and rail from Chicago to New York, while it cost 35-57 cents per bushel to carry it by all-rail. That is, all-rail transportation cost forty per cent more than lake-and-rail. In 1877 we find not very much change-lake-Mr. HENDERSON.	.
and-rail, 15-46 cents per bushel, all-rail 20-50 per bushel, or thirty-three per cent in excess of all-rail over lake-and-rail. Here seems to be a slight improvement. But now they are shouting about building a road from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Why ? Because the population has increased so fast since they have been in office. Well, the expense of finding out the population is what is increased, and that is about all. The minister of the Crown who had the census in hand had such hard work finding the population that it cost him $1,250,000 to discover it, as compared with .$500,000, which the previous census [cost. Since they have got into office they tell us that the people have ceased to leave the country. Well, Sir, right from a town not two hours' distant front here, 300 people have gone away since these hon. gentlemen came into power. Turn up the records of exports of settlers' effects, and what do they show ? They show that people are leaving by the hundred. The hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce used to make a good deal of capital out of the exodus. He harped so continually on the exodus that you would think lie was an Israelite, or Moses himself, frying to bring tlie people out of bondage. It will lie well for him if he does not turn out to he instead an Ishmaelite, with his hand against everybody. Not long ago his bail'd, and the hand of every one of his followers, was raised against the interests of tlie country, yet now they are boasting n limit our prosperity. Fortunately for tliem. there is no opposition to-day decrying the country and giving American immigration agents the best arguments they could have " Mr. BRODER.
for inducing the immigrants of Europe to choose the agricultural lands of tlie western states in preference to the Canadian Northwest. We on this side are not furnishing these agents with speeches such as hon. gentlemen opposite used to deliver when in opposition. Because our population is increasing is one of the reasons given for building this railway from ocean to ocean, but they are proposing to build It where there are no people. A man who will get on this railway in Winnipeg will not strike civilization until he reaches Quebec, 1,450 miles away. AVbat will lie do if he wants to see his clergyman, or get a pair of boots, or a barrel of flour, or And out what (lie Postmaster General is doing with the letters ? It is about time that they sent that pamphlet out to the country, and the danger is it will have Oeesar's image and superscription upon it, with the motto ' Render unto Cresar the things that are Caesar's.' While these hon. gentleman are boasting about a road from ocean to ocean, they are failing to .settle the serious question which has been demanding settlement for several years. I refer to the question of a cheaper rate of export on the products of the farm. Every cent you put upon the transportation of this country is a tax upon the people. These gentlemen are not going to relieve the people of one iota of that difficulty by the proposition before the House. Does the Minister of Justice pretend that this proposed railway will carry grain any cheaper than it is carried to-day? I do not wonder that the government would not let this Bill see daylight until they could not help themselves. It is evident that the Minister of Justice did not draft it, for when it did come down he could not conceal his disappointment. It was not drawn up by the Minister of Justice, but by the men who got what they wanted out of the bargain. The Granl Trunk Railway got what they wanted and left the rest for Canada. They got the tenderloin and the sirloin steak and we got a steak off the neck. And we will get it in the neck too, and no one knows that better than the hon. Minister of Justice. He cannot temper his justice with mercy in this case. Now they are going to write a pamphlet to give a character to that country. They should give such a letter as I gave to a gentleman who came to me and wanted a recommendation, i said :	' To whom it may concern ; here
is a man I never knew to do a hit of work he could get out of. If you can make use of such a man you are welcome to him. and he has my blessing.' that are being written somewhere about these buildings. The man is a good writer, and the pamphlet he will write will justify this scheme to the people of this country.
L need not tell the Minister of Justice his name, he knows all about it, and, Sir, that is the data upon which they intend to go to the country. A pamphlet giving this road a character, but which does not say where the road is going to go. They may talk about the height of land, they may talk about spruce and poplar and jack pine. No man in this country ever gave this territory as bad a character as the men who are trying to boom it up, and I advise the First Minister and the Minister of Finance [DOT]when they want to give a soil a character, not to say that it is covered with spruce and white birch and jack pine, because there is not a hard-headed man in this country who has any common sense and who known anything about the soil, who would not be convinced that there is no soil worth cultivating beneath such timber as that. It is a difficult matter for one great party to enhance and further the interest of the country while there is another great party sitting on the bent hindering the raisers, the one trying to build up the country and the other trying to pull it down. A pretty miserable man, a pretty poor sort of a man can pull down anything, but it takes a better man to build it up, and there is no stronger proof of the necessity of growth on the part of hon. gentlemen opposite, than that their whole object for nearly a quarter of a century has been to pull down what other men have built up. All they can do is to grease the cart, and they have greased it well, particularly when their old friends were driving it, the same old wheels, the same old axles, even the same old lynch pins-the ship of state with the same flag over the masthead, 'Canada for the Canadians' and they dare not say anything else. They may talk about having fixed policies, but look at their position on the trade question. If a speech is to be made in a locality where the people are in favour of free trade, they put up a minister to talk free trade-they have got him. Where there is a strong protective feeling, they put up a minister who talks protection-they have got him too. In an indifferent district, where the people do not know what they want, they put up a minister-and again they have got one or two-who does not know what he wants. They have men who cannot declare what they want.
That is what I call an omnibus government. You know what an omnibus is-it leaves the. hotel with all sorts of people and parcels. You can find anything you like in this omnibus government-free-traders, protectionists, revenue-tariff men, annexationists, no doubt people who are waiting, trying to find out what they are. and men who tell us that having a surplus means adding to our debt. They say they have a surplus greater than has been, taking the words used by the Postmaster General on his postage stamps. ' We hold an empire greater than has been.'

and, as I said once before, the Postmaster General could put a whole empire on a postage stamp, but he could not do anything to build up the country. try, and what will you do when you meet one of these ? There must be a detour. The government do not know whether it will be two hundred miles longer or shorter than they say. future, the flouring mills will be brought east instead of remaining in the west. Why?
